title: Wiki-supported collaborative learning in primary education: How a dialogic space is created for thinking together
authors: Manoli Pifarre & Judith Kleine Staarman
summary_haiku: This study examined how wikis support primary students' collaborative knowledge construction through a dialogic lens. Twenty-five students engaged in a science project using MediaWiki, combining asynchronous wiki interaction with synchronous face-to-face collaboration. Analysis revealed students developed exploratory, cumulative, and disputational talk patterns, establishing intersubjective understanding. The collaborative wiki text demonstrated greater complexity, length, and reasoning than initial individual proposals, supporting the claim that dialogic approaches enhance wiki-based collaborative learning.

title: A framework for conceptualizing, representing, and analyzing distributed interaction
authors: Daniel D. Suthers & Nathan Dwyer & Richard Medina & Ravi Vatrapu
summary_haiku: # Summary Suthers and colleagues present an uptake analysis framework for analyzing distributed technology-mediated interaction. The framework uses contingency graphs—abstract transcripts representing events as vertices and relationships between events as edges—to unify interaction data across multiple media and temporal scales. Uptake, defined as participants taking prior events as relevant for ongoing activity, serves as the conceptual foundation. The authors demonstrate the framework's utility through qualitative and quantitative analyses of synchronous and asynchronous collaborative learning data, arguing it enables both microanalysis and scaled statistical analysis while supporting dialogue across diverse CSCL methodologies.

title: Encouraging collaboration and building Community in Online Asynchronous Professional Development: designing for social capital
authors: Susan A. Yoon & Katherine Miller & Thomas Richman & Daniel Wendel & Ilana Schoenfeld & Emma Anderson & Jooeun Shim
summary_haiku: This study examined how online asynchronous professional development designed around social capital mechanisms supports science teachers' learning. Eight high school biology teachers participated in a six-week course combining discussion prompts, expert videos, and peer facilitation. Satisfaction surveys showed high ratings across all dimensions. Transactivity analysis revealed that collaborative prompts significantly increased peer interaction compared to content or implementation prompts. Interview data indicated positive perceptions of expertise access and interaction depth, though trust-building remained challenging in the asynchronous format.

title: Dialogues across time and space in a video‑based collaborative learning environment
authors: Charlotte Beal & Rolf Steier
summary_haiku: # Summary This design-based research study examines how pre-service teachers' dialogues emerged across time and space as they collaboratively constructed video-based mind maps using a Padlet platform. Through interaction analysis of 28 hours of video recordings, the researchers found that video-based mind maps supported multiple space-time constellations—synchronous small-group conversations, asynchronous group-to-group exchanges, and whole-class dialogues—enabling meaning-making across learning levels. The study demonstrates how shared video dialogues functioned as mediational artifacts connecting individual contributions into networked conversations that supported collaborative learning and exam preparation.

title: Enhancing students’ dialogic reflection through classroom discourse visualisation
authors: Pengjin Wang & Fan Chen & Deliang Wang & Gaowei Chen
summary_haiku: Visualisation-supported dialogic reflection (VSDR) using classroom discourse analysis enhanced primary students' collaborative learning. A 3-month intervention with 53 students showed significant knowledge gains in the high-dose group and increased student participation across both groups. Qualitative analysis revealed students engaged in deeper reflection on problem-solving strategies, group collaboration, and whole-class participation when reviewing visualised classroom discourse through discussion forums.

title: “I guess my question is”: What is the co-occurrence of uncertainty and learning in computer-mediated discourse?
authors: Michelle E. Jordan & An-Chih Janne Cheng & Diane Schallert & Kwangok Song & SoonAh Lee & Yangjoo Park
summary_haiku: This study examined how uncertainty expressions and learning co-occur in graduate students' computer-mediated discussions. Using inductive coding of 1,048 comments across synchronous and asynchronous online discussions, researchers found that 72% of paragraphs containing uncertainty also exhibited learning markers. Direct uncertainty expressions correlated with presenting new ideas and applications, while indirect expressions associated more with elaboration. Results suggest uncertainty expression facilitates productive learning through collaborative meaning-making in online environments.

title: Supporting classroom orchestration with real-time feedback: A role for teacher dashboards and real-time agents
authors: Mike Tissenbaum & Jim Slotta
summary_haiku: This design-based research study investigates how real-time software agents and teacher dashboards support orchestration of complex collaborative physics inquiry in high school classrooms. Using the Knowledge Community and Inquiry model, researchers developed SAIL Smart Space technology with four agent types to dynamically manage student grouping, material allocation, and teacher notifications. Results demonstrate that the tablet-based orchestration system successfully reduced teacher workload while enabling timely interventions that significantly improved student problem-solving outcomes.

title: A more reflective form of joint problem solving
authors: Richard Alterman & Kendall Harsch
summary_haiku: This study examines asynchronous online collaboration among university students completing wiki and blog-based writing assignments. Through qualitative analysis of over 7,000 lines of chat transcripts, the research identifies how participants create "venues"—virtual spaces anchoring joint problem-solving across different times and places. The findings reveal a shift toward more reflective, piecemeal collaboration compared to face-to-face interaction, with participants strategically selecting problems for joint attention while leveraging secondary participation through reading and reflection.

title: Students assessing their own collaborative knowledge building
authors: Eddy Y.C. Lee & Carol K.K. Chan & Jan van Aalst
summary_haiku: This study examined how knowledge-building portfolios and principles scaffold collaborative inquiry in computer forums. Using a quasi-experimental design with 119 ninth-grade students across three Knowledge Forum conditions, researchers found that students guided by knowledge-building principles demonstrated deeper inquiry, more high-level questions, and superior conceptual understanding compared to peers using forums alone or with portfolios only. Portfolio scores predicted domain understanding beyond individual participation measures, suggesting portfolios effectively characterize and foster collective knowledge advances.

title: Studying participation networks in collaboration using mixed methods
authors: Alejandra Martinez & Yannis Dimitriadis & Eduardo Gomez-Sanchez & Bartolome Rubia-Avi & Ivan Jorrin-Abellan & Jose A. Marcos
summary_haiku: This study validates a mixed-evaluation method combining social network analysis with qualitative and quantitative approaches to assess participatory learning in CSCL contexts. Applied across three diverse scenarios—blended learning, distance learning, and synchronous collaboration—the method demonstrates flexibility and appropriateness for measuring interaction structures. Results confirm that integrating multiple data sources and analysis techniques provides efficient, reliable evaluation while remaining accessible to practitioners, though resource demands remain substantial.

title: The joint organization of interaction within a multimodal CSCL medium
authors: Alan Zemel & Gerry Stahl
summary_haiku: This ethnomethodological case study examines how three students organize collaborative mathematical problem-solving in a synchronous dual-interaction online environment combining text chat and shared whiteboard. Through sequential interaction analysis, the authors reveal that students co-construct shared mathematical understanding by coordinating visual, narrative, and symbolic representations across media. The indexical field formed by referential links between chat messages and whiteboard drawings establishes common ground, enabling group cognition and deep mathematical learning through multiple realizations of mathematical objects.

title: PolyCAFe—automatic support for the polyphonic analysis of CSCL chats
authors: Stefan Trausan-Matu & Mihai Dascalu
summary_haiku: PolyCAFe applies the polyphonic framework—grounded in Bakhtin's dialogism and musical metaphor—to automatically analyze collaborative learning chats. Using Natural Language Processing and Social Network Analysis, the system identifies implicit links between utterances, detects voices and their inter-animations, and generates quantitative metrics for collaboration assessment. Evaluation experiments demonstrate that PolyCAFe significantly reduces tutor feedback preparation time while providing useful insights to learners about their participation.

title: Disengaged students and dialogic learning: the role of CSCL affordances
authors: Benzi Slakmon & Baruch B. Schwarz
summary_haiku: This study examines how three disengaged eighth-grade students gradually adopted dialogic norms through participation in computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) discussions using the Argunaut tool. Through temporal analysis of philosophical discussions, the research demonstrates that peer-mediated exposure to dialogic practices—rather than direct teacher intervention—enabled students to develop multivoicedness and expand their discursive repertoires. CSCL affordances, including delayed responses and reduced prosodic cues, facilitated this transformation.

title: Attending to others’ posts in asynchronous discussions: Learners’ online “listening” and its relationship to speaking
authors: Alyssa Friend Wise & Simone Nicole Hausknecht & Yuting Zhao
summary_haiku: Students' depth of listening—specifically rereading peers' posts—positively predicts responsiveness and argumentation quality in online discussions, while breadth alone does not. Using clickstream data from 31 undergraduates across six asynchronous discussions, multi-level regressions revealed that revisiting others' posts predicted more responsive comments, and reading (versus scanning) posts predicted richer argumentation. These listening-speaking relationships manifested differently across learner types over time.

title: Life history of a topic in an online discussion: a complex systems theory perspective on how one message attracts class members to create meaning collaboratively
authors: Jane S. Vogler & Diane L. Schallert & Michelle E. Jordan & Kwangok Song & Anke J. Z. Sanders & Yueh-hui Yan Te Chiang & Ji-Eun Lee & Jeongbin Hannah Park & Li-Tang Yu
summary_haiku: This qualitative study applied complex adaptive systems theory to analyze how meaning emerges in synchronous online classroom discussions. Researchers tracked one pivotal message (#43) and its resulting topic through multiple data sources including transcripts, screen recordings, and video observations of eight graduate students. Findings revealed that interdependent processes and content co-create understanding, private individual meaning-making mingles with public shared experiences, and topics follow developmental trajectories from inception through decline, demonstrating how collaborative learning emerges through system-level interactions.

title: Exploring college English language learners’ self and social regulation of learning during wiki-supported collaborative reading activities
authors: You Su & Yanyan Li & Hening Hu & Carolyn P. Rose
summary_haiku: This study examined self and social regulation of learning among 60 Chinese college English language learners during wiki-supported collaborative reading activities. Using content analysis and sequential analysis of chat logs, researchers found that high-performing groups demonstrated significantly more content monitoring, evaluation, and emotional regulation than low-performing groups. Sequential analysis revealed high-performing groups exhibited bidirectional patterns between co-regulation and socially shared regulation, while low-performing groups repeated self-regulation patterns.

title: A handheld classroom dashboard: Teachers’ perspectives on the use of real-time collaborative learning analytics
authors: Roberto Martinez-Maldonado
summary_haiku: This longitudinal study examined four teachers' perspectives on using a real-time analytics dashboard during 72 classroom sessions over ten weeks in a multi-tabletop collaborative learning environment. The handheld dashboard displayed group participation, task progress, script enactment, and automatically detected misconceptions. Through semi-structured interviews, teachers reported that visualizations enhanced awareness and decision-making, though they identified tensions regarding data incompleteness, immediate versus delayed feedback, orchestration load, and device portability, highlighting critical design considerations for effective CSCL classroom analytics tools.

title: Promoting regulation of equal participation in online collaboration by combining a group awareness tool and adaptive prompts. But does it even matter?
authors: Sebastian Strauss & Nikol Rummel
doi: Promoting regulation of equal participation in online collaboration by combining a group awareness tool and adaptive prompts. But does it even matter?
summary_haiku: This field experiment examined whether combining a group awareness tool (GAT) with adaptive prompts supports equal participation in online collaborative learning. Sixty-one students in groups received either no support, a GAT alone, or GAT plus prompts. While students showed higher satisfaction with more equal participation, the collaboration support produced only tentative effects on participation equality. Groups initiating collaboration early and coordinating continuously achieved better participation distribution and satisfaction, suggesting interaction patterns matter more than the technological interventions tested.

title: Deconstructing orchestration load: comparing teacher support through mirroring and guiding
authors: Ishari Amarasinghe & Davinia Hernandez-Leo & H. Ulrich Hoppe
summary_haiku: This study compared how mirroring and guiding support in teacher dashboards influence orchestration load during scripted collaborative learning. Six teachers conducted Pyramid-pattern activities under three conditions: no dashboard, mirroring support, and guiding support with alerts. Using epistemic network analysis, researchers found that guiding support enabled more targeted interactions and announcements compared to mirroring support. The findings deconstruct orchestration load into situation evaluation, goal formation, and action-taking facets.

title: Implementing learning analytics in wiki-supported collaborative learning in secondary education: A framework- motivated empirical study
authors: Xiao Hu & Jeremy T. D. Ng & Samuel K. W. Chu
summary_haiku: This study proposes a learning analytics framework for assessing wiki-supported collaborative learning quality across contribution, participation, transactivity, and social dynamics. Using mixed methods with 440 secondary students and six teachers, regression analyses and interviews revealed that students' and teachers' use of Wikiglass, an LA-enabled group awareness tool, significantly predicted collaboration quality metrics at individual and group levels, particularly when viewing other groups' analytics.

title: Studying teacher withitness in the wild: comparing a mirroring and an alerting & guiding dashboard for collaborative learning
authors: Reet Kasepalu & Pankaj Chejara & Luis P. Prieto & Tobias Ley
summary_haiku: This quasi-experiment examined how dashboards affect teacher withitness—situational awareness and interventions—during collaborative learning. Twenty-four teachers used three conditions: no dashboard, mirroring-only dashboard, and AI-assisted alerting & guiding dashboard. Results show mirroring dashboards increased situational awareness, while alerting & guiding dashboards significantly reduced teacher workload, particularly frustration and perceived failure. However, intervention rates didn't increase as hypothesized, suggesting teachers need extended training to effectively implement AI-suggested coregulation strategies in authentic classroom settings.

title: Scripting by assigning roles: Does it improve knowledge construction in asynchronous discussion groups?
authors: Tammy Schellens & Hilde Van Keer & Bram De Wever & Martin Valcke
summary_haiku: This design-based research compared two cohorts of university students (N=223 and N=286) across consecutive academic years to examine whether assigning rotating roles in asynchronous discussion groups enhances knowledge construction. Using multilevel analysis of coded discussion transcripts and exam scores, results showed that role assignment significantly improved students' knowledge construction levels and final exam performance, with an effect size of 0.5 standard deviations. However, differential effects emerged by role type, with summarizers benefiting most.

title: Distinguishing knowledge-sharing, knowledge- construction, and knowledge-creation discourses
authors: Jan van Aalst
summary_haiku: This study distinguishes three discourse modes—knowledge sharing, knowledge construction, and knowledge creation—using a coding scheme applied to secondary students' asynchronous online discussions in Knowledge Forum about SARS and Avian Flu. Analysis of four student groups' discourses revealed one group engaged in knowledge-creation discourse with superior knowledge advancement, one in knowledge-sharing discourse, and two in hybrid modes. Community sense emerged as the primary differentiating factor.

title: Wikis to support the “collaborative” part of collaborative learning
authors: Johann Ari Larusson & Richard Alterman
summary_haiku: Wikis provide an effective platform for supporting asynchronous, non-collocated collaborative learning when enhanced with awareness, navigation, and communication components. Two case studies demonstrate that prefabricated wiki structures function as coordinating representations, enabling both tightly coupled team design projects and loosely coupled co-blogging activities to maintain adequate intersubjective spaces for productive student collaboration.

title: Online moderation of synchronous e-argumentation
authors: Christa S. C. Asterhan
summary_haiku: This exploratory study examines effective online moderation of synchronous small-group argumentation in co-located classrooms. Through student questionnaires and protocol analyses of moderated discussions using Digalo software, researchers found that generic scaffolding prompts—effective in face-to-face settings—were ineffective in synchronous e-discussions. Instead, content-specific, involved moderation styles that disguised scaffolding as peer participation proved more effective and appreciated by students.

title: Scaffolding collaborative technical writing with procedural facilitation and synchronous discussion
authors: Shiou-Wen Yeh & Jia-Jiunn Lo & Jeng-Jia Huang
summary_haiku: Researchers developed Process-Writing Wizard, a computer-supported system combining procedural scaffolding and synchronous chat to facilitate collaborative technical writing among EFL students. An experimental study with 48 students compared the system against standard chat. Results showed experimental group students demonstrated significantly higher perceived usefulness, positive attitudes, and stronger intention to reuse the system. Their articles exhibited superior content and organization quality, and synchronous discussions focused more on article-related interactions rather than social exchanges.

title: Toward a classification of discourse patterns in asynchronous online discussions
authors: Jan van Aalst & Carol K. K. Chan & Ella L. F. Fu
summary_haiku: This study developed a classification of nine discourse patterns in asynchronous online discussions using qualitative coding and narrative analysis of Knowledge Forum databases across three classes. The patterns distinguished three modes of discourse—knowledge sharing, knowledge construction, and knowledge building—revealing how students engage in collaborative interactions. Knowledge-sharing discourse predominated, while knowledge-building discourse was rare, suggesting that supporting productive discourse requires explicit pedagogical guidance aligned with learning principles.

title: Real-time orchestrational technologies in
authors: Camillia Matuk & Michael Tissenbaum
summary_haiku: Real-time dashboards in computer-supported collaborative learning environments enable teachers to monitor student progress and provide timely, targeted guidance during complex collaborative activities. This special issue examines five empirical studies investigating how real-time data visualization supports classroom orchestration, finding that effective designs partner with teachers rather than replace their functions, balance automated support with teacher autonomy, and require participatory design involving educators throughout development.

title: Correction to: A handheld classroom dashboard: teachers’ perspectives on the use of real-time collaborative learning analytics
authors: Roberto Martinez-Maldonado
summary_haiku: This correction notice addresses duplicate images in the original article examining teachers' perspectives on a handheld classroom dashboard for real-time collaborative learning analytics. The correction republishes the correct versions of Figures 4 and 6, which display visualizations of group task progress, individual participation, and real-time feedback on learning design enactment.

title: Dialogic intervisualizing in multimodal inquiry
authors: Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver & Lap Ki Chan & Judith L. Green & Susan M. Bridges & Asmalina Saleh
summary_haiku: Medical students collaboratively constructed understanding of cardiovascular physiology through facilitated problem-based learning using multimodal digital texts. Using Interactional Ethnography to analyze one PBL cycle, researchers traced how students iteratively accessed, curated, and generated visual representations—from simple diagrams to complex cardiac cycle charts—within dialogic exchanges with their facilitator. The study proposes "dialogic intervisualizing" as a theoretical construct characterizing dynamic interplay between information problem-solving, textual negotiation, and purposeful dialogue for deep knowledge co-construction in computer-supported inquiry.

title: Affording embodied cognition through touchscreen and above-the-surface gestures during collaborative tabletop science learning
authors: Nikita Soni
summary_haiku: This study examined how family groups use touchscreen and above-the-surface gestures during collaborative learning with multi-touch tabletops displaying ocean temperature data. Using a user-centered design approach, researchers analyzed 11 family groups' utterances and gestures to identify embodied cognition instances. Four gesture types emerged: orienting the group, cooperative gestures, individual intentional gestures, and articulating conceptual understanding. Findings reveal specific gestural interactions that facilitate embodied-cognition-supported collaborative meaning-making in science learning.

title: Improving learning and writing outcomes: Influence of cognitive and behavioral group awareness tools in wikis
authors: Lisa Ollesch & Sven Heimbuch & Daniel Bodemer
summary_haiku: This study examined how cognitive and behavioral group awareness tools affect wiki-based collaborative learning through a 2×2 factorial experiment with 158 participants. Results show both tool types influence thread selection and discussion engagement, with behavioral awareness particularly motivating contributions. Critically, only the combination of cognitive and behavioral awareness improved article quality, suggesting complementary effects outweigh individual benefits in supporting wiki-based learning outcomes.

title: Exploring the impact of chat‑based collaborative activities and SRL‑focused interventions on students’ self‑regulation profiles, participation in collaborative activities, retention, and learning in MOOCs
authors: Georgios Psathas & Stergios Tegos & Stavros N. Demetriadis & Thrasyvoulos Tsiatsos
summary_haiku: This study examined how self-regulated learning (SRL) interventions combined with chat-based collaborative activities affect MOOC students' outcomes. Using a programming MOOC with 1,807 participants, researchers compared control, general intervention, and personalized intervention groups. Results showed personalized interventions significantly improved SRL profiles and course retention (87.5% vs. 62.5%), while both intervention types increased collaborative participation and learning outcomes compared to controls, demonstrating that targeted SRL support enhances engagement and completion in MOOCs.

title: Combining Danmaku and Discussion Boards: Toward A Scalable and Sociable Environment for Mass Collaboration in MOOCs
authors: Bo Yang
summary_haiku: This study examines how danmaku and discussion boards accommodate mass participation in MOOCs through mixed-method analysis of 2,435 danmaku messages and 739 discussion board posts. Findings reveal danmaku fosters collective indirect interaction emphasizing socio-emotional dimensions, while discussion boards organize learners into threaded small groups supporting direct cognitive discussions. The complementary tools enable scalable, sociable collaborative learning environments addressing both emotional and knowledge-sharing needs.

title: Accomplishing collaboration at scale: How professionals jointly frame problems on Stack Overflow
authors: Alena Seredko
summary_haiku: # Summary This study investigates how software developers collaboratively frame programming problems on Stack Overflow through asynchronous, fluid participation. Using trace ethnography and sequential analysis of selected threads, the research reveals that minimal reproducible examples (MREs) structured within the platform's dual-space design enable collaboration at scale. Standardized norm-enforcing requests and explicit referencing practices ensure mutual intelligibility among unknown contributors, facilitating effective problem-solving in large-scale online environments.

title: Students assessing their own collaborative knowledge building
authors: Eddy Y.C. Lee & Carol K.K. Chan & Jan van Aalst
summary_haiku: This study examined how electronic portfolio assessments guided by knowledge-building principles support collaborative inquiry in computer forums. Using a quasi-experimental design with 119 ninth-grade students across three Knowledge Forum conditions, researchers found that students receiving portfolios with knowledge-building principles demonstrated deeper inquiry, more high-level questions, and superior conceptual understanding compared to peers using forums alone or portfolios without principles. Portfolio scores predicted essay performance beyond individual participation metrics, suggesting portfolios effectively capture distributed, progressive knowledge advancement.

title: R-U-Typing-2-Me? Evolving a chat tool to increase understanding in learning activities
authors: Hugo Fuks & Mariano Pimentel
summary_haiku: This research investigates "Chat Confusion"—difficulties following conversations when multiple participants communicate simultaneously in chat tools used for educational debates. Through iterative design-based development, researchers identified six key problems: co-text loss, dynamics interruption, message overload, lack-of-visibility-of-turn-in-progress, reading difficulties, and decontextualization. Successive Mediated Chat versions implemented targeted solutions including message threading, structured conversation techniques, publication queues, interface improvements, and session history. Case studies demonstrated that combining structured dynamics with interface enhancements effectively reduced confusion and improved understanding in online learning activities.

title: The affordance of anchored discussion for the collaborative processing of academic texts
authors: J. van der Pol & W. Admiraal & P.R.J. Simons
summary_haiku: Anchored discussion systems, which integrate texts directly into online forums with message anchoring capabilities, promote more text-focused and constructive collaboration than traditional forum discussion. Comparing these systems with standard discussion boards in a pedagogy course, the study found anchored discussion produced more meaning-oriented discourse, more efficient communication, and fewer social digressions, making it more suitable for collaborative academic text comprehension among undergraduate students.

title: Barriers to online critical discourse
authors: Liam Rourke
summary_haiku: This qualitative case study examined barriers to critical discourse in online forums within a 15-week graduate humanities course. Through observation and interviews with five distance students, researchers identified three key obstacles: students held competing orientations toward the conference (some seeking critique, others socioemotional support), perceived critiques as personal attacks, and viewed critical discourse as burdensome for participation marks. Structured learning activities with defined roles and assessment methods reflecting engagement effort could mitigate these barriers.

title: Contextual perspective in analysing collaborative knowledge construction of two small groups in web-based discussion
authors: Maarit Arvaja
summary_haiku: This study presents a methodology for analyzing collaborative knowledge construction in asynchronous web-based discussions by examining two student groups' thematic structure, communicative functions, and contextual resources. Comparing novice and experienced teacher-education students, findings reveal that different backgrounds influenced how groups created and interpreted context, negotiated meanings, and selected resources—novices relied on course material and peer discussion, while experienced students drew primarily on personal teaching experience.

title: Argumentation in a changing world
authors: Baruch B. Schwarz
summary_haiku: # Summary This design-based research study examined a seven-month history course using the Kishurim program, which promotes critical reasoning through dialogic argumentation supported by the Digalo graphic tool. While traditional measures of argumentative components showed no significant improvement, students demonstrated significant gains in openness, coherence, and decisiveness. Analysis of e-discussions revealed that these criteria better reflect the program's dialogic pedagogical principles than conventional skill-based metrics, suggesting new evaluation standards for collaborative learning environments.

title: Rainbow: A framework for analysing computer-mediated pedagogical debates
authors: Michael Baker & Jerry Andriessen & Kristine Lund & Marie van Amelsvoort & Matthieu Quignard
summary_haiku: Rainbow is a seven-category analytical framework for analyzing computer-mediated pedagogical debates in CSCL environments. Developed through pragma-dialectical theory and dialogue analysis, it identifies when students broaden and deepen understanding of debate spaces through argumentative interaction. The framework synthesizes existing approaches into coherent functional categories, validated across multiple collaborative learning tasks and communication media with strong inter-coder reliability.

title: Supporting controversial CSCL discussions with augmented group awareness tools
authors: Juergen Buder & Daniel Bodemer
summary_haiku: Augmented group awareness tools that aggregate and visualize learner ratings of discussion contributions can strengthen minority influence in collaborative learning. An experimental study with groups discussing controversial physics topics found that groups using rating-based awareness tools made significantly better decisions and showed higher individual learning than unsupported groups, particularly by shifting majority members toward scientifically correct minority viewpoints through enhanced informational influence.

title: Context-oriented communication and the design of computer-supported discursive learning
authors: Thomas Herrmann & Andrea Kienle
summary_haiku: This theory-driven design experiment develops a context-oriented communication model to guide computer-supported discursive learning (CSDL) system design. Through iterative testing of the KOLUMBUS prototype across five classroom settings, researchers identified that integrating communicative annotations directly with segmented learning material as context significantly enhances mutual understanding in asynchronous discussions. The study extends traditional dyadic communication models by introducing the facilitator as a crucial third party, providing practical design guidelines emphasizing context integration, metadata support, and facilitation features.

title: The right tool for the wrong task? Match and mismatch between first and second stimulus in double stimulation
authors: Andreas Lund
summary_haiku: This study examines how Norwegian high school students learning English as a foreign language approach open-ended collaborative tasks using wiki technology. Using Vygotsky's double stimulation framework, researchers analyzed the relationship between task design (first stimulus) and available tools (second stimulus) in collaborative knowledge construction. Findings reveal that learners struggled to maintain awareness across individual, group, and whole-class levels. When the wiki application failed, students sustained collective working practices through alternative tools like PowerPoint and MSN chat, demonstrating that pedagogical and technological designs must be better aligned to support collaborative knowledge production.

title: The pedagogical challenges to collaborative technologies
authors: Diana Laurillard
summary_haiku: # Summary Collaborative technologies rarely address formal learning needs despite their educational potential. This paper proposes the Conversational Framework—a pedagogical model integrating instructionism, constructionism, socio-cultural, and collaborative learning theories—to establish user requirements for technology design. The framework emphasizes iterative interactions between teachers, learners, and peers across discursive and experiential levels, enabling educators to challenge technologies to deliver genuinely enhanced learning rather than merely digitizing conventional methods.

title: The logic of wikis: The possibilities of the Web 2.0 classroom
authors: Michael Glassman & Min Ju Kang
summary_haiku: Web 2.0 tools like wikis and blogs can enable Dewey's vision of democratic education by supporting abductive reasoning—the logic of hypothesis generation essential for creative problem-solving. Unlike traditional deductive approaches emphasizing certainty, abduction requires simultaneously maintaining multiple competing premises, a capability previously impossible in classrooms but now feasible through hypertext-based technologies that create scale-free networks of interconnected information nodes.

title: Participation and common knowledge in a case study of student blogging
authors: Richard Alterman & Johann Ari Larusson
summary_haiku: This case study examines how student blogging facilitates common knowledge emergence in a loosely coordinated learning environment. Through qualitative and quantitative analysis of 25 undergraduates' semester-long blogging activity in an Internet & Society course, researchers found that common knowledge develops through distributed participation across multiple conversations and topics. Longer conversations served as focal points attracting wider readership and participation, while persistent content enabled students to mine the blogosphere when preparing papers, with approximately 50% of paper topics foreshadowed by blogging activity.

title: Dialogical positions as a method of understanding identity trajectories in a collaborative blended university course
authors: M. Beatrice Ligorio & Fedela Feldia Loperfido & Nadia Sansone
summary_haiku: # Summary This study proposes a three-step qualitative-quantitative method for tracking identity trajectories in collaborative learning using Bakhtinian concepts of polyphony and chronotopes as dialogical indicators. Applied to online notes from two university students in a blended course, the method reveals unique, context-sensitive identity development patterns, demonstrating how students' positioning shifts across course modules in response to activities and personal circumstances.

title: Real-time mutual gaze perception enhances collaborative learning and collaboration quality
authors: Bertrand Schneider & Roy Pea
summary_haiku: Real-time gaze visualization during remote collaborative learning on neuroscience contrasting cases enhanced learning gains and collaboration quality compared to control conditions. Eye-tracking enabled dyads to achieve higher joint attention, with followers benefiting most. Joint attention emerged as the primary mediator of improved learning outcomes.

title: Social argumentation in online synchronous communication
authors: Esra Alagoz
summary_haiku: This study examined argumentative practices among adolescents in World of Warcraft synchronous guild chat using ethnographic methods. Analysis of 27 argumentative exchanges revealed that 81% employed counter-critiques—stronger arguments directly refuting opponents' claims—rather than weaker counter-alternatives. Quality argumentation peaked during discussions about avatar customization (race/class, gear, talent builds), suggesting that interest-driven, authentic contexts where players exercise control over personalization trigger sophisticated argumentative discourse skills.

title: The dialectical potential of Cultural Historical Activity Theory for researching sustainable CSCL practices
authors: Sue Timmis
summary_haiku: Cultural Historical Activity Theory (CHAT) offers a relational, dialectical framework for understanding sustainable computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) in authentic educational settings. This study proposes an integrated CHAT methodology that moves beyond descriptive triangle models to analyze contradictions and tensions across multiple activity levels. Through a five-stage analytical process applied to undergraduate online collaboration, the research demonstrates how CHAT's dialectical method reveals complex interrelations between discourse, actions, and community, explaining why collaborative practices succeed or fail to become institutionalized.

title: “Newbies” and “Celebrities”: Detecting social roles in an online network of teachers via participation patterns
authors: H. Smith Risser & SueAnn Bottoms
summary_haiku: This study used cluster analysis combining structural and behavioral data to identify social roles in an unstructured online teacher blog network. Analyzing 99 teachers' participation patterns across six months, researchers detected five distinct roles: "Newbies," "Inbound Participants," "Full Participants," "Celebrities," and "Peripheral Members." Results revealed that participation patterns and network position significantly influence both current role and trajectory of role change, with expertise and engagement type affecting status transitions independent of tenure.

title: Fixed group and opportunistic collaboration in a CSCL environment
authors: Tuya Siqin & Jan van Aalst & Samuel Kai Wah Chu
summary_haiku: This study examined 27 Chinese undergraduates' synchronous online discourse across two phases: fixed group collaboration (8 weeks) and opportunistic collaboration (8 weeks) using Knowledge Forum. Multi-faceted analysis revealed that while all groups showed similar interaction patterns, productive groups generated higher-level questions and ideas. Opportunistic collaboration enabled broader interactions and more constructive discourse but exhibited scattered interactions and reduced metacognition. Active participation and high-level idea contributions correlated positively with domain knowledge gains.

title: ReaderBench: Automated evaluation of collaboration based on cohesion and dialogism
authors: Mihai Dascalu & Stefan Trausan-Matu & Danielle S. McNamara & Philippe Dessus
summary_haiku: ReaderBench proposes two computational models for automated collaboration assessment in CSCL conversations. The dialogical voice inter-animation model evaluates collaboration through overlapping semantic chains representing different participants' viewpoints, while the social knowledge-building model analyzes longitudinal cohesion patterns. Validation against human annotations of ten chat conversations demonstrates both models reliably identify collaboration zones and predict overall collaboration quality, supporting cohesion and voice inter-animation as collaboration signatures.

title: Cultural ways of constructing knowledge: the role of identities in online group discussions
authors: Murat Oztok
summary_haiku: This study explores how students utilize multiple identification categories—such as gender, profession, ethnicity, and group affinity—during online group discussions to construct knowledge collaboratively. Through case analysis of asynchronous threaded discussions in a graduate education course, the research demonstrates that individuals flexibly enact different identities at various knowledge-construction phases, using personal experiences to negotiate meaning and advance collective understanding. The findings reveal that identification plays a central role in mediating between personal cognition and social learning processes.

title: Joint interactions in large online knowledge communities: The A3C framework
authors: Ulrike Cress & Heisawn Jeong & Johannes Moskaliuk & Joachim Kimmerle
summary_haiku: This conceptual article proposes the A3C framework distinguishing four types of joint interactions in large online knowledge communities: Attendance, Coordination, Cooperation, and Collaboration. These interaction types vary by how members share goals, processes, and outcomes, progressing from individualistic orientations to fully shared endeavors. The framework integrates cognitive and socio-cultural perspectives to explain diverse participation patterns in mass-scale communities like Wikipedia and Scratch.

title: Students’ engagement with real-time graphs in CSCL settings: scrutinizing the role of teacher support
authors: Line Ingulfsen & Anniken Furberg & Torunn Aanesland Stromme
summary_haiku: This study examined student-teacher interactions during collaborative real-time lab work on ocean acidification. Using interaction analysis of 49 student-teacher exchanges, researchers identified challenges students faced interpreting graphs and connecting experimental actions to scientific phenomena. The teacher provided crucial support through eliciting strategies—using gestures, prompts, and cued questions—and elaboration strategies, demonstrating how teacher guidance intersects with digital resources and instructional design to scaffold conceptual understanding in CSCL settings.

title: What information should CSCL teacher dashboards provide to help teachers interpret CSCL situations?
authors: Anouschka van Leeuwen & Nikol Rummel & Tamara van Gog
summary_haiku: Teachers struggle to interpret collaborative learning situations from dashboards. This experimental study (n=53) compared three dashboard types—mirroring, alerting, and advising—examining how different support levels affect teachers' detection and interpretation of student collaboration problems in fraction tasks. Results showed dashboard type did not influence detection speed or accuracy, but advising dashboards significantly improved interpretation depth, with teachers adopting more analytical stances toward situations.

title: Cohesion in online environments
authors: Maria Altebarmakian & Richard Alterman
summary_haiku: Online group cohesion emerges from students' engagement choices in asynchronous collaboration. This case study analyzed 29 students completing design assignments through a custom platform, measuring cohesion via behavioral engagement, interactivity, and cognitive engagement. Results show students prioritized thoughtful commenting over interactive dialogue, achieving moderate cohesion sufficient for reflective meaning-making but limited direct negotiation of ideas.

title: Initiating scientific collaborations across career levels and disciplines – a network analysis on behavioral data
authors: Julia Eberle & Karsten Stegmann & Alain Barrat & Frank Fischer & Kristine Lund
summary_haiku: This study examined how researchers initiate scientific collaborations at face-to-face academic events using network analysis of behavioral data. Analyzing 5,736 relations among 287 researchers at two technology-enhanced learning conferences, the researchers employed RFID devices to measure contact duration and social network questionnaires to identify collaboration intentions. Results revealed that longer face-to-face contact, reciprocity, and transitivity significantly predicted new collaboration formation. PhD students were less frequently selected as partners, and Information Technology researchers selected fewer partners overall. Group awareness support reduced disciplinary differences in partner selection, suggesting targeted interventions can facilitate interdisciplinary collaboration.

title: Collaborative analytics-supported reflective Assessment for Scaffolding Pre-service Teachers’ collaborative Inquiry and Knowledge Building
authors: Yuqin Yang & Gaoxia Zhu & Daner Sun & Carol K. K. Chan
summary_haiku: This study examined how collaborative analytics-supported reflective assessment enhances pre-service teachers' competencies in collaborative inquiry and knowledge building. Using a quasi-experimental design with 40 experimental and 28 comparison pre-service teachers over 18 weeks, the experimental group engaged in knowledge building enriched by KBDeX visualizations and rubrics, while the comparison group used portfolio assessment. Analysis of Knowledge Forum discourse revealed that the experimental group demonstrated significantly higher-level epistemic engagement, collaborative interactions, and metacognitive reflection. Epistemic network analysis showed stronger connections between higher-level actions in the experimental group, and cumulative degree centrality indicated greater community knowledge advancement. Results suggest collaborative analytics-supported reflective assessment effectively scaffolds pre-service teachers' development of collaborative inquiry competencies.

title: The temporal dynamics of online problem‑based learning: Why and when sequence matters
authors: Mohammed Saqr & Sonsoles Lopez-Pernas
summary_haiku: This study analyzed 8,009 qualitatively coded interactions from 204 medical students across four online problem-based learning courses using sequence and process mining. Findings revealed that interaction sequences and their temporal order predicted student achievement better than interaction frequency alone. High-cognitive interactions (argumentation, evaluation) triggered similar high-level responses, while low-cognitive interactions perpetuated low-level engagement. Initiating interactions, regardless of cognitive content, showed strongest association with performance, highlighting the importance of sequential dynamics over simple participation counts.

title: Taking a stance in the process of learning: Developing perspectival understandings through knowledge co‑construction during synchronous computer‑mediated classroom discussion
authors: Hannah Park & Diane L. Schallert & Kyle M. Williams & Rachel E. Gaines & Jeonghyun Lee & van de Sande
summary_haiku: This study examined how graduate students expressed perspectives through stancetaking during synchronous online classroom discussions. Using Du Bois' discourse framework, researchers analyzed 27 chat transcripts, coding for epistemic, affective, and evaluative stances alongside positioning, evaluation, and alignment acts. Findings revealed students predominantly adopted epistemic stances focused on knowledge acquisition, with shifts in discussion topics marking moments of perspectival understanding development. The analysis demonstrates how collaborative knowledge co-construction occurs through iterative combinations of subsidiary stance acts.

title: Capturing temporal pathways of collaborative roles: A multilayered analytical approach using community of inquiry
authors: Ramy Elmoazen & Mohammed Saqr & Laura Hirsto & Matti Tedre
summary_haiku: This longitudinal study analyzed 135 dental students' online problem-based learning discussions across four courses using Community of Inquiry framework coding combined with latent class analysis, epistemic network analysis, and process mining. Three distinct roles emerged: leaders, social mediators, and peripheral explorers. Students exhibited stable role trajectories across time, with active trajectories achieving higher grades than free riders, suggesting roles function as stable dispositions requiring intentional teacher intervention for change.

title: Understanding the role of I‑positions facilitating knowledge construction in a computer‑supported collaborative learning environment
authors: Aaron J. Peltoniemi & Joni Lamsa & Sami Lehesvuori
summary_haiku: This qualitative study applies discourse analysis and dialogical self theory to investigate how interpersonal and intrapersonal voices facilitate knowledge construction in computer-supported collaborative learning. Analyzing ten physics students in two groups, researchers identified discourse functions and I-positions (I–it, I–me, I–you, I–we) within dialogues. The successful group employed both interpersonal and intrapersonal voices, with intrapersonal voices peaking during empirical evaluation, while the unsuccessful group relied predominantly on interpersonal voices focused on individual-level concerns rather than collective elaboration.

title: The CoMPAS Framework for Modeling Individual Participation in Collaborative Learning Processes: a Systematic Review
authors: Shihui Feng & Ziyi Wei
summary_haiku: This systematic review of 66 studies (2005-2024) proposes the CoMPAS framework for modeling individual participation in collaborative learning using process data. The framework identifies six forms of participation—cognitive interactions, coordinative interactions, metacognitive interactions, passive participation, solo active participation, and socio-emotional interactions—analyzed through oral conversational, textual, log, and nonverbal physical data using descriptive, content, network, and clustering methods. Findings reveal bidirectional relationships between individual participation and group performance.

title: A dialogic understanding of the relationship between CSCL and teaching thinking skills
authors: Rupert Wegerif
summary_haiku: # Summary Wegerif argues that dialogue itself constitutes the primary thinking skill underlying creativity and learning-to-learn. Through literature review and case studies using Raven's reasoning tests, he demonstrates that teaching dialogue as an end in itself—rather than as a tool for knowledge construction—promotes general thinking skills. He proposes a dialogic interpretative framework for CSCL that emphasizes opening, deepening, and broadening reflective spaces through technology-supported dialogue.

title: Approaching institutional contexts: Systemic versus dialogic research in CSCL
authors: Hans Christian Arnseth
summary_haiku: # Summary This article distinguishes between systemic and dialogic research approaches in CSCL to address how institutional contexts shape tool meanings and functions. Systemic approaches identify variable correlations affecting collaboration and outcomes, while dialogic approaches examine how meanings emerge through social interaction. The authors argue that dialogic analysis of sequential activities reveals why CSCL applications often fail in ordinary classrooms, demonstrating that understanding institutional practice transformation requires attention to how participants actively constitute contexts through their actions.

title: Electronic [re]constitution of groups: Group dynamics from face-to-face to an online setting
authors: Lynn Clouder & Jayne Dalley & Julian Hargreaves & Sally Parkes & Julie Sellars & Jane Toms
summary_haiku: This three-year case study examined how group dynamics change when physiotherapy students transition from face-to-face to online collaboration during clinical placements. Using action research with six seminar groups, researchers analyzed discussion forums, focus groups, and evaluations. Findings reveal that group dynamics remain relatively stable across contexts once established face-to-face, though individual participation may shift online. Social presence proves essential for positive dynamics, yet groups must transcend sociability to develop cognitive presence and deeper learning. Effective facilitation significantly influences outcomes, particularly when managing emotionally charged discussions or low-engagement groups.

title: Putting the pieces together: Online argumentation vee diagrams enhance thinking during discussions
authors: E. Michael Nussbaum & Denise L. Winsor & Yvette M. Aqui
summary_haiku: Online argumentation vee diagrams (AVDs) significantly enhance students' ability to integrate opposing arguments in asynchronous discussions. Using a quasi-experimental design with 87 preservice teachers, students completing individual AVDs before discussions and collaborative group AVDs afterward demonstrated greater compromise-based reasoning and opinion change compared to controls. Scaffolding questions evaluating argument strength proved essential for effectiveness, suggesting structured support facilitates metacognitive reflection necessary for balanced argumentation.

title: A systemic and cognitive view on collaborative knowledge building with wikis
authors: Ulrike Cress & Joachim Kimmerle
summary_haiku: This article presents a theoretical framework integrating Luhmann's systems theory with Piaget's equilibration theory to explain collaborative knowledge building in wikis. The model distinguishes between social and cognitive systems, analyzing how externalization and internalization processes enable learning through assimilation and accommodation. Empirical Wikipedia examples demonstrate that medium-level incongruities between individual knowledge and wiki content motivate equilibration activities, driving both individual learning and collaborative knowledge building through co-evolution of systems.

title: A three-level analysis of collaborative learning in dual-interaction spaces
authors: Jacques Lonchamp
summary_haiku: This article presents a three-level qualitative interaction analysis methodology for dual-interaction spaces—CSCL systems combining shared artifact editing with synchronous communication. The approach analyzes collaborative learning traces at dialog, knowledge, and action levels to identify patterns and inform system customization. Applied to software engineering diagram construction, the method reveals how learners negotiate categorization rules through prototypical examples, enabling evidence-based improvements to learning environment design.

title: Distributed leadership in online groups
authors: Julia Gressick & Sharon J. Derry
summary_haiku: In an asynchronous online learning environment, pre-service teachers working in small groups demonstrated highly distributed leadership across all members, with different leadership forms showing varying distribution patterns. While successful group performance was not directly predicted by overall leadership distribution patterns, qualitative analysis revealed that effective groups developed internal organizational structures and positive interpersonal dynamics that facilitated both peer and instructor engagement, suggesting emergent distributed leadership offers a viable alternative to scripted collaborative roles.

title: Temporality matters: Advancing a method for analyzing problem-solving processes in a computer-supported collaborative environment
authors: Manu Kapur
summary_haiku: This study advances Lag-sequential Analysis (LsA) as a quantitative method for examining temporal patterns in computer-supported collaborative learning groups. Applied to synchronous online problem-solving discussions, LsA revealed significant sequential interaction patterns invisible to traditional "coding and counting" approaches. Critically, temporal transition patterns between process categories emerged as the strongest predictor of group performance, demonstrating that analyzing the order and sequence of collaborative interactions—not merely their frequency—is essential for understanding collaborative learning processes.

title: Exploring e-learners’ perceptions of net-based peer-reviewed English writing
authors: Zi-gang Ge
summary_haiku: This study examined asynchronous, blind peer review for improving Chinese adult e-learners' English writing. Thirty-six students divided into three ability groups participated in a year-long experiment with rotating cross-group peer reviews mediated by the instructor. Results showed all groups improved, with lower-ability students making greater progress than higher-ability students. However, high-ability students became discouraged when paired with lower-ability peers for extended periods, suggesting flexible grouping strategies may be necessary.

title: Perspective taking and synchronous argumentation for learning the day/night cycle
authors: Baruch B. Schwarz & Yaron Schur & Haim Pensso & Naama Tayer
summary_haiku: Combining perspective-taking through pictures and synchronous computer-supported argumentation promotes conceptual learning of the day/night cycle in Grade 8 students. Using the Digalo tool and design-research methodology with pre-post testing, the study found significant improvements in mental models, elaboration, and knowledge integration. However, teacher mediation during small-group discussions did not enhance learning outcomes, suggesting that meticulous task design and peer argumentation were primary drivers of conceptual change.

title: Student use of Facebook for organizing collaborative classroom activities
authors: Cliff Lampe & Donghee Yvette Wohn & Jessica Vitak & Nicole B. Ellison & Rick Wash
summary_haiku: Two survey studies examined how undergraduate students repurpose Facebook for classroom organizing. Study 1 (N=302) found that Facebook intensity and willingness to contact instructors predicted collaboration propensity. Study 2 (N=214) revealed two distinct collaboration types: positive (instructor-approved) and negative (unapproved), with different predictors including self-efficacy and relational communication strategies, suggesting how students use Facebook matters more than frequency.

title: Identity presence and knowledge building: Joint emergence in online learning environments?
authors: Fengfeng Ke & Alicia F. Chavez & Pei-Ni L. Causarano & Antonio Causarano
summary_haiku: This mixed-method study examined identity presence in seven online courses and its relationship to knowledge building. Using discourse analysis of 1,817 discussion posts, researchers found that posts expressing personal experiences, cultural perspectives, and age-related views elicited significantly more responses and correlated with knowledge-sharing interactions. However, identity presence did not significantly predict higher-level collaborative knowledge construction, suggesting online learners prioritize self-expression over negotiating shared understanding.

title: The impact of scripted roles on online collaborative learning processes
authors: Francesca Pozzi
summary_haiku: This pilot study examined how scripted "opinion-centered" roles impact online collaborative learning in an asynchronous text-based environment. Using content analysis of 209 student messages and post-activity questionnaires, researchers evaluated four dimensions: participative, social, cognitive, and teaching. Results showed roles effectively fostered group cohesion and knowledge building, though metacognition remained underdeveloped. Students' perceptions largely aligned with message analysis, indicating awareness of the collaborative process.

title: Explaining authors’ contribution to pivotal artifacts during mass collaboration in the Wikipedia’s knowledge base
authors: Iassen Halatchliyski & Johannes Moskaliuk & Joachim Kimmerle & Ulrike Cress
summary_haiku: This empirical study examined how authors' contribution experience relates to their involvement in pivotal Wikipedia articles across two knowledge domains. Using network analysis on German Wikipedia data, researchers identified two types of pivotal articles: those central within single domains and those bridging domains. Results showed domain specialists predominantly contributed to domain-central articles, while generalists contributed to boundary-crossing articles. Article experience positively predicted contributions to both article types regardless of specialization.

title: Peer interaction and social network analysis of online communities with the support of awareness of different contexts
authors: Jian-Wei Lin & Li-Jung Mai & Yung-Cheng Lai
summary_haiku: This study directly compares social-context awareness (SA) and knowledge-context awareness (KA) in online learning communities using identical experimental settings. Through a semester-long investigation with repeated measurements, researchers found that SA stimulated significantly more quantitative peer interaction than KA, particularly in later stages. However, both approaches had limited capacity to enhance message quality. Despite similar midterm performance, the SA community demonstrated significantly better learning outcomes on the final posttest, likely attributed to more extensive peer interaction patterns.

title: A Habermasian perspective on joint meaning making online: What does it offer and what are the difficulties?
authors: Michael Hammond
summary_haiku: Habermas's theory of communicative action—emphasizing genuine consensus through unconstrained dialogue where only "the better argument" prevails—offers a critical framework for understanding online meaning-making. This theoretical perspective values truth-seeking over technological affordances, distinguishes emancipatory from strategic communication, and interrogates techno-romantic assumptions. However, challenges include abstractness, limited practical guidance, and questions about consensus feasibility.

title: Role taking and knowledge building in a blended university course
authors: Donatella Cesareni & Stefano Cacciamani & Nobuko Fujita
summary_haiku: Assigning scripted roles aligned with knowledge-building principles significantly enhances student participation in blended university courses. Two studies examined 143 students across three modules, comparing role-takers with non-role-takers using quantitative participation metrics and qualitative content analysis. Results demonstrated that role-takers demonstrated higher reading and writing activity, varied their conversational functions more broadly, and engaged in greater synthesis and metacognitive reflection, supporting collective cognitive responsibility for knowledge advancement.

title: Deliberative emotional talk
authors: Benzi Slakmon & Baruch B. Schwarz
summary_haiku: This study demonstrates that high-quality deliberative discussions about controversial issues can integrate strong emotions with argumentative rigor. Using design-based research, the authors developed the Hot Discussions Platform (HDP), a CSCL tool enabling teachers to design, moderate, and reflect on emotionally-engaged discussions. Through a 30-hour professional development course with 25 teachers, analysis revealed teachers recognize emotions as essential to democratic education and develop sophisticated moderation practices balancing authentic expression with critical thinking standards, establishing proof-of-concept for "deliberative emotional talk."

title: Capturing regulatory patterns in online collaborative learning: A network analytic approach
authors: Si Zhang & Juan Chen & Yun Wen & Hongxian Chen & Qianqian Gao & Qiyun Wang
summary_haiku: This study examined 45 student teachers' regulatory patterns during online collaborative learning using content analysis and epistemic network analysis (ENA). Findings revealed that high-performing groups demonstrated significantly more content monitoring and emotional regulation behaviors than low-performing groups across different activity stages. The analysis identified distinct regulatory patterns: high-performing groups emphasized planning and evaluation, while low-performing groups relied on routine-level regulatory strategies throughout collaboration.

title: Prompting collaborative and exploratory discourse: An epistemic network analysis study
authors: Zarifa Zakaria & Jennifer Tsan & Anna Iwanski & Jessica Vandenberg & Collin Lynch & Kristy Elizabeth Boyer & Eric Wiebe
summary_haiku: This study examined how simple prompting interventions affect elementary students' collaborative discourse during pair programming. Using Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA) to analyze coded dialogue from 62 fourth graders, researchers compared intervention students receiving empirically-derived prompts supporting exploratory talk with control students. Results revealed intervention students significantly increased justification, alternative ideas, and simple questions, demonstrating qualitatively different collaboration patterns through network visualizations showing stronger connections between exploratory talk codes.

title: Educational dialogues and computer supported collaborative learning: critical analysis and research perspectives
authors: Michael J. Baker & Baruch B. Schwarz & Sten R. Ludvigsen
summary_haiku: This critical analysis proposes that educational dialogue research in CSCL requires theoretically grounded integration of diverse data types across multiple timescales. The authors argue the object of study should be collective thinking development in dialogue, with the exchange as the basic analytical unit. They introduce digital platforms as an intermediary analytical level between micro-dialogic exchanges and macro-institutional contexts, emphasizing the need for coherent theoretical frameworks connecting automatic and human analyses to avoid fragmentation.

title: iTalk–iSee: A participatory visual learning analytical tool for productive peer talk
authors: Liru Hu & Jiajun Wu & Gaowei Chen
summary_haiku: iTalk–iSee is a participatory visual learning analytics tool designed to support primary school students' productive peer talk in dialogic collaborative problem-solving. Grounded in Bakhtinian dialogism theory, the tool maps 18 productive talk moves onto three DCPS goals (equality/respect, open-mindedness, convergence) and employs visualization design principles with a three-step macro-script (code→visualize→reflect) to strengthen learner agency. Field study evaluation with 59 fourth-graders demonstrated usability improvements through iterative refinement and positive user experience ratings.

title: Shared meaning-making in online intergroup discussions around sensitive topics
authors: Tugce Aldemir & Marcela Borge & Jose Soto
summary_haiku: This study identifies four communication patterns associated with multicultural collaborative competence (MCC) in online intergroup discussions about sensitive identity topics: grounding with narratives, exploring differences and commonalities, critical reflection, and emotional support. Through qualitative analysis of four undergraduate teams' discussions, the researchers found that existing general collaborative competence frameworks inadequately capture these socio-political dynamics, though some overlap exists between MCC sophistication and traditional collaboration quality measures.

title: Emotion expression and recognition in written digital discussions on Civic Issues
authors: Benzi Slakmon & Omer Keynan & Orly Shapira
summary_haiku: This study examined emotion expression and recognition in written digital discussions on controversial civic issues among nine undergraduate students. Using mixed methods—analyzing 23 discussion turns through follow-up interviews—researchers compared how participants labeled their own emotions with how peers recognized them. Findings revealed low correlation between composers' emotion labeling and others' recognition, lack of shared emotional vocabulary, and two key recognition strategies: attributing emotions based on perceived closeness/belonging to topics, and using iconized visual imagery. Despite poor alignment, participants successfully communicated emotionally through dialogic engagement.

title: Mediating and perspective‑taking manipulatives: Fostering dynamic perspective‑taking by mediating dialogic thinking and bolstering empathy in role‑play and reflection for microteaching
authors: Toshio Mochizuki & Hiroshi Sasaki & Takehiro Wakimoto & Yoshihiko Kubota & Brendan Eagan & Ryoya Hirayama & Yuta Yamaguchi & Natsumi Yuki & Hideo Funaoi & Hideyuki Suzuki & Hiroshi Kato
summary_haiku: This study examined how tangible puppets and 3D manipulable animations support student teachers' perspective-taking in microteaching. Using epistemic network analysis on discourse from 72 preservice teachers across three sessions, results showed that combining mediating manipulatives (puppets) with perspective-taking manipulatives (3D viewpoint switching) significantly enhanced student-centered reflection compared to video-only conditions. The intervention fostered authentic imaginary student voices and sustained dialogic teaching perspectives in subsequent role-plays.

title: An artificial intelligence-driven learning analytics method to examine the collaborative problem-solving process from the complex adaptive systems perspective
authors: Fan Ouyang & Weiqi Xu & Mutlu Cukurova
summary_haiku: This study proposes a three-layered AI-driven analytical framework integrating learning analytics to examine collaborative problem-solving from a complex adaptive systems perspective. Analyzing multimodal data from 24 online group sessions using optimal matching, clustering, and hidden Markov modeling, researchers identified three distinct collaborative patterns: behavior-oriented (medium performance), communication-behavior-synergistic (high performance), and communication-oriented (low performance), revealing the multimodal, dynamic, and synergistic nature of group collaboration.

title: Gesture‑mediated collaboration with augmented reality headsets in a problem‑based astronomy task
authors: James Planey & Robin Jephthah Rajarathinam & Emma Mercier & Robb Lindgren
summary_haiku: This qualitative study examined 15 undergraduate groups collaborating on an astronomy problem using augmented reality headsets and tablets. Analysis revealed that gesture—particularly spatial pointing and representational gestures—mediated collaborative knowledge construction, especially during complex tasks. Groups with higher AR experience showed greater engagement. Gesture facilitated five key affordances: exploration, orientation, perspective-sharing, synthesizing representations, and symbolic conception. The findings demonstrate how embodied gesture bridges digital and physical spaces, enabling groups to create shared situated conceptual spaces that enhance collaborative problem-solving in extended reality environments.

title: The role of first‑language heterogeneity in the acquisition of online interaction self‑efficacy in CSCL
authors: Natalia Reich-Stiebert & Jennifer Raimann & Stefan Sturmer
summary_haiku: Students in linguistically heterogeneous CSCL groups exhibited lower gains in online interaction self-efficacy than those in homogeneous groups, regardless of their own language status. This nine-week pretest-posttest study of 1,525 distance education students found that task-related communication during initial collaboration moderated this negative effect, while social bonding activities paradoxically amplified perceived heterogeneity and impaired self-efficacy development.

title: Effects of group awareness support in CSCL on students’ learning performance: A three‑level meta‑analysis
authors: Dengkang Chen & Yi Zhang & Heng Luo & Zhifang Zhu & Jingsi Ma & Yuru Lin
summary_haiku: Group awareness support in computer-supported collaborative learning shows moderate positive effects on student learning performance (g = 0.46). A three-level meta-analysis of 46 studies found greatest impact on cognitive development, followed by behavioral participation and social emotion. Combined awareness types outperformed individual types, and larger groups benefited more than smaller groups from awareness support.

title: Using generative ai as a simulation to support higher‑order thinking
authors: M. Borge & B. K. Smith & T. Aldemir
summary_haiku: # Summary This case study examines whether generative AI can support higher-order thinking through human-computer collaboration. An expert in collaborative learning engaged in extended dialogue with ChatGPT, practicing metacognitive and sociometacognitive skills while reflecting on interaction quality using a framework of six communication patterns. Findings indicate ChatGPT feasibly supports both individual metacognition and collective sensemaking when users actively regulate conversations and employ structured reflection prompts, though limitations like tendency toward definitive unsupported claims require human oversight for effective learning.

title: Collaboration in virtual and remote laboratories for education: A systematic literature review
authors: Azzeddine Benabbou & Catherine Pons
summary_haiku: This systematic literature review examined 62 educational virtual and remote laboratories published 2011-2025 to assess collaboration support. While communication and group awareness tools are well-integrated, guidance and regulation tools remain underrepresented. Most laboratories support synchronous, non-co-located collaboration in STEM disciplines. Evaluation studies show predominantly positive learning outcomes, yet only one-third assess collaboration quality, indicating a significant research gap requiring future investigation.

title: Age‑related differences in explanatory activities during collaborative learning with concept maps: experimental investigation using epistemic network analysis
authors: Shigen Shimojo & Yugo Hayashi
summary_haiku: Younger adults demonstrated significantly higher learning performance and concept map quality than older adults during collaborative learning with concept maps using attribution theory. While younger adults engaged more frequently in active utterances and showed stronger connections between constructive and interactive behaviors, older adults exhibited higher constructive and interactive utterance frequencies but stronger active-interactive connections. Epistemic network analysis revealed that older adults required knowledge reactivation during elaboration, suggesting age-related cognitive decline hinders knowledge integration in computer-supported collaborative learning environments.

title: Co-reﬂection in online learning: Collaborative critical thinking as narrative
authors: Joyce Yukawa
summary_haiku: This study examined two graduate students' learning in an online action research course using narrative analysis. The research identifies co-reflection—a collaborative critical thinking process combining cognitive and affective interactions with relationship building—as central to knowledge co-construction. Two co-reflection types emerged: tacit (indirect, subtle) and active (explicit, discursive). Simple, flexible software tools effectively supported inquiry learning by accommodating diverse communication and learning styles.

title: Supporting synchronous collaborative learning: A generic, multi-dimensional model
authors: Jacques Lonchamp
summary_haiku: Lonchamp proposes Omega+, a multi-dimensional model-based generic synchronous collaborative learning environment addressing limited applicability of existing CSCL systems. The system uses separate explicit models for collaborative situations, interactions, processes, and performance monitoring, enabling flexible combinations of scaffolding techniques. Evaluation occurs through functional equivalence demonstrations and a dedicated web platform supporting real-world usage analysis and teacher customization.

title: Code talk: Student discourse and participation with networked handhelds
authors: Tobin White
summary_haiku: Networked handheld computers in a middle school mathematics classroom expanded collaborative problem-solving participation beyond traditional discourse. Through interactional analysis of two student groups using the Code Breaker cryptography software, the study found that students demonstrating largest achievement gains gave more instructions and responded less frequently. Importantly, shared mathematical objects across devices enabled non-discursive participation forms, allowing lower-status students to contribute meaningfully despite limited verbal participation.

title: From dialogue to monologue and back: Middle spaces in computer-mediated learning
authors: Noel Enyedy & Christopher M. Hoadley
summary_haiku: This study develops a framework distinguishing communication interfaces supporting dialogue from information interfaces supporting monologue in computer-mediated learning. Through design-based research with the Knowledge Integration Environment, the authors examine how students transition between these modes using SpeakEasy and SenseMaker tools. Case analyses reveal that successful learners strategically moved between dialogue and monologue, reflecting on ideas and identifying knowledge gaps, while less successful learners failed to leverage these transitions, suggesting that "middle spaces" bridging both modes enhance learning trajectories.

title: Investigating patterns of interaction in networked learning and
authors: Maarten de Laat & Vic Lally & Lasse Lipponen
summary_haiku: Social Network Analysis (SNA) combined with content analysis and critical event recall provides valuable insights into networked learning communities. This multi-method study examined interaction patterns in an online master's program, revealing how participant roles and network density evolve over time. SNA effectively visualizes collaboration structures and identifies central versus peripheral members, complementing traditional qualitative methods to deepen understanding of computer-supported collaborative learning dynamics.
