title: How do argumentation diagrams compare when student pairs use them as a means for debate or as a tool for representing debate?
authors: Kristine Lund & Gaelle Molinari & Arnauld Sejourne & Michael Baker
summary_haiku: This study compared two instructional approaches for using argumentation diagrams during online debates among 36 secondary students. Using the ADAM analysis method, researchers examined individual diagrams created before and after debate, plus collaborative diagrams produced during debate. Results revealed that students instructed to represent their chat debate in diagrams added more non-argumentative relations (examples, causes, consequences), while those using diagrams simultaneously during debate expressed more opinions about arguments. These findings suggest different cognitive mechanisms emerge depending on whether diagrams mediate debate or represent completed debate.

title: The role of floor control and of ontology in argumentative activities with discussion-based tools
authors: Baruch B. Schwarz & Amnon Glassner
summary_haiku: This study examined how informal argumentative ontologies and floor control in synchronous e-discussions affect knowledge co-elaboration among 54 seventh-grade students using the Digalo tool. Using a 2×2 factorial design, researchers compared conditions with/without ontology and with/without floor control. Results showed that combining informal ontology with floor control produced significantly more relevant claims and arguments while reducing chat-style expressions and non-productive peer references, suggesting these design features facilitate collaborative knowledge construction.

title: A Community of Practice among tutors enabling student participation in a seminar preparation
authors: Bernhard Nett
summary_haiku: A tutor community of practice overcame institutional barriers to implementing computer-supported collaborative learning in a Computer and Law seminar. Through informal collaboration and shared identity, tutors self-organized to design and conduct an educational experiment using JurMOO, a text-based virtual platform, for seminar preparation. This bottom-up approach enabled student participation and learning where top-down professor coordination had failed, demonstrating that tutor communities can effectively support educational innovation.

title: Group awareness and self-presentation in computer-supported information exchange
authors: Joachim Kimmerle & Ulrike Cress
summary_haiku: This experimental study examined how group awareness tools and protective self-presentation (PSP) influence knowledge-sharing behavior in computer-supported information exchange. Using a laboratory task simulating a social dilemma, 119 participants worked in three conditions: control, group-feedback, and individual-feedback. Results showed that individual feedback identifying each participant's contributions significantly increased cooperation rates, particularly among high-PSP individuals. An interaction effect emerged: high protective self-presenters were most cooperative when identifiable but least cooperative anonymously, suggesting self-presentation concerns drive knowledge-sharing behavior in collaborative digital environments.

title: Analyzing collaborative learning processes automatically: Exploiting the advances of computational linguistics in
authors: Carolyn Rose & Yi-Chia Wang & Yue Cui & Jaime Arguello & Karsten Stegmann & Armin Weinberger & Frank Fischer
summary_haiku: Researchers applied computational linguistics text classification technology to automatically analyze collaborative learning discourse using a multi-dimensional coding scheme. Testing on 1,250 coded segments, they achieved acceptable reliability (Kappa ≥0.7) on several dimensions by designing linguistically-informed features reflecting thread structure and discourse context, demonstrating that feature engineering proved more effective than sophisticated algorithms for this task.

title: Automatic coding of dialogue acts in collaboration protocols
authors: Gijsbert Erkens & Jeroen Janssen
summary_haiku: Researchers developed an automatic coding system to identify dialogue acts (communicative functions) in online collaboration protocols using discourse markers. Testing on 1,000 messages showed 79% agreement with manual coding (Cohen's kappa=0.75). Validity analyses confirmed the system reliably distinguished gender differences in communication patterns and detected experimental intervention effects, supporting its utility for analyzing collaborative learning processes.

title: Genre and CSCL: The form and rhetoric of the online posting
authors: Norm Friesen
summary_haiku: This study applies genre analysis to online discussion postings in CSCL contexts, hypothesizing that educational postings share rhetorical characteristics with their epistolary precursor, the letter. Through content analysis of 136 postings, the author identifies 240 rhetorical markers reflecting epistolary dynamics, including salutations, present-tense references, and temporal references. Findings suggest that cultural and historical factors embedded in familiar genres significantly shape how students engage in online collaborative learning, beyond technological affordances alone.

title: Exploring metaskills of knowledge-creating inquiry in higher education
authors: Hanni Muukkonen & Minna Lakkala
summary_haiku: This study investigates metaskills required for knowledge-creating inquiry in higher education through an 11-week undergraduate psychology course using progressive inquiry and web-based collaboration. Qualitative analysis of database discourse and student self-reflections revealed three student groups exhibited varying engagement levels in collaborative object-oriented inquiry. Group C demonstrated superior skills in monitoring individual, collective, and object-oriented aspects of inquiry, while Groups A and B struggled with shared knowledge advancement. Findings suggest metaskills for collaborative knowledge creation develop through sustained socialization into inquiry practices emphasizing iterative development of shared epistemic objects.

title: Web 2.0: Inherent tensions and evident challenges for education
authors: Nina Bonderup Dohn
summary_haiku: Web 2.0 practices and educational systems embody fundamentally incompatible learning metaphors. While Web 2.0 emphasizes participatory, distributed knowledge construction with internal goals, education prioritizes individual knowledge acquisition for external purposes. This conceptual tension manifests practically in challenges regarding collaboration, evaluation criteria, and material authenticity when Web 2.0 tools are integrated into educational settings.

title: Analyzing temporal patterns of knowledge construction in a role-based online discussion
authors: Alyssa Friend Wise
summary_haiku: This study analyzed temporal patterns of knowledge construction in role-based online discussions using content analysis and statistical discourse analysis. Examining 252 posts from 21 university students, researchers identified pivotal posts that divided discussions into distinct segments. Results showed most discussions progressed from lower to higher knowledge construction phases, with mid-discussion summaries by Synthesizer and Wrapper roles acting as pivotal posts that elevated subsequent discussion quality, supporting the progressive nature of collaborative knowledge construction.

title: Building a community among teachers, researchers and university students. A blended approach to training
authors: Donatella Cesareni & Francesca Martini & Ilaria Mancini
summary_haiku: # Summary This case study examined a blended learning community of 45 Italian teachers, researchers, and university students participating in the ITCOLE project. Using qualitative analysis of face-to-face and online interactions, researchers found that expert teachers assumed central roles while novice teachers engaged in legitimate peripheral participation, gradually becoming more competent community members. Teachers recognized CSCL's innovative potential for student motivation and collaborative knowledge building, though they identified challenges including technical infrastructure limitations and heavy workload demands.

title: The multivoicedness of game play: Exploring the unfolding of a student’s learning trajectory in a gaming context at school
authors: Kenneth Silseth
summary_haiku: This qualitative case study examines how classroom interactions facilitate a student's learning trajectory while playing the educational game Global Conflicts: Palestine. Using sociocultural and dialogic analysis of video-recorded gameplay and discussions, the research demonstrates that computer games become learning resources through collaborative meaning-making. The teacher's role in orchestrating dialogic spaces where multiple perspectives "inter-animate" each other proved crucial for developing nuanced understanding of the Israeli-Palestinian conflict's complexity.

title: Personal and shared experiences as resources for meaning making in a philosophy of science course
authors: Maarit Arvaja
summary_haiku: Health education students in an online philosophy of science course used personal work experiences and peer contributions as meaning-making resources. Analysis of individual writings and discussions revealed three epistemic activities: applying theoretical concepts to practice, forming conceptions, and critiquing. Peer interactions involved elaboration and sharing discourse. Results demonstrate that connecting abstract philosophical knowledge to lived experience enhanced understanding while fostering boundary crossing between institutional and personal knowledge contexts.

title: The ACODEA framework: Developing segmentation and classification schemes for fully automatic analysis of online discussions
authors: Jin Mu & Karsten Stegmann & Elijah Mayfield & Carolyn Rose & Frank Fischer
summary_haiku: The ACODEA framework enables fully automatic analysis of online discussions by extracting syntactic and semantic features through part-of-speech tagging and named-entity recognition before segmentation and classification. Applied to 84 students' collaborative discussions about attribution theory, the three-layer approach achieved high reliability (Cohen's Kappa ≥0.81) for micro-argumentation coding across different contexts, demonstrating that context-independent automated analysis is feasible for collaborative learning environments.

title: Recalibrating reference within a dual-space interaction environment
authors: Alan Zemel & Timothy Koschmann
summary_haiku: # Summary Middle school students collaborating in the Virtual Math Teams system develop shared understanding of mathematical problems through sequential recalibration of referential practices. Using ethnomethodological analysis of chat and whiteboard interactions, the study demonstrates how students progressively specify indexical properties of underspecified problems and solutions. Rather than treating representations as static objects, the research reveals how problem-solving emerges from the situated, interactive work of producing and refining references to mathematical concepts across dual-space modalities.

title: Enhancing student knowledge acquisition from online learning conversations
authors: Evren Eryilmaz & Jakko van der Pol & Terry Ryan & Philip Martin Clark & Justin Mary
summary_haiku: This experimental study compared linked and parallel artifact-centered discussion systems with 106 pharmacy students. Annotation functionality in the linked system decreased coordination activities while increasing assertion and conflict knowledge construction activities. Mediation analysis revealed that assertion, conflict, and clarification activities significantly predicted individual learning gains, with the treatment group achieving greater post-test improvements than controls.

title: Crossing boundaries in Facebook: Students’ framing of language learning activities as extended spaces
authors: Annika Lantz-Andersson & Sylvi Vigmo & Rhonwen Bowen
summary_haiku: This ethnographic case study examined how 60 students aged 13-16 from four countries framed English language learning activities in a Facebook group. Using frame analysis and sociocultural theory, researchers found that students initially adopted formal school-task framing but gradually negotiated boundary-crossing interactions creating extended learning spaces. However, maintaining these dynamic spaces proved difficult, requiring deliberate collaborative negotiation between educators and students to balance everyday social media practices with educational goals.

title: Advancing knowledge‐building discourse through judgments of promising ideas
authors: Bodong Chen & Marlene Scardamalia & Carl Bereiter
summary_haiku: Grade 3 students demonstrated capability in making promisingness judgments—evaluating ideas for their potential to advance knowledge—when supported by explicit discussion and a digital tool integrated into Knowledge Forum. Design-based research revealed students could distinguish ideas worth developing from mere facts, and promisingness judgments significantly enhanced collaborative discourse and scientific knowledge advancement compared to control classrooms.

title: Exploring the relationship between resistance and perspectival understanding in computer-mediated discussions
authors: SoonAh Lee & Kwangok Song
summary_haiku: This discourse analytic study examined how graduate students expressed resistance while negotiating ideas in computer-mediated discussions. Findings revealed that resistance expressions frequently accompanied perspectival understanding as students elaborated on course readings and peer ideas. Resistance functioned as a constructive discourse tool, facilitating both individual and collaborative knowledge construction. The study demonstrates resistance's integral role in developing sophisticated perspectives within online classroom discussions.

title: Conversational agents for academically productive talk: a comparison of directed and undirected agent interventions
authors: Stergios Tegos & Stavros Demetriadis & Pantelis M. Papadopoulos & Armin Weinberger
summary_haiku: This study compared directed versus undirected conversational agent interventions promoting academically productive talk in 96 computer science students working in dyads. Using a pre-test/post-test experimental design with discourse analysis, results showed directed interventions—addressing individual students—significantly enhanced individual domain knowledge and explicit reasoning compared to undirected interventions addressing both peers. Explicit reasoning mediated the agent's effect on dyad performance, with directed methods proving more effective at stimulating productive discourse.

title: Comparing effects of two collaboration scripts on learning activities for wiki-based environments
authors: Sven Heimbuch & Lisa Ollesch & Daniel Bodemer
summary_haiku: This experimental study compared two wiki collaboration scripts for educational knowledge construction. The Discuss-Deliberate-Revise (DDR) script, emphasizing upfront discussion before edits, was tested against Wikipedia's Be Bold-Revert-Discuss (BRD) script promoting frequent individual edits. Across a pre-study with dyads and main study with larger groups, DDR encouraged more discussion and produced higher-quality, error-free articles, though direct learning gains were minimal. Individual differences in cognitive closure, metacognitive strategies, and motivation moderated script effectiveness.

title: When coding-and-counting is not enough: using epistemic network analysis (ENA) to analyze verbal data in CSCL research
authors: Brendan Eagan & Ingo Kollar & David Williamson Shaffer
summary_haiku: Traditional coding-and-counting analyses of collaborative learning discourse ignore temporal relationships between learning actions, potentially missing important patterns. This study compared traditional frequency-based analysis with Epistemic Network Analysis (ENA), which models temporal co-occurrences of coded actions. Analyzing pre-service teachers' problem-solving discourse, ENA revealed that evidence evaluation was central to dyadic reasoning but not individual reasoning—a pattern invisible to traditional methods. Results confirm that temporal structure, not merely code frequency, drives these findings.

title: Data wrangling practices and collaborative interactions with aggregated data
authors: Shiyan Jiang & Jennifer Kahn
summary_haiku: Youth engaged in data wrangling—selecting and managing large datasets to create models and stories—using interactive visualization tools to explore family migration. Analysis of talk-in-interaction identified ten sociotechnical practices and four learning activity categories: addressing missing data, understanding aggregation, exploring historical events, and varying visual encoding. Collaborative interactions with instructors and peers supported critical inquiry and meaning-making about data's social significance.

title: Students’ multimodal knowledge practices in a makerspace learning environment
authors: Anu Kajamaa & Kristiina Kumpulainen
summary_haiku: This sociocultural study examined how students' collaborative knowledge practices are mediated multimodally in a school makerspace during STEAM challenges. Through discourse and multimodal interaction analysis of 350 minutes of video data from two student groups, researchers identified four intertwined knowledge practices: orienting to, interpreting, concretizing, and expanding knowledge. Findings reveal that discourse, materials, embodied actions, and spatial arrangements jointly mediated students' joint attention and knowledge creation, with peer guidance proving more influential than teacher support or pre-given instructions.

title: Group awareness and regulation in
authors: Lenka Schnaubert & Daniel Bodemer
summary_haiku: This article conceptualizes group awareness (GA) in computer-supported collaborative learning as a conscious, current, individual cognitive construct about social entities that learners perceive as valid. The authors identify six defining aspects of GA and propose it operates within three regulatory cycles: regulating GA itself through metacognitive monitoring, regulating social interaction based on GA, and regulating partner schema building. The framework connects GA to working memory processes and suggests implications for designing support tools and conducting empirical research on collaborative learning mechanisms.

title: Integrating a collaboration script and group awareness to support group regulation and emotions towards collaborative problem solving
authors: Matias Rojas & Miguel Nussbaum & Orlando Guerrero & Pablo Chiuminatto & Samuel Greiff & Rodrigo Del Rio & Danilo Alvares
summary_haiku: This study examined how a game-based collaboration script with group awareness tools affects elementary students' collaborative problem-solving skills. Using a quasi-experimental design with 223 sixth-graders, researchers compared an experimental group playing a six-level collaborative game to a control group receiving regular instruction. Results showed the intervention significantly improved attitudes toward collaboration and increased shared regulation and co-regulation processes. Qualitative analysis revealed positive emotions like satisfaction emerged through co-regulation, suggesting collaboration scripts combined with group awareness effectively support regulation skills and emotional development during collaborative problem-solving.

title: Fostering growth orientations in students’ identities as knowledge builders
authors: Shiri Kashi & Yotam Hod
summary_haiku: This study examined how students develop growth orientations in humanistic knowledge building communities (HKBCs). Using grounded analysis of 322 utterances from graduate students' reflective diaries and discussions, researchers identified five dimensions of fixedness-growth orientations: feelings, mindset, personal responsibility, self-constructs, and attitudes toward change. Statistical analysis revealed significant increases in growth orientation across the semester. Case studies illustrated how students transformed from fixed to growth orientations through community support and reflection, with implications for self-regulated learning and emergent roles in collaborative environments.

title: An automated group learning engagement analysis and feedback approach to promoting collaborative knowledge building, group performance, and socially shared regulation in CSCL
authors: Lanqin Zheng & Miaolang Long & Jiayu Niu & Lu Zhong
summary_haiku: This study examined an automated group learning engagement analysis and feedback approach using deep neural networks in computer-supported collaborative learning. A quasi-experimental design with 120 college students in 40 groups compared the proposed approach to traditional online collaboration. Results showed significant improvements in cognitive, metacognitive, behavioral, emotional, and social engagement; collaborative knowledge building; group performance; and socially shared regulation, without increasing cognitive load.

title: Understanding young children’s science learning through embodied communication within an MR environment
authors: Xintian Tu & Joshua Danish & Megan Humburg & Mengxi Zhou & Nitasha Mathayas & Noel Enyedy
summary_haiku: This study examines how first and second graders use embodied communication—gestures and body movements—within a mixed-reality environment to learn about particle states of matter. Using interaction analysis and coding schemes, researchers found students developed shared gestures representing challenging concepts during classroom activities and subsequently used these gestures in interviews to clarify understanding. Results reveal embodied communication serves both individual and collective functions, supporting collaborative knowledge construction about microscopic particle behavior and macroscopic state changes.

title: Co‑constructing knowledge with generative AI tools: Reflections from a CSCL perspective
authors: Ulrike Cress & Joachim Kimmerle
summary_haiku: # Summary Cress and Kimmerle examine how generative AI tools like ChatGPT can support human knowledge construction from a computer-supported collaborative learning perspective. While AI lacks conceptual understanding, they argue that appropriate prompts enabling argumentative dialogue between humans and AI can facilitate knowledge transformation beyond simple information exchange. The authors propose future CSCL research directions including ethnomethodological studies, experimental investigations of prompting strategies, and exploration of whether genuine collaborative knowledge construction occurs between human-AI dyads.

title: Reflective assessment using analytics and artifacts for scaffolding knowledge building competencies among undergraduate students
authors: Yuqin Yang & Carol K. K. Chan & Gaoxia Zhu & Yuyao Tong & Daner Sun
summary_haiku: # Summary This study develops a comprehensive framework of knowledge building (KB) competencies encompassing conceptual, metacognitive, socio-emotional, and epistemic dimensions. Using qualitative discourse analysis of 1,390 Knowledge Forum notes from 41 undergraduates, the research demonstrates that reflective assessment enriched with super synthesis notes, KB interaction rubrics, and KBDeX learning analytics visualizations significantly fosters development of these competencies. Results show undergraduates engaged in higher-level productive discourse moves across all dimensions, with sequential pattern analysis revealing progressive improvements in socio-emotional interactions and epistemic engagement between pre- and post-intervention stages.

title: Learning to notice collaboration: examining the impact of professional development on mathematics teachers’ enhanced awareness in CSCL settings
authors: Benzi Slakmon & Rotem Abdu
summary_haiku: # Summary This study examined how professional development affects mathematics teachers' ability to notice dialogue in computer-supported collaborative learning. Fourteen teachers analyzed video excerpts of student pairs solving parabola tasks before and after an 80-minute intervention focused on Bakhtinian dialogic concepts. Using think-aloud interviews and dialogic framework analysis, results showed significant improvements in teachers' attending to and responding to dialogic attributes, particularly regarding student relationships, inter-animation, and multivoicedness, though challenges remain in balancing mathematical correctness with dialogue support.

title: Toward multimodal learning analytics in simulation‑based collaborative learning: A design ethnography of maritime training
authors: Charlott Sellberg & Amit Sharma
summary_haiku: # Summary This design ethnography examines maritime simulator-based training to inform multimodal learning analytics (MMLA) development. Through detailed video analysis of master mariner students' collaborative bridge activities, the researchers identified how instructors deliver embedded assessments and feedback using multiple social and material resources. The study proposes specific technologies—system logs, eye-tracking, and speech recognition—necessary for capturing professional performance, communication, and collaboration in simulation-based learning environments.

title: How do new ideas come to be adopted during discourse?
authors: Deanna Kuhn & Teresa Fraguada & Mariel Halpern
summary_haiku: This study examines how adolescents adopt and revise ideas during electronic peer argumentation. Two case studies traced participants' evolving positions across eight successive dialogs on juvenile justice. Results revealed contrasting patterns: one participant readily adopted partners' ideas but struggled defending positions, while the other maintained firm beliefs with strong counterargument skills but limited openness to new ideas. Findings highlight how argumentation skills, epistemological understanding, and metacognitive reflection jointly influence belief change in collaborative discourse.

title: Technology affordances for intersubjective meaning making: A research agenda for CSCL
authors: Daniel D. Suthers
summary_haiku: Suthers proposes intersubjective meaning making—how groups jointly compose interpretations of dynamically evolving contexts—as CSCL's integrating research agenda. Through conceptual analysis, he argues that technology should be designed as fundamentally social to afford such meaning-making processes. He advocates hybrid methodologies combining experimental, descriptive, and design approaches, with "uptake" relations serving as a boundary object enabling dialogue across theoretical traditions.

title: Using graphical tools in a phased activity for enhancing dialogical skills: An example with Digalo
authors: Nathalie Muller Mirza & Valerie Tartas & Anne-Nelly Perret-Clermont & Jean-Francois de Pietro
summary_haiku: This study examined how university students developed argumentative and historical knowledge through a phased learning activity using Digalo, graphical argument-mapping software. Using descriptive analysis of two collective debates about the Valladolid Controversy, researchers found that students constructed complex understanding of the historical topic while developing sophisticated argument-counterargument-reply sequences. The software's visual representations and structured functionalities supported both topic meaning-making and argumentative processes, enabling students to elaborate justifications and integrate opposing perspectives into their reasoning.

title: Using activity-oriented design methods to study collaborative knowledge-building in e-learning courses within higher education
authors: Christine Greenhow & Brad Belbas
summary_haiku: Activity-Oriented Design Methods (AODM) operationalize Activity Theory to analyze collaborative knowledge-building in e-learning courses. Using qualitative case study methodology, researchers applied AODM's six-stage framework to examine course design teams and students in online higher education. Findings revealed that peer collaboration, facilitated through small-group assignments and discussion guidelines, supported students' development of statistical knowledge through exploratory talk and iterative refinement of shared learning objects.

title: Facilitating argumentative knowledge construction with computer-supported collaboration scripts
authors: Karsten Stegmann & Armin Weinberger & Frank Fischer
summary_haiku: Computer-supported collaboration scripts significantly improve argumentative knowledge construction in online discussions. A 2×2 factorial study with 120 educational science students examined scripts supporting single argument construction and argumentation sequences. Results showed scripts substantially enhanced formal argument quality and argumentation sequence quality. Scripts also facilitated knowledge on argumentation but not domain-specific knowledge, suggesting learners focused effort on argumentation skills rather than content mastery.

title: Cultural practices in networked classroom learning environments
authors: Nancy Ares
summary_haiku: Networked classroom simulations enable underserved secondary mathematics students to leverage cultural practices as learning resources. This case study examined the Gridlock Participatory Simulation, analyzing how coordination and co-construction activities—supported by multiple communication modes including informal language, gesture, and graphical representations—invited students to draw on community-based interaction patterns while engaging in rigorous mathematical discourse and practice.

title: Book review: Exploring thinking as communicating in CSCL
authors: Anna Sfard
summary_haiku: Sfard's theory conceptualizes mathematical objects as products of discursive processes rather than mental acquisitions, arguing that deep understanding emerges through participation in social routines of mathematical discourse. The review examines how students collaboratively construct mathematical meaning through communication, proposing that extending this participationist framework to computer-mediated group interaction could advance CSCL research while requiring integration with broader social and cultural dimensions.

title: Leveraging online communities in fostering adaptive schools
authors: David Hung & Kenneth Y. T. Lim & Der-Thanq Victor Chen & Thiam Seng Koh
summary_haiku: Online communities function as "para-communities" that should remain distinct from formal schools rather than being integrated into them. Through conceptual analysis, the authors argue that schools and online communities serve fundamentally different goals: schools emphasize intentional learning and efficiency, while online communities prioritize intrinsic motivation and innovation. They propose that adaptive schools leverage external para-communities through internal Communities of Interest, enabling complementary relationships that cultivate social capital and innovation without compromising organizational efficiency.

title: Exploring whether students’ use of labelling depends upon the type of activity
authors: Eva Mary Bures & Philip C. Abrami & Richard F. Schmid
summary_haiku: This mixed-methods study examined whether graduate students use labeling features less frequently during structured versus unstructured online dialogue. Participants (n=37) engaged in two activities: an unstructured discussion and a HipBone Game with predetermined structure. Results showed significantly reduced label usage during the structured activity, with 62% using labels multiple times unstructured versus 46% structured. Students preferred the structured dialogue but reported mixed satisfaction with labeling. Findings suggest structured activities provide alternative scaffolding, potentially rendering labeling features redundant.

title: Scripting a distance-learning university course: Do students benefit from net-based scripted collaboration?
authors: Joerg M. Haake & Hans-Rudiger Pfister
summary_haiku: This experimental field study examined whether scripted collaboration benefits net-based learning in a semester-long university operating systems course. Forty-two student groups performed brainstorming, clustering, and essay-writing tasks either with system-enforced scripts or non-scripted instructions. Results showed no general advantage of scripting for knowledge acquisition or task performance. However, principal component analysis revealed scripting slightly improved essay coherence and comprehensibility, suggesting benefits for complex tasks requiring deeper understanding.

title: Can the interactive whiteboard support young children’s collaborative communication and thinking in classroom science activities?
authors: Ruth Kershner & Neil Mercer & Paul Warwick & Judith Kleine Staarman
summary_haiku: Interactive whiteboards can support young children's collaborative communication and thinking in primary science, but effectiveness depends on multiple interacting factors. Through observational analysis of twelve classrooms, researchers found the IWB facilitates productive dialogue when combined with teacher scaffolding, established "talk rules," and appropriate classroom participation structures. However, the technology alone is not pedagogically transformative; success requires careful integration with other classroom resources and attention to both social and cognitive dimensions of collaborative learning.

title: Sharing and cultivating tacit knowledge in an online learning environment
authors: Meng Yew Tee
summary_haiku: Online graduate business students cultivated tacit knowledge through a strategic management course using naturalistic inquiry methodology. The course combined readings, threaded discussions, and a simulation game, creating a "ba" (shared context) that encouraged socialization, externalization, combination, and internalization processes aligned with Nonaka's knowledge creation model. Students reported learning tacit dimensions impossible to acquire from textbooks alone.

title: A multimodal approach to coding discourse: Collaboration, distributed cognition, and geometric reasoning
authors: Michael A. Evans & Eliot Feenstra & Emily Ryon & David McNeill
summary_haiku: Researchers developed a multimodal coding framework to analyze distributed cognition in young children's collaborative problem-solving. Using speech, gesture, and gaze analysis, they tracked "coreferences"—shared references to objects, participants, and concepts—across three discourse levels. Applied to 7-8-year-olds solving tangrams physically and virtually, findings revealed increased meta-level communication and coalition formation in computer-supported settings, with dominant participants showing greater influence in virtual versus physical environments.

title: Collaboration amidst disagreement and moral judgment: The dynamics of Jewish and Arab students’ collaborative inquiry of their joint past
authors: Sarah Pollack & Yifat Ben-David Kolikant
summary_haiku: Israeli Jewish and Arab students collaboratively investigated a historical event through computer-supported learning, analyzing conflicting narratives via wiki-based discussion. Despite persistent disagreement, students' post-activity individual answers demonstrated enriched historical understanding, incorporating multiple perspectives and reduced one-sidedness. The researchers propose "fission"—moments when opposing voices create cracks in individual perspectives, fostering polyphonic thinking without requiring consensus.

title: Context matters: The value of analyzing human factors within educational contexts as a way of informing technology-related decisions within design research
authors: Kim MacKinnon
summary_haiku: Design research in educational technology often overlooks systematic analysis of contextual factors. This study adapts Cognitive Work Analysis (CWA), an engineering method, to systematically identify human factors constraints—political, organizational, team, psychological, and physical—within a teacher education program. Through interviews, documentation analysis, and observations, 358 constraints were identified. The modified CWA approach made contextual information explicit and organized, enabling informed technology design decisions for supporting student research projects through an online mentorship environment.

title: Online class size, note reading, note writing and collaborative discourse
authors: Mingzhu Qiu & Jim Hewitt
summary_haiku: This mixed-methods study examined 25 online graduate courses (341 students, 25 instructors) using tracking logs and interviews to investigate how class size affects note reading and writing loads. Findings revealed class size positively correlates with total notes read but negatively with percentage read, indicating information overload in larger classes. Students wrote shorter, simpler notes in larger classes. Dividing large classes into subgroups reduced overload. An optimal class size of 13-15 students was identified for effective collaborative discourse.

title: 4SPPIces: A case study of factors in a scripted collaborative-learning blended course across spatial locations
authors: Mar Perez-Sanagustin & Patricia Santos & Davinia Hernandez-Leo & Josep Blat
summary_haiku: This case study evaluates the 4SPPIces model—a conceptual framework combining Space, Pedagogical Method, Participants, and History factors—for designing computer-supported collaborative blended learning scripts. Researchers implemented a geography fieldwork activity with 34 students across Barcelona using mobile devices and GPS. Results demonstrate that considering 4SPPIces factors successfully enhanced the activity, promoting collaborative skills, motivation, and learning about multiple urban districts while effectively supporting teacher orchestration through integrated technologies.

title: Participatory learning through behavioral and cognitive engagements in an online collective information searching activity
authors: Chia-Ching Lin & Chin-Chung Tsai
summary_haiku: This study investigated how college students' behavioral and cognitive engagements relate during online collective information searching using social bookmarking. Through cluster analysis of 101 engineering students' activity logs and annotations, researchers identified four behavioral patterns (Hitchhiker, Individualist, Active, Commentator) and two cognitive levels (Deep, Surface). Results revealed that students exhibiting "Active" behavioral engagement demonstrated "Deep" cognitive engagement, while those with "Hitchhiker" or "Individualist" patterns showed "Surface" engagement, with deeper engagement correlating to better assignment performance.

title: Inducing socio-cognitive conflict in Finnish and German groups of online learners by CSCL script
authors: Armin Weinberger & Miika Marttunen & Leena Laurinen
summary_haiku: This cross-cultural study examined how a peer-critique collaboration script affects socio-cognitive conflict in online learning. Using a 2×2 design with 132 Finnish and German university students, researchers analyzed discussion patterns and knowledge acquisition. Results revealed German groups engaged in more conflict-oriented consensus building than Finnish groups, who preferred integration-oriented approaches. The script strengthened conflict-oriented discourse in German groups but proved incompatible with Finnish collaborative norms, suggesting CSCL environments require culturally sensitive design.

title: Capturing and analyzing verbal and physical collaborative learning interactions at an enriched interactive tabletop
authors: Roberto Martinez-Maldonado & Yannis Dimitriadis & Alejandra Martinez-Mones & Judy Kay & Kalina Yacef
summary_haiku: This study developed an approach to automatically capture and analyze verbal and physical interactions at an enriched interactive tabletop to distinguish collaborative from less collaborative student groups. Using sequence pattern mining on data from 60 students in concept-mapping triads, the researchers identified interaction patterns—including speech timing, turn-taking, and peer engagement—that differentiated high from low collaboration groups, demonstrating the potential of multimodal data analysis for supporting collaborative learning awareness.

title: Toward collaboration sensing
authors: Bertrand Schneider & Roy Pea
summary_haiku: Researchers applied network analysis to dual eye-tracking data from collaborative learning dyads, representing fixations as nodes and saccades as edges. Network metrics correlated with collaboration quality dimensions, and machine learning algorithms predicted collaboration quality with 85-100% accuracy, suggesting eye-tracking networks can serve as "collaboration-sensing" tools for assessing and potentially improving student teamwork.

title: Appropriation of a representational tool in a second-language classroom
authors: Yun Wen & Chee-Kit Looi & Wenli Chen
summary_haiku: This case study examined how secondary school students appropriated Group Scribbles, a representational tool, during collaborative Chinese-language writing in a networked classroom. Through microanalysis of cross-media interactions between face-to-face and online spaces, researchers identified five functions inscriptional devices served in group-understanding development: referencing, pinpointing, prompting notice, realizing parallels, and promoting synergy. Findings revealed that representational tools supplement face-to-face communication by enabling balanced participation, helping learners notice linguistic problems, and serving as resources for elaborating ideas.

title: The impact of hierarchical positions on communities of learning
authors: Martin Rehm & Wim Gijselaers & Mien Segers
summary_haiku: Hierarchical positions significantly influence participants' activity and performance in online Communities of Learning within organizations. Analyzing 249 staff members across 25 CoLs, this empirical study found that higher-ranked employees contributed more frequently and achieved better exam grades. However, cluster analysis revealed a "Stars" group of exceptional performers transcending hierarchical constraints, suggesting that while organizational hierarchy shapes collaborative behavior, individual motivation can overcome these structural barriers.

title: Learning to learn together with CSCL tools
authors: Baruch B. Schwarz & Reuma de Groot & Manolis Mavrikis & Toby Dragon
summary_haiku: This design-based research study introduces Learning to Learn Together (L2L2)—learning to collaborate while engaging in inquiry and argumentation on challenging tasks. Using the Metafora CSCL platform integrating planning tools, microworlds, and discussion features, researchers observed three classroom cases where students developed collaborative practices including collective reflection, mutual engagement, and peer assessment. Results demonstrate L2L2 is an attainable educational goal, partially achieved through technology-mediated affordances supporting integrated inquiry-argumentation-collaboration practices.

title: Tracing the change in discourse in a collaborative dynamic geometry environment: From visual to more mathematical
authors: Diler Oner
summary_haiku: This case study examined three middle-school students' mathematical discourse development while solving geometry construction problems in the Virtual Math Teams collaborative environment. Using Sfard's commognitive framework, the researcher traced changes in students' word usage, visual mediators, and problem-solving routines across six episodes. The team progressively shifted from visual, perception-based approaches to more formal mathematical discourse emphasizing geometric dependencies, demonstrating that well-designed collaborative virtual learning environments can support significant mathematical development comparable to expert instruction.

title: Developing & using interaction geography in a museum
authors: Ben Rydal Shapiro & Rogers P. Hall & David A. Owens
summary_haiku: Researchers developed "interaction geography," an integrative approach combining conversation analysis, movement tracking, and spatial design to study visitor engagement in museum settings. Using Mondrian Transcription and the Interaction Geography Slicer visualization tool, they analyzed 22 visitor groups' complete museum visits. A CSCL environment enabled museum professionals to reframe their understanding of visitor behavior—particularly children's movement—from disruptive to purposeful learning, supporting evidence-based design decisions for equitable learning opportunities.

title: Connecting levels of activity with classroom network technology
authors: Tobin White
summary_haiku: Classroom network technology enables fluid transitions between individual, small-group, and whole-class mathematics instruction. Through design-based research analyzing two learning environments, this study identifies mechanisms—appropriation, mediation, emergence, and orchestration—that support multilevel activity. Findings reveal that rather than sequential shifts between levels, classroom activity often exhibits simultaneous, overlapping interactions across planes, with shared mathematical objects mediating connections between groups and facilitating dynamic classroom participation.

title: Orchestrating the emergence of conceptual learning: a case study in a geometry class
authors: Baruch B. Schwarz & Naomi Prusak & Osama Swidan & Adva Livny & Kobi Gal & Avi Segal
summary_haiku: # Summary This case study investigates whether teachers can orchestrate conceptual learning across multiple student groups working simultaneously on geometry tasks. Using SAGLET, a system that monitors parallel group work and alerts teachers to critical moments via machine learning, the researchers observed one experienced teacher guiding eight groups through challenging quadrilateral hierarchy problems. Analysis revealed five intervention types—collaboration encouragement, task supervision, justification requests, argumentation scaffolding, and social validation—with scaffolding being most frequent. Results demonstrate successful orchestration: seven of eight groups solved difficult tasks requiring abstract geometric reasoning, suggesting that real-time alerts and visibility tools enable adaptive guidance across multiple groups in classroom settings.

title: Using big data techniques for measuring productive friction in mass collaboration online environments
authors: Peter Holtz & Joachim Kimmerle & Ulrike Cress
summary_haiku: Researchers analyzed Wikipedia using big data techniques—text classification, social network analysis, and clustering—to examine how "productive friction" (resolving socio-cognitive conflicts) drives learning and knowledge construction at both individual and collective levels. Findings demonstrated that knowledge development occurs when diverse contributors engage across different perspectives, while homogeneous groups risk polarization and stagnation.

title: Providing different types of group awareness information to guide collaborative learning
authors: Lenka Schnaubert & Daniel Bodemer
summary_haiku: # Summary This experimental study with 260 university students examined how different types of group awareness information guide collaborative learning. Dyads discussed blood-sugar regulation while receiving either cognitive information about peers' assumptions, metacognitive information about peers' confidence levels, both, or neither. Results showed that visualized information strongly influenced task selection strategies—learners focused on conflicting assumptions or uncertain topics based on available information. However, providing awareness information did not significantly improve learning outcomes, suggesting that guiding study behavior alone may be insufficient without additional support for collaborative knowledge construction processes.

title: Imagining with improvised representations in CSCL environments
authors: Magdalena Kersting & Kenneth Silseth & Rolf Steier
summary_haiku: This study examines how upper secondary physics students collaboratively improvise and introduce representations outside designed learning environments to solve problems. Through video analysis of small groups using an interactive map task comparing two- and three-dimensional spatial representations, researchers identified emergent improvised representations including gestures, physical objects, and digital tools like GoogleEarth. Findings reveal that imagination—conceptualized as a social, embodied, and materially distributed process—enables students to recognize representational needs and discover new possibilities, with multimodal shifts facilitating sophisticated meaning-making across digital, physical, gestural, and dimensional boundaries.

title: Socio-cognitive openness in online knowledge building discourse: does openness keep conversations going?
authors: Frank P. C. M. de Jong & Jan van Aalst & Natascha de Hoog & Hennie van Heijst & Paul A. Kirschner
summary_haiku: This study analyzes socio-cognitive openness in online knowledge-building discourse among Master's students using a framework with four social and four cognitive components. Analyzing 638 Knowledge Forum contributions, researchers found moderate openness levels with higher social than cognitive openness. Cognitive openness indicators—particularly elaboration, justification, and inviting response—positively predicted follow-up contributions, while social openness showed no significant relationship. Expressing uncertainty emerged as key to sustaining knowledge-building conversations.

title: Capturing the participation and social dimensions of
authors: Mohammed Saqr & Olga Viberg & Henriikka Vartiainen
summary_haiku: This study validates social network analysis centrality measures for analyzing computer-supported collaborative learning. Using data from 12 university courses with 598 students, researchers examined how different network configurations (multigraph, simplified, weighted) affect the reproducibility of centrality measures as indicators of student performance. Results show multigraph configuration produces the most consistent and robust measures, with degree centralities reliably indicating participation and eigenvector centrality consistently reflecting social dimensions across configurations.

title: The impact of a gamified mobile question‑asking app on museum visitor group interactions: an ICAP framing
authors: Jesse Ha & Luis E. Perez Cortes & Man Su & Brian C. Nelson & Catherine Bowman & Judd D. Bowman
summary_haiku: This study examined how a gamified mobile question-asking app affects museum visitor group interactions using the ICAP framework. Researchers compared two app modes—Ask Mode (baseline) and Game Mode (gamified)—across 1,539 visitor groups at two museums. Results showed gamified versions significantly increased group discussion frequency and collaborative question-asking, particularly among family groups and when children controlled the device, supporting mobile apps' potential for fostering informal collaborative learning.

title: Modelling diffusion in computer-supported collaborative learning: a large scale learning analytics study
authors: Mohammed Saqr & Sonsoles Lopez-Pernas
summary_haiku: This large-scale study of 69 courses (3,277 students) examines whether diffusion-based network centrality measures capture information exchange and predict academic success in computer-supported collaborative learning. Using meta-analysis across all courses, the research demonstrates that diffusion centralities—measuring how ideas spread through networks—show stronger and more consistent correlations with student achievement than traditional network measures. Clustering analysis identified three student roles: influencers, mediators, and isolates, validated through manual coding of interactions.

title: Self‑efficacy and behavior patterns of learners using a real‑time collaboration system developed for group programming
authors: Ting-Chia Hsu & Hal Abelson & Evan Patton & Shih-Chu Chen & Hsuan-Ning Chang
summary_haiku: This study examined how adult learners' self-efficacy and collaborative behaviors differ when using a real-time collaboration (RTC) system integrated with MIT App Inventor for block-based programming. Using sequential behavior analysis on 13 participants grouped by disciplinary background, researchers found that RTC enabled simultaneous task execution and enhanced communication through annotations. Computer Science majors in homogeneous groups demonstrated significantly higher programming self-efficacy during collaboration than non-majors and heterogeneous groups, though individual versus collaborative self-efficacy remained comparable overall.

title: CSsCL: the performance of collaborative learning
authors: Charles Crook
summary_haiku: This commentary examines three foundational concepts in computer-supported collaborative learning: collaboration scripts, self-regulation, and group awareness. Through analysis of five special issue papers, Crook proposes that regulation operates in layered structures requiring "meta-metacognition," and that group awareness involves both social cognition and intersubjectivity. He reconceptualizes scripted collaboration using a theatre metaphor, emphasizing performance, direction, and audience perspectives to better integrate these concepts within classroom ecosystems.

title: Integrating collaboration scripts, group awareness, and self‑regulation in computer‑supported collaborative learning
authors: Lenka Schnaubert & Freydis Vogel
summary_haiku: This special issue examines three interconnected concepts in computer-supported collaborative learning: group awareness, collaboration scripts, and self-regulation. Through conceptual and empirical papers, the collection explores how these mechanisms—which support learners' social interactions, cognitive processes, and metacognitive monitoring—can be combined to enhance collaborative learning design. The papers demonstrate that integrating these approaches yields more effective CSCL environments than addressing them separately.

title: The impact of scripts on blended and online socially shared regulation of learning: A role‑playing game theory perspective
authors: Clyde A. Warden & Chi-Cheng Chang & James O. Stanworth & Judy F. Chen
summary_haiku: Researchers examined how brief "mere exposure prompts" (MEP) affect collaborative learning in role-playing game simulations across online and blended course formats. Using behavioral trace data and social network analysis with 185 students completing business negotiation tasks, they found MEP scripts significantly influenced planning behaviors in fully online learners but not blended learners, despite both groups recalling the prompt message. Results suggest online environments enable script-based interventions more effectively than traditional classroom settings.

title: The mechanism and effect of class-wide peer feedback on conceptual knowledge improvement: Does different feedback type matter?
authors: Jesmine S. H. Tan & Wenli Chen & Junzhu Su & Guo Su
summary_haiku: Class-wide peer feedback in computer-supported collaborative learning significantly improved students' conceptual knowledge about biological adaptations. Using mixed methods with 38 sixth-graders, researchers found that feedback seeking clarity and providing suggestions yielded highest response rates and knowledge improvement. Elaborated comments with moderate depth were most effective, while excessive elaboration proved cognitively demanding. Results demonstrate that intergroup peer feedback supports knowledge advancement when group-level cognitive capacity is maximized.

title: Does matching peers at finer‑grained levels of prior performance enhance gains in task performance from peer review?
authors: Zheng Zong & Christian D. Schunn
summary_haiku: This study examined whether matching peer reviewers and authors by four performance levels (rather than binary high/low) enhances task performance gains in online peer feedback. Using regression analysis on 766 biology students across multiple assignments, results revealed that providing feedback to same-level peers benefits reviewers, while receiving feedback shows mixed effects. Simulations indicated that performance-based matching algorithms produce better cumulative outcomes than random assignment across all student performance levels.

title: Promoting knowledge building through meta‑discourse and epistemic discourse understanding
authors: Yuyao Tong & Carol K. K. Chan
summary_haiku: # Summary This quasi-experimental study examined how meta-discourse—students' reflection on and inquiry into their collaborative discourse—promotes epistemic discourse understanding and productive knowledge-building inquiry. Ninth-grade visual arts students (n=63) in two classes used Knowledge Forum for online collaboration. The experimental class engaged in classroom meta-discourse reflecting on discourse processes, principles, and idea development, while the comparison class used regular discussion. Results showed experimental students developed deeper epistemic discourse understanding and domain knowledge, engaged in more sophisticated knowledge-building discourse moves, and demonstrated stronger relationships between epistemic understanding and productive inquiry, suggesting meta-discourse effectively supports collaborative learning.

title: Exploring students’ immersive VR experiences as resources for collaborative meaning making and learning
authors: Kenneth Silseth & Rolf Steier & Hans Christian Arnseth
summary_haiku: Students viewing a cinematic VR film about exclusion and discrimination, followed by teacher-facilitated group dialogues, experienced the VR as highly social. Through interaction analysis of reflective dialogues, researchers identified four dimensions characterizing meaning-making: feeling part of conversations, attending to others' bodily expressions, students' own bodily responses, and teacher guidance. The study demonstrates how immersive VR experiences become collaborative learning resources when integrated into structured activity sequences emphasizing dialogue.

title: Situating CoWeb: a scholarship of application
authors: Jochen Rick & Mark Guzdial
summary_haiku: Researchers developed CoWeb, a wiki-based platform for collaborative learning, and deployed it across diverse academic contexts at Georgia Tech. Through design-based research, they found that collaborative learning success depends critically on cultural compatibility: CoWeb succeeded in architecture and composition where collaboration aligned with disciplinary values, but failed in STEM courses due to competitive cultures. By redesigning an introductory computing course around collaborative principles, they overcame these barriers, demonstrating that culture can be intentionally shaped to support technology adoption.

title: Knowledge-building activity structures in Japanese elementary science pedagogy
authors: Jun Oshima & Ritsuko Oshima & Isao Murayama & Shigenori Inagaki & Makiko Takenaka & Tomokazu Yamamoto & Etsuji Yamaguchi & Hayashi Nakayama
summary_haiku: # Summary This design study examined how to transform Japanese elementary science classrooms into knowledge-building communities by integrating traditional activity structures with CSCL technology. Across two consecutive years, researchers refined lesson designs using Knowledge Forum to support idea-centered, collaborative inquiry. Results showed that improving task authenticity and participatory structures—particularly blending online and offline communication—significantly enhanced students' collective knowledge advancement and engagement with conceptual artifacts compared to initial implementations.

title: Knowledge building in mathematics: Supporting collaborative learning in pattern problems
authors: Joan Moss & Ruth Beatty
summary_haiku: Grade 4 students using Knowledge Forum, a collaborative online platform, demonstrated sophisticated mathematical reasoning when solving pattern generalization problems. Students found multiple algebraic rules per problem, revised their conjectures over weeks, and increasingly provided detailed justifications—behaviors rarely observed in traditional instruction. Knowledge-building principles of epistemic agency and idea improvement fostered this inquiry orientation, with students spontaneously recognizing structural similarities across problems.

title: A rating scheme for assessing the quality of computer-supported collaboration processes
authors: Anne Meier & Hans Spada & Nikol Rummel
summary_haiku: Researchers developed a nine-dimension rating scheme for assessing computer-supported collaboration quality by combining qualitative analysis of student dialogue with theoretical frameworks. Applied to 40 dyads solving interdisciplinary patient cases via videoconferencing, the scheme demonstrated satisfactory inter-rater reliability and successfully detected instructional effects on collaboration processes, offering an efficient alternative to time-consuming transcription-based coding methods.

title: Supporting students’ participation in authentic proof activities in computer supported collaborative learning (CSCL) environments
authors: Diler Oner
summary_haiku: This paper proposes integrating dynamic geometry software with knowledge-building pedagogy in CSCL environments to support high school students' mathematical proof activities. The author argues that proof instruction should incorporate both empirical exploration and deductive reasoning, reflecting authentic mathematical practice. The study recommends software modifications, particularly adding shared dynamic geometry components and problematizing mechanisms, to help students distinguish between empirical conviction and formal proof while engaging in collaborative knowledge construction.

title: Learning to collaborate while being scripted or by observing a model
authors: Nikol Rummel & Hans Spada & Sabine Hauser
summary_haiku: Observing a worked-out collaboration model with elaboration support proved most effective for improving computer-mediated collaborative problem-solving among medical and psychology students. Using an experimental design with five conditions, researchers found that model-based learning outperformed scripted collaboration on process quality and knowledge measures. Results challenge the prevailing positive view of collaboration scripts in CSCL research, suggesting adaptive scripting approaches instead.

title: Collaborative corrections with spelling control: Digital resources and peer assistance
authors: Asta Cekaite
summary_haiku: Swedish eighth-graders collaboratively corrected spelling errors using Microsoft Word's spellchecker during English writing tasks. Through conversation analysis of video-recorded sessions, the study identified how diagnostic tools and spelling lists configured different correction practices. Students preferentially used diagnostic feedback for autonomous problem-solving before requesting peer assistance or spelling suggestions, demonstrating that underspecified software instructions created space for creative collaborative engagement and language learning.

title: Computer-supported argumentation: A review of the state of the art
authors: Oliver Scheuer & Frank Loll & Niels Pinkwart & Bruce M. McLaren
summary_haiku: Computer-supported argumentation systems have evolved over 15-20 years to support and teach argumentation skills across domains. This literature review examines 50 systems, analyzing argument representations, interaction designs, ontologies, automated analysis techniques, and empirical findings. Key results show that visual representations and structured interaction designs improve argumentative discourse, while macro-level pedagogical scripts enhance learning outcomes. However, conflicting empirical results reveal the need for comprehensive theoretical frameworks and systematic comparative studies.

title: Mr. Vetro: A Collective Simulation for teaching health science
authors: Andri Ioannidou & Alexander Repenning & David Webb & Diane Keyser & Lisa Luhn & Christof Daetwyler
summary_haiku: Mr. Vetro is a collective simulation where students collaboratively control physiological organs on networked computers to learn about system interactions. Formal evaluation across 400 high school students demonstrated significant learning gains in physiological knowledge and vocabulary, increased inquiry-based teaching practices, and positive real-life health behavior changes, though attitudes toward science remained relatively stable.

title: Animation and grammar in science education: Learners’ construal of animated educational software
authors: Goran Karlsson
summary_haiku: This case study examines how two upper-secondary students collaboratively interpret animated biochemical processes through written reports. Using interaction analysis of video-recorded sessions, the research reveals that students' grammatically constructed narratives prioritize perceptually salient animated features as active subjects, deriving noun phrases from animation and educational text while substituting verbs with everyday language. Without sufficient subject-matter knowledge, students cannot evaluate adequacy and rely solely on grammatical correctness, resulting in non-scientific explanations. The findings emphasize that technology-supported science education requires consideration of both cultural and semiotic processes.

title: Bridging research and practice: Implementing and sustaining knowledge building in Hong Kong classrooms
authors: Carol K. K. Chan
summary_haiku: # Summary This article examines how computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) research translates into classroom practice through a case study of knowledge-building implementation in Hong Kong schools. Using design-based research across macro (policy), meso (teacher networks), and micro (classroom) levels, the study identifies three critical themes: systemic alignment across educational levels, capacity building through principle-based teacher communities, and innovation as continuous inquiry. Findings demonstrate that sustained CSCL adoption requires coordinating institutional policies, teacher professional development networks, and classroom design while adapting research models to local socio-cultural contexts.

title: Multi-touch tables and the relationship with collaborative classroom pedagogies: A synthetic review
authors: Steven E. Higgins & Emma Mercier & Elizabeth Burd & Andrew Hatch
summary_haiku: Multi-touch tables offer significant potential for supporting collaborative classroom learning through their design features. This synthetic review proposes a typology categorizing hardware characteristics—surface geometry and display type, touch sensing capabilities, and connectivity—to analyze how technical affordances align with pedagogical goals. Evidence suggests horizontal multi-touch surfaces enable more equitable participation and task-focused interaction than traditional single-touch technologies, though text entry limitations and teacher orchestration challenges require further investigation.

title: Making rounds: The routine work of the teacher during collaborative learning with computers
authors: Christian Greiffenhagen
summary_haiku: This ethnomethodological study analyzes teacher interventions during collaborative computer-based learning using video recordings of English lessons with storyboarding software. Through detailed conversation analysis of naturally occurring classroom interactions, the author identifies five types of teacher practices: ratifying pupil work, reminding pupils of task requirements, making suggestions for improvement, maintaining classroom control, and making whole-class announcements. The analysis reveals that classroom management and pedagogy are intertwined rather than separate, and tensions between teacher and pupil perspectives are collaborative rather than antagonistic.

title: How gamers manage aggression: Situating skills in collaborative computer games
authors: Ulrika Bennerstedt & Jonas Ivarsson & Jonas Linderoth
summary_haiku: Using ethnomethodological analysis of boss encounters in a massively multiplayer online game, this study examines skills gamers develop during collaborative gameplay involving portrayed aggression. The researchers found that "aggression" and "collaboration" manifest as highly specialized, game-specific practices—particularly aggro management—rather than transferable general skills. The analysis challenges assumptions underlying both positive and negative gaming effects research, arguing that claims about behavioral transfer require explicit theoretical justification and risk oversimplification.

title: How to improve collaborative learning with video tools in the classroom? Social vs. cognitive guidance for student teams
authors: Carmen Zahn & Karsten Krauskopf & Friedrich W. Hesse & Roy Pea
summary_haiku: Social interaction-related guidance proved more effective than cognitive task-related guidance for student teams using video tools in collaborative history learning. In a 2×2 experimental design with 148 sixteen-year-old students, teams receiving guidance emphasizing communication norms and cooperation demonstrated superior learning outcomes in historical skills and design product quality, regardless of video tool type. Results suggest focusing instructional support on group dynamics rather than task procedures.

title: Interactive visual tools as triggers of collaborative reasoning in entry-level pathology
authors: Markus Nivala & Hans Rystedt & Roger Saljo & Pauliina Kronqvist & Erno Lehtinen
summary_haiku: Virtual microscopy enables collaborative pathology learning through multimodal referential practices. This qualitative video analysis of 15 medical student pairs examined how interactive visual tools mediate diagnostic reasoning. Students organized shared visual fields using gestures, zooming, and paced negotiations to construct joint understanding. Key strategies included framing diagnostic processes, negotiating visual evidence, and extending reasoning frames when uncertain. The study demonstrates that technology becomes constitutive of face-to-face collaboration, and understanding image production techniques proves integral to medical interpretation.

title: Multi-player epistemic games: Guiding the enactment of classroom knowledge-building communities
authors: Katerine Bielaczyc & John Ow
summary_haiku: Researchers extended epistemic games—strategic knowledge-building practices—to "multi-player" versions where students collectively advance ideas through distributed contributions in Knowledge Forum. Using design-based research in Singapore primary science classrooms, they developed scaffolding tools (Think Cards and hypothetical game-configurations) to help students learn the Progressive-Improvement Game. Analyses showed students improved significantly in generating valid knowledge-building moves, supporting classroom enactment of knowledge-building communities.

title: Contemporary intellectual structure of CSCL research (2006–2013): a co-citation network analysis with an education focus
authors: Kai-Yu Tang & Chin-Chung Tsai & Tzu-Chiang Lin
summary_haiku: This study employed document co-citation analysis, exploratory factor analysis, and social network analysis to map the intellectual structure of CSCL research (2006–2013). Analyzing 403 source papers and 5,351 citing articles, researchers identified six research subfields: representation and discourse patterns, factors influencing CSCL, intervention and comparison, critical reasoning, social construction processes, and design and modeling. Results revealed seminal works and core publications, with representation and discourse emerging as the dominant research stream, demonstrating the field's maturity and interconnectedness.

title: The new information literate: Open collaboration and information production in schools
authors: Andrea Forte
summary_haiku: This qualitative study examined high school students' information assessment practices while contributing to a collaborative online wiki. Through 57 interviews and classroom observations, the researcher identified two information literacy strategies: first-order strategies involving established heuristics for evaluating sources, and second-order strategies involving reflective analysis of how information is produced. Findings reveal that participating in information production enhanced students' understanding of source credibility and fostered individual responsibility for contributing accurate information to public resources.

title: Whoa! We’re going deep in the trees!: Patterns of collaboration around an interactive information visualization exhibit
authors: Pryce Davis & Michael Horn & Florian Block & Brenda Phillips & E. Margaret Evans & Judy Diamond & Chia Shen
summary_haiku: This study analyzed how child dyads collaboratively explored DeepTree, an interactive multi-touch tabletop exhibit visualizing 70,000+ species in a phylogenetic tree. Using qualitative interaction analysis of museum visitors, researchers identified four distinct collaboration patterns organized by coordination level and action target: reactive, autonomous, planning, and contemplative. Results showed that DeepTree supported learning of macroevolutionary concepts like common descent, with design features like the "fly-through" mechanic facilitating meaning-making across different interaction patterns.

title: Group-level formative feedback and metadiscourse
authors: Monica Resendes & Marlene Scardamalia & Carl Bereiter & Bodong Chen & Cindy Halewood
summary_haiku: Grade 2 students engaged in knowledge building with visualization-based formative feedback tools showed significant improvements in domain vocabulary use, scientific accuracy, explanation complexity, and discourse connectivity compared to a comparison class. Using comparative word clouds and epistemic discourse move graphs, students demonstrated productive metadiscourse—reflection on their collective knowledge-building process—though primarily with teacher facilitation, suggesting young children possess greater metacognitive capacity than typically assumed.

title: AMOEBA: Designing for collaboration in computer science classrooms through live learning analytics
authors: Matthew Berland & Don Davis & Carmen Petrick Smith
summary_haiku: AMOEBA is a learning analytics tool designed to support teachers in orchestrating real-time collaboration among novice programmers using the IPRO visual programming environment. The study examined how pairing students based on a "surprising similarity" metric—operationalizing Zone of Proximal Development for computer science—affected programming outcomes across eight classes. Results showed that paired students produced programs with greater complexity, depth, and novelty compared to unpaired work, with improvements persisting after pairing ended.

title: Reflective assessment in knowledge building by students with low academic achievement
authors: Yuqin Yang & Jan van Aalst & Carol K. K. Chan & Wen Tian
summary_haiku: Students with low academic achievement engaged in sustained knowledge-building discourse when supported by reflective assessment using the Knowledge Connections Analyzer tool. Analysis of 20 Grade 11 visual arts students' online discussions revealed they generated theories, built on peers' ideas, and synthesized concepts. Reflective assessment helped students focus on knowledge-building goals including community collaboration, idea improvement, and synthesis, demonstrating that low-achieving students can successfully participate in higher-order collaborative inquiry.

title: Group practices: a new way of viewing CSCL
authors: Gerry Stahl
summary_haiku: Stahl proposes analyzing group practices—observable, routinized behaviors enacted by small collaborative teams—as central to understanding computer-supported collaborative learning. Using design-based research with the Virtual Math Teams project, he demonstrates that groups adopt practices through breakdowns and negotiation, mediating between individual cognition and cultural knowledge. This approach provides systematic methodology for CSCL design, theory, and analysis beyond traditional pre/post comparisons.

title: Experiences, appearances, and interprofessional training: The instructional use of video in post-simulation debriefings
authors: Oskar Lindwall & Hans Rystedt & Elin Johansson
summary_haiku: This study uses conversation analysis to examine 40 video-supported debriefings following simulation-based healthcare training. The research reveals that video enables students to discuss their interprofessional teamwork from a third-person perspective, while facilitators' instructional questions guide students to reconceptualize their performance by contrasting audiovisual appearances with their subjective experiences, facilitating collaborative sense-making about professional conduct.

title: Cracking her codes: understanding shared technology resources as positioning artifacts for power and status in CSCL environments
authors: Amber Simpson & Nicole Bannister & Gretchen Matthews
summary_haiku: Researchers used positioning theory and interaction analysis to examine how two pairs of female students negotiated power and status around shared technology during cryptography tasks. Analysis revealed that technology control functioned as a positioning artifact reflecting and reinforcing power dynamics: one pair exhibited stark dominance limiting participation, while the other showed subtle status imbalances without apparent learning impact. The study concludes that interactions around technology serve as critical indicators of negotiated power and status in collaborative learning environments.

title: Leveraging mobile eye-trackers to capture joint visual attention in co-located collaborative learning groups
authors: Kshitij Sharma & Bertrand Schneider & Sebastien Cuendet & Guillaume Zufferey & Pierre Dillenbourg & Roy Pea
summary_haiku: Mobile eye-trackers reveal that joint visual attention correlates with collaborative learning quality in co-located dyads, but high coordination alone doesn't guarantee learning. Qualitative analysis of two high-coordination groups showed that imbalanced participation—where one student dominates initiating joint attention—predicts lower learning gains, suggesting that productive collaboration requires balanced visual leadership between partners.

title: Why and how do middle school students exchange ideas during science inquiry?
authors: Camillia Matuk
summary_haiku: This study investigates how the Idea Manager tool supports middle school students' peer idea exchange during science inquiry on cancer and cell division. Using the Knowledge Integration framework with 297 grade 7 students, researchers found that students generated more ideas independently than copying peers' ideas, and that collecting redundant self-generated ideas correlated with higher-quality scientific explanations, contrary to expectations favoring diverse ideas. Teachers reported enhanced formative assessment capabilities through monitoring student progress.

title: Improving the quality of vocational students’ collaboration and knowledge acquisition through instruction and joint reflection
