authors: Judith ter Vrugte & Anjo Anjewierden & Lars Bollen & Elise H. Eshuis & Jakob Sikken & Ton de Jong
summary_haiku: Combining conventional instruction with an online reflection tool incorporating self-assessment, peer feedback, and goal-setting significantly improved vocational students' collaborative behavior and knowledge acquisition in computer-supported learning environments. Analysis of chat logs and knowledge tests from 198 first-year technical students revealed that instruction alone proved ineffective, but instruction paired with the reflection tool fostered higher-quality collaboration and superior learning outcomes compared to control conditions.

title: Towards a micro-ecological approach to CSCL
authors: Marcela Borge
summary_haiku: # Summary Current CSCL theories prioritize single-level analysis, limiting understanding of complex orchestration processes. This paper proposes a micro-ecological framework analyzing interactions across individual, group, and classroom levels simultaneously. Through a design club case study, the authors identify "transecological disruptions"—critical moments where actions at one level propagate across levels—demonstrating how this approach reveals orchestration complexity and learning opportunities that traditional single-level analyses miss.

title: Capturing the dynamic and cyclical nature of regulation: Methodological Progress in understanding socially shared regulation in learning
authors: Hanna Jarvenoja
summary_haiku: This review examines methodological progress in researching socially shared regulation (SSRL) of learning in collaborative and computer-supported collaborative learning contexts. The authors identify three key challenges: capturing regulation's cyclical, temporal nature; understanding how self-regulation, co-regulation, and SSRL jointly contribute to learning; and studying SSRL in authentic contexts. They advocate for multimodal data collection methods, technological tools for prompting regulation, and analyzing learning challenges as triggers for regulatory processes.

title: Give student ideas a larger stage: support cross-community interaction for knowledge building
authors: Guangji Yuan & Maria Bogouslavsky & Jianwei Zhang
summary_haiku: Two grade 5/6 science classrooms engaged in knowledge building about human body systems using Knowledge Forum over ten weeks. Students created "super notes"—synthesized summaries of inquiry progress—as epistemic boundary objects shared in a cross-classroom meta-space. Qualitative analysis revealed students conceived super notes as refined, accessible "big ideas" reflecting their learning journey. Super notes facilitated cross-community interaction, enabling students to encounter diverse perspectives, deepen inquiry, and develop integrated system-level understandings, demonstrating how scaling CSCL practices across classrooms fosters high-level epistemic engagement.

title: Gaze awareness and metacognitive suggestions by a pedagogical conversational agent: an experimental investigation on interventions to support collaborative learning process and performance
authors: Yugo Hayashi
summary_haiku: A 2×2 experimental study examined how real-time gaze feedback and pedagogical conversational agent suggestions independently and jointly affect collaborative learning. Eighty dyads completed a knowledge integration task while receiving various combinations of these interventions. Results showed gaze feedback more effectively facilitated coordination processes, while agent suggestions better improved learning gains. Combined interventions produced synergistic effects on performance, with successful coordination strongly predicting learning outcomes only when both supports were present.

title: Social sensitivity: a manifesto for CSCL research
authors: Jaana Isohatala & Piia Naykki & Sanna Jarvela & Michael J. Baker & Kristine Lund
summary_haiku: Current educational technologies inadequately support collaborative learning as both cognitive and socio-emotional processes, risking hindered idea exchange and negative interactions. This manifesto argues CSCL research is fragmented across theoretical silos, failing to communicate coherent evidence to practitioners and developers. The authors propose "social sensitivity"—an interdisciplinary framework emphasizing constructively critical, respectful, and cohesive collaboration—and call for concrete actions: crossing theoretical boundaries, conducting multimodal empirical research, and transferring evidence to educational practices and policies.

title: Agency to transform: how did a grade 5 community co‑configure dynamic knowledge building practices in a yearlong science inquiry?
authors: Dan Tao & Jianwei Zhang
summary_haiku: This study investigates how a fifth-grade science classroom co-configured dynamic knowledge-building practices through "reflective structuration"—a process where students and teacher collaboratively constructed and adapted shared inquiry structures over a yearlong human body systems investigation. Using qualitative analysis of classroom observations, online discourse, and student artifacts, researchers documented how students co-formulated nine evolving "big questions" that guided inquiry directions. Analysis revealed students' agentic moves expanded, deepened, and reframed collective work, with social network analysis and pre-post testing demonstrating productive knowledge building outcomes and improved scientific understanding.

title: The trade‑off between individuals and groups: role interactions under different technology affordance conditions
authors: Cixiao Wang & Shuling Li
summary_haiku: This study examined how technology affordances—specifically device-to-student ratios (1:1 versus 1:m) and external scripts—influence role-based interactions during collaborative scientific inquiry. Using thematic analysis, descriptive statistics, and social network analysis with 130 fifth-grade students across three inquiry experiments, researchers identified eleven emergent roles organized into five categories. Key findings revealed that limited technology resources and external scripts promoted collective awareness, while personal device ownership encouraged individual-focused behavior. Stable group action orientations facilitated better coordination and learning outcomes, though close interaction density did not guarantee collaborative effectiveness.

title: Many are the ways to learn identifying multi-modal behavioral profiles of collaborative learning in constructivist activities
authors: Jauwairia Nasir & Aditi Kothiyal & Barbara Bruno
summary_haiku: This study identifies three distinct multi-modal behavioral profiles of dyads engaged in collaborative open-ended learning with interactive tabletops and a robot mediator. Using combined learning analytics and interaction analysis on video, audio, and log data from 32 teams, researchers discovered two learning profiles—Expressive Explorers and Calm Tinkerers—and one non-learning profile, Silent Wanderers. Key findings reveal that speech overlap and reflection behaviors strongly distinguish learners from non-learners, while problem-solving strategy interacts with emotional expressivity to characterize different pathways to learning.

title: Patterns of action transitions in online collaborative problem solving: A network analysis approach
authors: Shupin Li & Johanna Poysa-Tarhonen & Paivi Hakkinen
summary_haiku: This study examined 166 Finnish sixth graders' action transition patterns during computer-based collaborative problem-solving using social network analysis. Researchers created transition networks from log file data and calculated network measures including density, centralization, and reciprocity. Results showed pairs with at least one member possessing high social and cognitive skills conducted significantly more actions with higher transition frequencies, suggesting more productive collaborative problem-solving than other pair compositions.

title: Cross-community knowledge building with idea thread mapper
authors: Guangji Yuan & Jianwei Zhang & Mei-Hwa Chen
summary_haiku: # Summary This design-based research study investigated how four Grade 5 classrooms collaboratively built knowledge about human body systems using the Idea Thread Mapper (ITM) platform. Students engaged in local classroom inquiry while generating "super notes"—reflective syntheses—shared in a cross-community meta-space. Through cross-classroom "Super Talk" discussions on how people grow, students integrated diverse ideas from multiple classrooms into sophisticated, multifaceted understandings. Results demonstrated that students produced high-quality reflections and that cross-community collaboration created expansive learning contexts enabling knowledge advancement across social levels.

title: Evolution of the academic emotions of academically low‑achieving students in knowledge building
authors: Yuqin Yang & Gaoxia Zhu & Carol K. K. Chan
summary_haiku: Low-achieving secondary students engaged in Knowledge Building through Knowledge Forum exhibited predominantly positive emotions, with joy comprising 53% of expressed emotions. Sequential pattern analysis revealed emotions tend to transition to similar emotions, and five primary emotional evolution paths emerged, with confusion serving as a critical juncture determining whether students progress toward joy or negative emotions like boredom and frustration.

title: Coordinating modalities of mathematical collaboration in shared VR environments
authors: Wen Huang & Candace Walkington & Mitchell J. Nathan
summary_haiku: This study examines how in-service teachers collaboratively construct geometric knowledge in shared VR environments using a novel multimodal analysis method. Analyzing 108 episodes across three groups, researchers identified strong simultaneous relationships between actions on virtual objects and collaborative speech, plus five emergent interaction themes. Results demonstrate that virtual objects effectively mediate collaborative knowledge-building, with structured activity design and moderate avatar realism supporting equitable, adaptable learning.

title: Mobile augmented reality supporting families’ immersive collaborative learning: Learning‑on‑the‑move for place‑based geoscience sense‑making
authors: Heather Toomey Zimmerman & Susan M. Land & Lillyanna Faimon & Yu-Chen Chiu
summary_haiku: This study investigated how families experienced immersion while using a mobile augmented reality app called Time Explorers to collaboratively learn about geologic time and geoscience processes during outdoor learning-on-the-move. Using interaction analysis of video recordings and interviews from 17 families (51 participants), researchers found that sensory and social immersion supported sense-making conversations and observational inquiry, while narrative and actional immersion enabled deep engagement with geoscience content about rock-water interactions shaping Appalachia.

title: Common “place” observations about embodiment and CSCL
authors: Victor R. Lee
summary_haiku: This commentary examines embodied computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) by arguing that shared physical or digital "place" is central to how multiple bodies coordinate learning. Unlike earlier embodied learning research focusing on individual sensorimotor experience, embodied CSCL leverages three key resources: differing relative perspectives, body motion/gesture, and common referents. The author proposes that foregrounding place in future embodied CSCL research and design could advance understanding of how technology mediates collaborative meaning-making among co-located learners.

title: Understanding the effect of differences in prior knowledge on middle school students’ collaborative interactions and learning
authors: Sadhana Puntambekar & Dana Gnesdilow & Sinan Yavuz
summary_haiku: # Summary This study examined how prior knowledge variance within collaborative groups affects middle school students' science learning and interactions. Using hierarchical linear modeling on 102 groups and social network analysis of two contrasting groups, researchers found that students in homogeneous groups achieved significantly greater learning gains than those in heterogeneous groups. Qualitative analysis revealed homogeneous groups exhibited more distributed, reciprocal interactions with mutual scaffolding, while heterogeneous groups showed centralized interactions dominated by the highest-knowledge member, resulting in lower engagement and learning for less-knowledgeable peers.

title: Students’ use of technological tools to engage in collective mathematical proof activity
authors: Tenchita Alzaga Elizondo & David Brown
summary_haiku: Using instrumental genesis theory, this study examined how students in a remote introduction to proofs course operationalized Google Docs and Zoom to engage in collaborative proof activity. Analysis of six episodes revealed students developed collective utilization schemes coordinating visual mediators with verbal communication to enable collective argumentation and co-construct solutions through iterative text refinement. Google Docs' simultaneous editing and referencing features particularly supported active, process-oriented proof writing.

title: Contesting sociocomputational norms: Computer programming instructors and students’ stancetaking around refactoring
authors: Morgan M. Fong & David DeLiema & Virginia J. Flood & Oia Walker-van Aalst
summary_haiku: This interaction analysis study examines how elementary and middle school students and instructors negotiate refactoring—revising working code—in a programming workshop. Using stancetaking, sociocomputational norms, and inequity frameworks, researchers analyzed 20 minutes of classroom discourse. Findings reveal that while students initially debated coding approaches, instructors progressively endorsed loops as superior, amplifying relational inequity by devaluing alternative strategies and limiting discussion of efficiency's multiple interpretations.

title: Correction: Contesting sociocomputational norms: computer programming instructors and students’ stancetaking around refactoring
authors: Morgan M. Fong & David DeLiema & Virginia J. Flood & Oia Walker-van Aalst
summary_haiku: This correction clarifies a discrepancy in the theoretical framework section of an interaction analysis study examining how computer programming instructors and students contest sociocomputational norms through classroom discourse. The researchers use stancetaking analysis to investigate participatory and relational inequities without assuming participants' inner experiences, focusing on how meanings are publicly negotiated.

title: Disagreeing softly: Supporting students in managing disagreement in peer critique
authors: Jinzhi Zhou & Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver & Zach Ryan & Christina Stiso & Danielle Murphy & Joshua Danish & Clark A. Chinn & Ravit Golan Duncan
summary_haiku: Fifth-grade students engaged in peer critique within a computer-supported collaborative learning environment predominantly used soft disagreements (64%) rather than direct forms when critiquing groupmates' scientific models. Using conversation analysis, researchers found that students effectively resolved disagreements consensually in 88.6% of episodes, advancing collective knowledge through both direct and soft disagreement forms, while maintaining positive group dynamics.

title: Collaborative science? Formalism and a unified language: Future directions for computer‑supported collaborative learning
authors: Sten Ludvigsen & Hans C. Arnseth & Kenneth Silseth & Rolf Steier
summary_haiku: # Summary This article responds to calls for unified language and formalism in computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL). Rather than endorsing computational modeling approaches, the authors propose a meta-stance centered on learning mechanisms that integrate cognitive, socio-cognitive, and sociocultural perspectives. They advocate for analyzing moment-by-moment meaning-making through dialogue, mediational tools, and meaning potentials, arguing this approach better captures collaborative learning processes than probabilistic models alone. The authors present an exchange structure formalism and emphasize mechanistic causality in qualitative research to build cumulative CSCL knowledge.

title: Collaborative knowledge building using the Design Principles Database
authors: Yael Kali
summary_haiku: The Design Principles Database (DPD) supports collaborative knowledge building among educational technology researchers through a structured system of interconnected design features and principles at multiple abstraction levels. Using design-based research methodology across three iterations of a peer-evaluation activity, the study demonstrates how researchers extract principles from literature, test them in practice, and contribute refined knowledge back to the community database, exemplifying second-order collaborative learning environments.

title: Consistent practices in artifact-mediated collaboration
authors: Nathan Dwyer & Daniel D. Suthers
summary_haiku: This study examined how dyads collaboratively solve problems using flexible paper-based media while restricted to written communication. Through video analysis of six pairs discussing wicked problems, researchers identified invariant communicative practices across different materials and participants. Despite varied interaction styles and artifacts, consistent patterns emerged in managing attention, awareness, and ownership of contributions. Findings challenge conventional CSCL design assumptions and suggest that effective collaborative technologies should support flexible semiotic resources rather than rigid representational structures.

title: Supporting collaborative learning and problem-solving in a constraint-based CSCL environment for UML class diagrams
authors: Nilufar Baghaei & Antonija Mitrovic & Warwick Irwin
summary_haiku: COLLECT-UML is a constraint-based intelligent tutoring system that teaches UML class diagram design while supporting collaborative learning. Using meta-constraints to model collaboration alongside domain constraints, the system provides feedback on both problem-solving and teamwork. Evaluation studies with 48 students showed significant improvements in UML knowledge and collaboration skills, with experimental group participants acquiring greater declarative knowledge about effective collaboration and demonstrating more balanced, active participation.

title: What does it mean? Students’ procedural and conceptual problem solving in a CSCL environment designed within the field of science education
authors: Ingeborg Krange & Sten Ludvigsen
summary_haiku: This study examined procedural versus conceptual problem-solving in a CSCL environment where secondary students built a 3D insulin protein model using a codon table. Through interaction analysis of video-recorded collaborative sessions, researchers found that procedural problem-solving dominated student interactions, while conceptual knowledge construction occurred only when necessary for task completion. The authors conclude that institutional pressures to complete curriculum-based problems, combined with how the knowledge domain and tools were designed, prioritized procedural efficiency over deeper scientific understanding.

title: Annotations and the collaborative digital library: Effects of an aligned annotation interface on student argumentation and reading strategies
authors: Joanna Wolfe
summary_haiku: Aligned annotation interfaces—where reader comments appear in text margins—significantly enhance student critical thinking and argumentation. Two complementary studies found that annotations, particularly pairs presenting conflicting viewpoints, prompted students to move beyond passive comprehension toward active evaluation and perspective-taking. Students receiving annotated materials demonstrated reduced reliance on summary strategies and greater engagement with competing positions, suggesting annotations provide valuable scaffolding for developing critical reading and writing practices.

title: Exploring embedded guidance and self-efficacy in educational multi-user virtual environments
authors: Brian C. Nelson & Diane Jass Ketelhut
summary_haiku: This exploratory study examined how student self-efficacy in scientific inquiry affects guidance system use and learning outcomes in River City, an educational multi-user virtual environment. Using a sample of 96 middle school students, researchers found that students with low self-efficacy viewed significantly fewer guidance messages than higher-efficacy peers. While embedded reflective guidance improved learning across all efficacy levels, it only partially mitigated low self-efficacy's negative impact on performance. Notably, low-efficacy students with heavy guidance use achieved comparable outcomes to high-efficacy students without guidance.

title: Productive failure in CSCL groups
authors: Manu Kapur & Charles K. Kinzer
summary_haiku: Groups solving unstructured physics problems without support struggled initially but subsequently outperformed peers who solved well-structured problems on individual transfer tasks. This confirmatory study with 177 eleventh-grade students demonstrates productive failure: complex, divergent collaborative processes seemingly leading to failure paradoxically enhanced later problem-solving performance, suggesting that the nature of collaborative interaction rather than prior knowledge or solution quality drives learning gains.

title: The power of natural frameworks: Technology and the question of agency in CSCL settings
authors: Annika Lantz-Andersson
summary_haiku: # Summary This study analyzes how secondary school students frame computer-supported collaborative learning situations using video analysis of mathematics problem-solving with educational software. Results reveal students shift between social frameworks where they assume responsibility for understanding tasks and natural frameworks where they attribute difficulties to technology design. When receiving incorrect feedback without explanation, students often cease engaging with mathematical reasoning and instead attempt procedural workarounds, potentially avoiding accountability for learning while preserving self-esteem.

title: A knowledge-practice perspective on technology-mediated learning
authors: Kai Hakkarainen
doi: A knowledge-practice perspective on technology-mediated learning
summary_haiku: Technology enhances learning through transformed social practices, not merely through tool implementation. While knowledge-building theory emphasizes idea advancement, this perspective argues that genuine educational transformation requires cultivating epistemic practices—socially embedded ways of working with knowledge—that channel intellectual efforts toward collective knowledge advancement. Material artifacts and social practices constitute dialectical unity in knowledge creation.

title: Contrasting the use of tools for presentation and critique: Some cases from architectural education
authors: Gustav Lymer & Jonas Ivarsson & Oskar Lindwall
summary_haiku: This ethnomethodological video analysis of architectural design reviews examines how presentation technologies shape critique practices. Comparing poster-based, digital slideshow, and hybrid setups across 143 sessions, the study reveals that digital technologies fundamentally transform sequential organization, shared attention, and part-whole relations during discussion and assessment. The findings suggest that presentation tools designed primarily for delivery may inadequately support subsequent critique, highlighting the need for spatially organized interfaces better suited to collaborative design review practices.

title: Toward a dialectic relation between the results in CSCL: Three critical methodological aspects of content analysis schemes
authors: Marc Clara & Teresa Mauri
summary_haiku: This paper proposes a framework of indicators based on three critical methodological aspects—units of analysis, relations between theoretical levels, and dimensions of analysis—to facilitate reciprocal positioning of content analysis results in CSCL research. Rather than seeking theoretical integration across diverse approaches, the authors argue for dialectical relations that reveal tensions and enable mutual theoretical development within the field's inherent methodological diversity.

title: Promoting metacognitive skills through peer scaffolding in a CSCL environment
authors: Manoli Pifarre & Ruth Cobos
summary_haiku: A longitudinal case study of 18 university students using the KnowCat knowledge-building system over two semesters examined how peer scaffolding develops metacognitive skills in computer-supported collaborative learning. Content analysis of student annotations revealed statistically significant increases in metacognitive processes, particularly in monitoring and clarity-seeking behaviors. Results suggest pedagogical use of CSCL environments with structured peer feedback effectively enhances students' self-regulation and collaborative problem-solving capabilities.

title: Scaffolding problem-based learning with CSCL tools
authors: Jingyan Lu & Susanne P. Lajoie & Jeffrey Wiseman
summary_haiku: Interactive whiteboards fundamentally altered teacher scaffolding in medical problem-based learning. This case study compared traditional whiteboard versus interactive whiteboard conditions during deteriorating patient simulations with medical students. Results revealed that interactive whiteboards enabled teachers to visualize all student groups' work simultaneously, allowing them to increase problem complexity and reduce task-structuring guidance. Technology expanded scaffolding choices by externalizing collaborative problem-solving processes.

title: How digital concept maps about the collaborators’ knowledge and information influence computer-supported collaborative problem solving
authors: Tanja Engelmann & Friedrich W. Hesse
summary_haiku: Digital concept maps displaying collaborators' knowledge structures and information resources enhance computer-supported collaborative problem-solving. This experimental study compared 40 triads—20 with access to partners' concept maps and 20 without—on problem-solving tasks. Results demonstrated that groups with map access acquired greater knowledge-and-information awareness, focused on problem-relevant information, and solved problems faster and more accurately than control groups.

title: Revealing preconditions for trustful collaboration in CSCL
authors: Anne Gerdes
summary_haiku: This philosophical analysis examines preconditions for trust in virtual learning environments. Through phenomenological inquiry and case analysis, the author argues that self-surrender—fundamental to human communication—is undermined by surveillance and impression management in online learning systems. Drawing on open-source community models, the study concludes that volunteerism, self-articulation of goals, and inquiry-based teaching methods can foster mastery-oriented learning and authentic collaborative engagement.

title: The Singapore experience: Synergy of national policy, classroom practice and design research
authors: Chee-Kit Looi & Hyo-Jeong So & Yancy Toh & Wenli Chen
summary_haiku: Singapore's systemic approach to CSCL integration demonstrates how design research methodology bridges macro-level policy, meso-level school implementation, and micro-level classroom interactions. Through the GroupScribbles project across multiple schools, researchers co-designed collaborative learning activities with teachers, developed design principles for rapid collaborative knowledge improvement, and achieved sustainable adoption. This multi-level alignment of policy, practice, and research provides a model for scaling CSCL innovations while addressing real classroom constraints.

title: Interactive tabletops in education
authors: Pierre Dillenbourg
summary_haiku: Interactive tabletops support co-located collaborative learning through hands-on manipulation of objects, conveying socio-constructivist pedagogical approaches. This analytical framework examines 33 design considerations across four levels: user-system interaction, teamwork dynamics, classroom orchestration, and socio-cultural contexts. The authors argue that tabletops' educational effectiveness depends on thoughtful design addressing these specific affordances rather than inherent technological properties.

title: Collaboration within large groups in the classroom
authors: Eyal Szewkis & Miguel Nussbaum & Tal Rosen & Jose Abalos & Fernanda Denardin & Daniela Caballero & Arturo Tagle & Cristian Alcoholado
summary_haiku: This study investigates large-group classroom collaboration using Single Display Groupware with multiple mice and minimal hardware. Through an experimental design comparing 42 students using the system for 40% of class time against 32 control students, researchers found that "silent collaboration"—a negotiation mechanism enabling object exchanges—effectively facilitated synchronous learning in Spanish language tasks. Results demonstrated significant learning gains and successful achievement of collaborative conditions, suggesting this low-cost approach enables effective large-group computer-supported collaborative learning.

title: Scaffolding of small groups’ metacognitive activities with an avatar
authors: Inge Molenaar & Ming Ming Chiu & Peter Sleegers & Carla van Boxtel
summary_haiku: Avatar-based metacognitive scaffolding in small group learning environments influences student knowledge acquisition through mediation by metacognitive activities. Multivariate multilevel analysis of 51,339 conversation turns from 54 elementary students revealed that problematizing scaffolds (eliciting student explanations) produced greater domain knowledge than structuring scaffolds (providing examples), with metacognitive activities mediating these effects. Both scaffold types enhanced metacognitive knowledge primarily through increased metacognitive engagement.

title: Linking teacher beliefs, practices and student inquiry-based learning in a CSCL environment: A tale of two teachers
authors: Yangjie Song & Chee-Kit Looi
summary_haiku: Teachers holding innovation-oriented beliefs about inquiry-based learning enacted mathematics lessons with inquiry principle-based practices and technology-enhanced orchestration, while teachers with teacher-centered beliefs used traditional approaches. Comparative case analysis of two teachers using Group Scribbles technology revealed that innovation-oriented beliefs directly shaped progressive inquiry practices, which subsequently fostered student collaborative knowledge construction and effective technology use.

title: Instrumental genesis in technology-mediated learning: From double stimulation to expansive knowledge practices
authors: Giuseppe Ritella & Kai Hakkarainen
summary_haiku: Technology-mediated collaborative learning requires transforming social practices through instrumental genesis—the developmental process of appropriating technological tools as learning instruments. Drawing on sociocultural theory, the authors argue that epistemic mediation through external artifacts enables knowledge creation, but productive integration demands extended iterative efforts reformatting cognitive-cultural operating systems at personal and collective levels, explaining why innovative CSCL practices remain difficult to implement in educational systems.

title: Computational analysis and mapping of ijCSCL content
authors: Jacques Lonchamp
summary_haiku: This empirical study employs co-word analysis to map content in the International Journal of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning (2006-2011). Using hierarchical clustering and multidimensional scaling on full-text corpora, the research identifies three major thematic categories: interaction analysis, technical/organizational issues, and applications. Key findings include dominant themes like scripting, monitoring, community-based learning, and argumentation, revealing the intellectual structure of CSCL research.

title: Using augmented reality and knowledge-building scaffolds to improve learning in a science museum
authors: Susan A. Yoon & Karen Elinich & Joyce Wang & Christopher Steinmeier & Sean Tucker
summary_haiku: A quasi-experimental study examined how augmented reality and knowledge-building scaffolds enhance science learning in a museum setting. Using four conditions with varying levels of digital augmentation and pedagogical support, researchers tested 119 middle-grade students on electrical conductivity concepts. Results showed digital augmentation alone improved conceptual knowledge, while knowledge-building scaffolds combined with augmented reality significantly enhanced students' ability to theorize about scientific phenomena, suggesting collaborative supports amplify technology-based informal learning.

title: On the bridge to learn: Analysing the social organization of nautical instruction in a ship simulator
authors: Magnus Hontvedt & Hans Christian Arnseth
summary_haiku: This qualitative study examines how nautical students collaboratively construct simulated learning contexts through role-play in a ship simulator. Using interaction analysis of video data, the researchers identify two competing activity contexts: students enacting professional crew roles and students participating in educational training. The analysis reveals that while role-play enables situated learning opportunities for professional tasks, maintaining credible simulations requires substantial interactional effort and can conflict with instructional objectives like meta-reflection and debriefing.

title: Student sensemaking with science diagrams in a computer-based setting
authors: Anniken Furberg & Anders Kluge & Sten Ludvigsen
summary_haiku: This study examined how upper secondary students collaboratively made sense of solar panel diagrams in a computer-based learning environment. Using interaction analysis of one student group's expert-group session, researchers found that science diagrams functioned as productive social and cognitive resources, enabling students to slow conceptual reasoning and negotiate scientific meanings. However, students faced significant challenges translating oral accounts into written explanations and coordinating multiple diagram representations. The analysis reveals that students' sensemaking involved not only conceptual understanding but also navigating institutional norms and practices embedded within schooling contexts.

title: Measuring prevalence of other-oriented transactive contributions using an automated measure of speech style accommodation
authors: Gahgene Gweon & Mahaveer Jain & John McDonough & Bhiksha Raj & Carolyn P. Rose
summary_haiku: Researchers developed an unsupervised Dynamic Bayesian Network model grounded in Speech Accommodation Theory to automatically detect other-oriented transactive contributions in dyadic speech discussions. Testing on debate recordings, they found significant positive correlation between automatic speech style accommodation measures and prevalence of other-oriented transacts (R=.36, p<.05), demonstrating that theoretically-informed computational models effectively assess collaborative learning processes.

title: Vocational education approach: New TEL settings—new prospects for teachers’ instructional activities?
authors: Raija Hamalainen & Bram De Wever
summary_haiku: This design-based research study examined vocational teachers' instructional activities in a 3D game environment using content analysis of 8,188 utterances from four teacher-student groups. Findings revealed teachers employed two distinct approaches: "knowledge-providing" and "joint problem-solving," with different student responses. Teachers asked more contextual questions and engaged in shared problem-solving than students, while students provided more knowledge. The study demonstrates teachers spontaneously develop innovative instructional strategies in technology-enhanced vocational learning settings, shifting from classroom management toward empowering collaborative knowledge construction.

title: Collaborative drawing on a shared digital canvas in elementary science education: The effects of script and task awareness support
authors: Hannie Gijlers & Armin Weinberger & Alieke Mattia van Dijk & Lars Bollen & Wouter van Joolingen
summary_haiku: This study examined how scripting and task awareness support affect elementary students' collaborative drawing on photosynthesis. Ninety-four fifth-graders worked in dyads using a shared digital canvas under three conditions: control, awareness prompts, or structured script. Both support types increased transactive discourse and deeper conceptual understanding compared to controls. Scripted students acquired significantly more conceptual knowledge, while awareness and scripting both facilitated integrative consensus-building and process-related discussions.

title: Preventing undesirable effects of mutual trust and the development of skepticism in virtual groups by applying the knowledge and information awareness approach
authors: Tanja Engelmann & Richard Kolodziej & Friedrich W. Hesse
summary_haiku: This experimental study examined whether a knowledge and information awareness (KIA) approach—providing digital concept maps of collaborators' knowledge—mitigates negative effects of mutual trust in virtual groups. Comparing 40 triads (20 with KIA, 20 without), researchers found that high initial trust reduced effectiveness in control groups but not experimental groups, while both conditions showed equal efficiency gains. Additionally, poor collaboration quality increased skepticism in control groups but not experimental groups, suggesting KIA facilitates mutual control independent of trust levels.

title: Constructing liminal blends in a collaborative augmented-reality learning environment
authors: Noel Enyedy & Joshua A. Danish & David DeLiema
summary_haiku: This study examines how augmented-reality environments support physics learning through "liminal blends"—conceptual integrations of students' embodied experiences, physical materials, peer contributions, and symbolic representations. Using interaction analysis of second-graders learning about friction, the researchers demonstrate how students blend their bodies, game narratives, material surfaces, and AR symbols to reason about force and motion, revealing cognition as distributed across individuals, materials, and social interaction.

title: Investigating the effects of prompts on argumentation style, consensus and perceived efficacy in collaborative learning
authors: Owen M. Harney & Michael J. Hogan & Benjamin Broome & Tony Hall & Cormac Ryan
summary_haiku: Process-level prompts during collaborative learning sessions significantly enhance group outcomes compared to task-level prompts. In an experimental study using Interactive Management with 75 psychology students, process-level prompts increased perceived consensus and perceived efficacy of the methodology. Analysis of group dialogue revealed more sophisticated argumentation patterns and greater complexity in consensus-based problem models among process-level groups, suggesting that facilitator prompting style substantially influences collaborative learning effectiveness.

title: Group emotions: the social and cognitive functions of emotions in argumentation
authors: Claire Polo & Kristine Lund & Christian Plantin & Gerald P. Niccolai
summary_haiku: Emotions serve dual functions in group argumentation: socially, they signal recognition and engagement in specific talk types (cumulative, disputational, exploratory); cognitively, they frame discourse objects through schematization. Analysis of student debates reveals low-intensity emotional framing correlates with cumulative talk, while high-intensity framing correlates with disputational talk, suggesting optimal emotional engagement supports higher-quality collaborative reasoning.

title: Quantitative approach to collaborative learning: performance prediction, individual assessment, and group composition
authors: Ling Cen & Dymitr Ruta & Leigh Powell & Benjamin Hirsch & Jason Ng
summary_haiku: This study applies machine learning techniques to predict group performance in computer-supported collaborative learning using interaction data from 122 students across three assignments. The research develops normalized features capturing collaboration patterns and proposes a comparative model to assess individual student contributions within groups. Results demonstrate 79% classification accuracy and reveal that heterogeneous groups with mixed genders and diverse skill levels achieve significantly greater collaborative synergy than homogeneous groups.

title: Socially shared regulation of learning in CSCL: understanding and prompting individual- and group-level shared regulatory activities
authors: Sanna Jarvela & Paul A. Kirschner & Allyson Hadwin & Hanna Jarvenoja & Jonna Malmberg & Mariel Miller & Jari Laru
summary_haiku: This review examines socially shared regulation of learning (SSRL) in computer-supported collaborative learning. The authors identify gaps in existing CSCL support tools, which focus on knowledge construction and social awareness but neglect regulatory processes. They present conceptual frameworks distinguishing self-regulated, co-regulated, and socially shared regulation, then describe multiple tools (AIRE, SEST, planning tools, VCRI+SSRL, S-REG) designed to prompt metacognitive awareness and support individual and group-level regulation of cognition, motivation, and emotion during collaborative tasks.

title: Improving collaborative learning in the classroom: Text mining based grouping and representing
authors: Daniel Bodemer & Melanie Erkens & H. Ulrich Hoppe
summary_haiku: This study developed and tested the Grouping and Representing Tool (GRT), which uses text mining to automatically form heterogeneous learning groups and visualize students' knowledge. Comparing Latent Dirichlet Allocation and Vector Space Models, researchers found LDA superior for visualizing cognitive information while Euclidean distance-based clustering better identified text differences for grouping. An experimental evaluation with 54 high school students showed GRT-supported dyads achieved twice the knowledge gains compared to unsupported groups, demonstrating text mining's effectiveness for supporting collaborative learning.

title: This is the size of one meter: Children’s bodily-material collaboration
authors: Jacob Davidsen & Thomas Ryberg
summary_haiku: Two nine-year-old children collaborating around a touchscreen demonstrate that bodily-material resources—gestures, movements, and touch—function as primary vehicles for learning about scale and measurement, not merely supplementary to language. Through detailed video analysis, the study reveals children use bodies communicatively to illustrate understanding, cognitively as auxiliary tools scaffolding knowledge, and physically to shepherd each other's learning in the space between themselves and the screen.

title: All in good time: knowledge introduction, restructuring, and development of shared opinions as different stages in collaborative writing
authors: Johannes Moskaliuk & Ulrike Cress
summary_haiku: This study examined how secondary school student dyads with differing theoretical perspectives on media effects collaborated to write shared texts. Using quantitative and qualitative content analysis of eight text versions, researchers identified three distinct sequential stages: early knowledge introduction, middle restructuring activities, and late shared opinion development. Results demonstrated that collaborative writing progresses through predictable phases, with different activities dominating each stage as participants integrate divergent perspectives into unified conclusions.

title: How to combine collaboration scripts and heuristic worked examples to foster mathematical argumentation – when working memory matters
authors: Matthias Schwaighofer & Freydis Vogel & Ingo Kollar & Stefan Ufer & Anselm Strohmaier & Ilka Terwedow & Sarah Ottinger & Kristina Reiss
summary_haiku: This study examined how sequencing and fading collaboration scripts and heuristic worked examples affect university students' mathematical argumentation skills. Using a 2×2 factorial design with 108 freshmen, researchers found that fading the initially presented scaffold improved dialogic skills regardless of sequence. For dialectic skills, working memory capacity moderated fading effects: low-capacity learners benefited most from fading the collaboration script when presented first, while high-capacity learners benefited from simultaneous scaffold availability.

title: The value of learning talk: applying a novel dialogue scoring method to inform interaction design in an open-ended, embodied museum exhibit
authors: Jessica Roberts
summary_haiku: # Summary Researchers developed SQuILD, a novel dialogue-scoring method for quantifying learning talk in open-ended museum exhibits. Testing this method on 119 visitor groups interacting with an interactive census data map, they compared full-body versus handheld tablet controls and single versus multi-user input configurations. Contrary to theoretical predictions, handheld tablet controls produced significantly higher-quality learning dialogue than full-body interaction, suggesting that intuitive, familiar interfaces may better support collaborative meaning-making than physically immersive designs.

title: Learning to monitor and regulate collective thinking processes
authors: Yann Shiou Ong & Marcela Borge & Carolyn Penstein Rose
summary_haiku: Students using a computer-supported framework for monitoring collaborative discussions significantly improved discourse quality over ten weeks. The study examined 37 students across 13 teams engaging in five discussion sessions, comparing two reflective scripting conditions. Results showed teams enhanced collaborative processes through individual assessment of communication patterns followed by collective sense-making, with evidence-based reflection prompts yielding higher-quality discourse than future-thinking prompts.

title: Community technology mapping: inscribing places when everything is on the move
authors: Katie Headrick Taylor & Reed Stevens & Deborah Silvis
summary_haiku: Community Technology Mapping (CTM) combines interactive digital mapping with structured interviews to support children's reflection on spatiotemporal organization of technology use across daily routines. Through ethnographic analysis of twelve children's mapping activities in Google Earth, researchers identified three inscription processes: making places visible through wayfinding, making places coherent through narrative reconciliation, and making places mobile through dynamic interaction. CTM functions as both pedagogical tool for developing locative literacies and methodological innovation for examining children's place-based learning beyond home observations.

title: Challenges in online collaboration: effects of scripting shared task perceptions
authors: Allyson F. Hadwin & Aishah Bakhtiar & Mariel Miller
summary_haiku: This study examined how different types of planning visualizations affect collaborative learning challenges and regulatory strategies. Undergraduate students (N=180) completed collaborative tasks under three conditions: quantified visualization, nominal visualization, or no visualization of group members' planning perceptions. Results showed groups without visualization support reported greater planning challenge severity and experienced cascading difficulties across multiple challenge types. Groups receiving visualization support reported more effective strategy use. Findings support integrating planning awareness tools into computer-supported collaborative learning environments.

title: Rendering controversial socioscientific issues legible through digital mapping tools
authors: Asa Makitalo & Thomas Hillman & Anne Solli
summary_haiku: Digital mapping tools developed for Science and Technology Studies enable upper secondary students to collaboratively explore controversial socioscientific issues online. Through video analysis of students using network visualization software (Gephi), researchers found that tool-mediated activity slowed categorization processes, prompting productive negotiation of how to interpret controversies. Misalignments between algorithmic tool logic and students' content-focused reasoning generated valuable collaborative discussion about distinguishing controversies from their visualizations.

title: Guiding collaborative revision of science explanations
authors: Libby Gerard & Ady Kidron
summary_haiku: Combining automated explanation scoring with teacher guidance in a computer-supported collaborative learning environment, this study examined how one sixth-grade teacher customized adaptive feedback to guide 98 student pairs in revising science explanations about plate tectonics. Analysis of classroom interactions revealed five distinct teacher guidance strategies that leveraged automated scores to personalize support. Results showed nearly all pairs engaged in meaningful revision, with significant improvements in explanation quality and individual posttest gains, demonstrating how teacher-computer partnerships can effectively promote collaborative knowledge integration.

title: Are we together or not? The temporal interplay of monitoring, physiological arousal and physiological synchrony during a collaborative exam
authors: Jonna Malmberg & Eetu Haataja & Tapio Seppanen & Sanna Jarvela
summary_haiku: This study examined metacognitive monitoring during collaborative exams using video analysis and physiological sensors measuring electrodermal activity. Results showed all group members contributed to monitoring, with monitoring frequency significantly correlating with physiological arousal peaks. Physiological synchrony occurred in groups experiencing task difficulties, suggesting it may indicate meaningful collaborative learning events requiring intervention.

title: Distributed spatial Sensemaking on the augmented reality sandbox
authors: Yotam Hod & Daniel Twersky
summary_haiku: This study uses Interaction Analysis to examine how small collaborative groups engage in distributed spatial sensemaking while using an Augmented Reality Sandbox for topographical learning. Findings reveal that AR features (contour lines, water simulations) coordinated with a 2D monitor representation enable groups to rapidly develop intrinsic-dynamic spatial thinking, facilitate quick trouble-repair sequences, and support divergent-to-convergent turn-taking patterns essential for advancing spatial understanding.

title: Unpacking the relationship between existing and new measures of physiological synchrony and collaborative learning: a mixed methods study
authors: Bertrand Schneider
summary_haiku: This mixed-methods study examined how electrodermal activity (EDA) measures physiological synchrony in collaborative learning. Forty-two dyads programmed robots while wearing EDA sensors. Pearson's correlation and directional agreement showed modest associations with learning gains and collaboration quality. Qualitative analysis of high and low-performing groups revealed that synchrony peaks during external events, oscillates during collaboration, and drops during independent work. A novel measure—cycles between low and high synchrony—strongly correlated with collaboration quality and learning outcomes, suggesting it captures distinct collaborative dynamics.

title: Talking about group (but not individual) process aids group performance
authors: Noel Capon & Hueiyi Lai & Deanna Kuhn
summary_haiku: # Summary This study examined how group discourse relates to collaborative problem-solving performance. Graduate business students worked in small groups through a computer-supported marketing simulation over eight sessions. Discourse analysis revealed that groups discussing their collective process (Meta-group talk) achieved superior outcomes, while talk focused on individual perspectives (Meta-self talk) correlated negatively with performance. Meta-group discourse included understanding others, defining group position, planning, and evaluating—functions that facilitate coordinated action essential for effective collaboration.

title: Finding a place for equity in CSCL: ambitious learning practices as a lever for sustained educational change
authors: Suraj Uttamchandani & Ayesha Bhimdiwala & Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver
summary_haiku: This conceptual article argues that computer-supported collaborative learning (CSCL) should prioritize educational equity by implementing ambitious learning practices—pedagogies emphasizing collaboration, dialogue, and disciplinary engagement. The authors contend that centering equity through student agency, shared meaning-making, and disruption of social inequality positions CSCL to meaningfully contribute to sustained educational change. They examine adaptive collaborative learning support as a case study, highlighting tensions between technological structure and learner agency while proposing that CSCL innovations can support equitable educational transformation when equity considerations guide development throughout.

title: Social practices in teacher knowledge creation and innovation adoption: a large-scale study in an online instructional design community for inquiry learning
authors: Luis P. Prieto & Tobias Ley & Ton de Jong & Maria Jesus Rodriguez-Triana & Denis Gillet
summary_haiku: This large-scale study analyzed 40,235 inquiry learning designs created in Graasp, an online platform used by 35,000+ teachers, to examine how social practices relate to classroom implementation of pedagogical innovations. Using the Knowledge Appropriation Model framework, researchers found that knowledge maturation, expert scaffolding, and knowledge appropriation practices were significantly associated with increased adoption rates of learning designs in classrooms, with maturation showing the strongest effect.

title: The spiral model of collaborative knowledge improvement: an exploratory study of a networked collaborative classroom
authors: Wenli Chen & Jesmine S. H. Tan & Zhongling Pi
summary_haiku: This exploratory case study introduces the Spiral Model of Collaborative Knowledge Improvement (SMCKI), a five-phase pedagogical framework designed to scaffold multi-layered collaborative learning in networked classrooms. Pre-service teachers collaboratively designed technology-enhanced learning activities through individual ideation, intra-group synergy, inter-group critique, intra-group refinement, and individual achievement phases. Results demonstrate significant quality improvements in technology-enhanced learning designs across all SMCKI phases, with participants progressively advancing from simple to complex knowledge dimensions.

title: Net.Create: Network Visualization to Support Collaborative Historical Knowledge Building
authors: Kalani Craig & Joshua Danish & Megan Humburg & Cindy Hmelo-Silver & Maksymilian Szostalo & Ann McCranie
summary_haiku: # Summary This study examines Net.Create, a collaborative network visualization tool designed to help undergraduate history students analyze complex texts. Using activity theory, researchers analyzed how the tool and accompanying activities help students reconcile contradictions between detail and context, active learning and large lectures, and memorization versus historical reasoning. Analysis of log data, video recordings, and student papers from 76 students reveals that quality of historical significance annotations—not quantity of entries—correlates with stronger final papers. Students successfully moved between local details and aggregate patterns, with high-performing groups engaging in deeper "why" analysis compared to low-performing groups focused on "who" and "what."

title: Guidance in computer‑supported collaborative inquiry learning: Capturing aspects of affect and teacher support in science classrooms
authors: Tarja Pietarinen & Tuire Palonen & Marja Vauras
summary_haiku: Teachers in computer-supported collaborative science inquiry learning primarily focused on task management and content knowledge while extensively observing groups. Mixed-methods analysis of four classrooms revealed teachers preferentially guided groups perceived as motivated and collaborative, regardless of prior competence. Notably, socio-emotional support was minimal. Teachers' positive affect correlated with student affect, suggesting reciprocal emotional influences on learning outcomes.

title: A classification of Challenges encountered in Complex Teamwork Settings
authors: Maedeh A. Kazemitabar & Susanne P. Lajoie & Tianshu Li
summary_haiku: This study examined teamwork challenges in a computer-supported collaborative learning environment using a hackathon as the research context. Through multimodal data collection including questionnaires, interviews, and video recordings of 48 participants, researchers employed qualitative theory-driven coding to identify 16 distinct challenges. These challenges were categorized into seven macro-level themes: cognitive, motivational, emotional, behavioral, cognitive/behavioral, general, and external. The analysis revealed which challenges specifically impede mutual trust and shared mental models—key team coordination mechanisms—providing educators with insights for supporting effective collaboration in CSCL settings.

title: Visions of the good in
authors: Etan Cohen & Dani Ben-Zvi & Yotam Hod
summary_haiku: This article examines ethical dimensions of design-based research in computer-supported collaborative learning. Using a Knowledge Building Community case study, the authors propose three ethical frameworks—aretaic, deontological, and consequentialist—to help CSCL researchers systematically articulate their ideological commitments and visions of the good. They present a seven-question framework for unpacking these ethical foundations across design phases and demonstrate how empirical findings can refine moral principles iteratively.

title: Facilitated model‑based reasoning in immersive virtual reality: Meaning‑making and embodied interactions with dynamic processes
authors: Michelle Lui & Kit-Ying Angela Chong & Martha Mullally & Rhonda McEwen
summary_haiku: This study examined how 34 undergraduate students engaged with a lac operon VR simulation using head-mounted displays while a facilitator viewed a mirrored display. Using the Structure-Behavior-Function framework to code facilitator-participant interactions, researchers identified four patterns supporting model-based reasoning: spontaneous structural observations, immediate situated feedback, multiple simulated states comparison, and inquiry spanning structural-behavioral-functional levels. Findings demonstrate that facilitated VR simulations effectively support abstract scientific concept understanding through embodied interaction and dialogue.

title: Fostering collaborative and embodied learning
authors: Jacob Fortman & Rebecca Quintana
summary_haiku: Extended reality (XR) environments—including augmented, virtual, and mixed reality—offer significant potential for collaborative and embodied learning by enabling learners to use body-based resources for meaning-making. This special issue examines empirical research demonstrating how XR technologies support collaborative embodied learning across diverse contexts, from family geoscience exploration to teacher mathematics reasoning, addressing the gap between XR adoption in education and research grounded in collaborative learning theory.

title: Zooming in: The role of nonverbal behavior in sensing the quality of collaborative group engagement
authors: Lisa Paneth & Loris T. Jeitziner & Oliver Rack & Klaus Opwis & Carmen Zahn
summary_haiku: This study examined how nonverbal behaviors relate to collaborative group engagement quality in computer-supported learning. Using video analysis of 38 university groups completing a design task, researchers applied quantitative mixed-effects models to 2,617 one-minute sequences and qualitative case analysis. Findings revealed that nodding, eye contact, and gesturing positively correlate with social, cognitive, and conceptual engagement, while laughing shows complex relationships across dimensions. The research demonstrates nonverbal behaviors serve as meaningful indicators of multifaceted, dynamic group engagement in collaborative learning contexts.

title: The perceptions of task cohesion in collaborative learning teams
authors: Andrew Zamecnik & Georg Grossmann & Djazia Ladjal & Abelardo Pardo
summary_haiku: # Summary This mixed-methods study examined task cohesion development in 194 collaborative learning teams using temporal network motif analysis combined with survey data. Teams were classified into four transition groups based on cohesion perception changes across a three-week work-integrated learning program. Findings revealed that teams maintaining aligned perceptions demonstrated higher performance and greater triadic interaction patterns, while teams with divergent perceptions showed lower performance and dyadic interactions. Temporal network motifs proved effective as proxies for task cohesion, validating the approach for understanding team dynamics in collaborative learning environments.

title: Emergent group understanding: Investigating intersubjectivity in sociotechnical interdependencies
authors: Anders I. Mørch & Renate Andersen & Siv Eie & Louise Mifsud
summary_haiku: This study investigates how shared understanding emerges in computer-mediated learning using Minecraft for social studies. Through design-based research with student teachers reconstructing historical industrial sites, researchers identified "emergent group understanding"—a phenomenon where spontaneous individual knowledge contributions trigger focused group action toward shared learning goals. The framework integrates sociotechnical congruence, intersubjectivity, and emergence theories, revealing how social and technological objects co-evolve through six states of intersubjectivity toward knowledge objects.

title: Revealing the interplay of cognitive, meta‑cognitive, and social processes in university students’ collaborative problem solving: a three‑stage analytical framework
authors: Shuowen An & Si Zhang & Zhihui Cai & Wei Pan & Mingwei Li & Mingwen Tong
summary_haiku: This study proposes a three-stage analytical framework to examine collaborative problem-solving (CPS) patterns among 24 university students completing instructional design and multimedia development tasks. Using dynamic time warping for clustering and process mining analysis, the researchers identified two distinct CPS subgroups: solution-driven groups that effectively transitioned from divergent to convergent thinking through meta-cognitive monitoring, and problem-driven groups that focused on task requirements but lacked comprehensive evaluation processes, resulting in lower performance outcomes.

title: Correction: An artificial intelligence‑driven learning analytics method to examine the collaborative problem‑solving process from the complex adaptive systems perspective
authors: Fan Ouyang & Weiqi Xu & Mutlu Cukurova
summary_haiku: This is a correction notice for an article on artificial intelligence-driven learning analytics examining collaborative problem-solving through complex adaptive systems theory. The correction addresses an erroneous figure that appeared in the original publication, replacing it with the correct framework diagram of complex adaptive systems theory adapted from Holland's work.

title: How does collaborative task design shape collaborative knowledge construction and group‑level regulation of learning? A study of secondary school students’ interactions in two varied tasks
authors: Kateryna Zabolotna & Liv Nøhr & Megumi Iwata & Daniel Spikol & Jonna Malmberg & Hanna Jarvenoja
summary_haiku: Task design significantly shapes collaborative learning processes. This study compared a conceptual physics drawing task and a hands-on robotics task involving secondary students, analyzing collaborative knowledge construction and group-level regulation using video coding and network analysis. Conceptually oriented tasks promoted prolonged cognitive engagement and stronger connections between cognitive regulation and negotiation, while hands-on tasks featured frequent but brief knowledge construction episodes emphasizing socioemotional interactions for maintaining collaboration.

title: Optimizing group formation with a mixed genetic algorithm: an empirical study in active reading using marker data
authors: Changhao Liang & Yuko Toyokawa & Hiroaki Ogata
summary_haiku: A mixed genetic algorithm embedded in a learning platform optimizes group formation for EFL active reading by balancing homogeneous and heterogeneous student characteristics using marker data. Implemented in a Japanese high school classroom with 39 students, the system significantly improved vocabulary learning gains and demonstrated positive group dynamics through Wordcloud visualization, with 85% of students reporting the tool's helpfulness for collaborative tasks.

title: The CSCL community in its ﬁrst decade: development, continuity, connectivity
authors: Andrea Kienle & Martin Wessner
summary_haiku: The CSCL community's first decade (1995–2005) demonstrates growth and increasing internationalization despite low individual continuity. Using quantitative analysis of conference proceedings, participant lists, and program committees combined with qualitative surveys, researchers found that while 79% of authors contributed to only one conference, international connectivity grew substantially through citations and co-authorships across countries, with conference location rotation and diverse program committee composition supporting this development.

title: A relational, indirect, meso-level approach to CSCL design in the next decade
authors: Chris Jones
summary_haiku: This theoretical paper proposes a relational approach to CSCL design, arguing that technology, affordances, and infrastructure should be understood as emerging through relationships rather than as fixed properties. Drawing on two European research networks, the authors advocate for meso-level analysis bridging micro-group and macro-institutional processes, and recommend indirect design strategies that acknowledge contingency in how learners enact technological affordances within networked learning environments.

title: Community-based learning: The core competency of residential, research-based universities
authors: Gerhard Fischer & Markus Rohde
summary_haiku: Residential research universities can maintain competitive advantage against online education by adopting community-based learning grounded in socio-cultural theory. The authors present case studies from University of Colorado and University of Siegen demonstrating how integrating students into communities of practice through apprenticeships, peer collaboration, and regional industry partnerships creates meaningful learning experiences that transcend traditional instructionist models, requiring significant cultural change and faculty risk-taking.

title: Patterns as a paradigm for theory in community-based learning
authors: John M. Carroll & Umer Farooq
summary_haiku: Carroll and Farooq propose design patterns as a theoretical framework for understanding community-based IT learning. Through 12 years of participatory action research with volunteer organizations, they present two patterns: "Informal Developmental Learning" addresses lack of IT control through reflection, analysis, and enactment; "Scaffolded Documentation" manages knowledge loss from volunteer turnover via technology assessment, contingency planning, and lightweight documentation. Patterns serve as middle-level abstractions capturing recurring problems and solutions intelligible to practitioners themselves.

title: Dealing with multiple documents on the WWW: The role of metacognition in the formation of documents models
authors: Marc Stadtler & Rainer Bromme
summary_haiku: This study examined whether metacognitive prompting helps laypersons form documents models—integrated representations of content and sources—when researching medical information online. Using an experimental design with 79 participants assigned to groups receiving evaluation prompts, monitoring prompts, both, or neither, researchers found that monitoring prompts enhanced factual knowledge acquisition, while evaluation prompts improved source knowledge and source attribution in essays, supporting metacognition's importance in multiple-document comprehension.

title: Specifying computer-supported collaboration scripts
authors: Lars Kobbe & Armin Weinberger & Pierre Dillenbourg & Andreas Harrer & Raija Hamalainen & Paivi Hakkinen & Frank Fischer
summary_haiku: This paper proposes a comprehensive framework for specifying computer-supported collaboration scripts by consolidating prior approaches. Through conceptual analysis, the authors identify five core components (participants, activities, roles, resources, groups) and three mechanisms (task distribution, group formation, sequencing) that enable platform-independent script description. The framework facilitates systematic research, practical design, and computational formalization of collaborative learning scripts across diverse educational contexts.

title: Future technology workshop: A collaborative method for the design of new learning technologies and activities
authors: Giasemi N. Vavoula & Mike Sharples
summary_haiku: The Future Technology Workshop (FTW) is a collaborative design method enabling participants with domain knowledge to envision and prototype interactions between current/future technologies and activities. Through seven structured sessions combining brainstorming, low-tech prototyping, role-play, and scenario analysis, participants progress from imagining far-future possibilities to grounding ideas in present constraints, ultimately generating implementable technology requirements. Successfully applied with children and adults across multiple projects, FTW provides cost-effective, pragmatic outcomes directly informing human-centered systems design.

title: The mechanics of CSCL macro scripts
authors: Pierre Dillenbourg & Fabrice Hong
summary_haiku: Macro scripts structure collaborative learning by strategically distributing resources, roles, and knowledge among team members to increase interaction intensity. Using pedagogical design principles and computational data structure transformations, scripts trigger knowledge-productive interactions like argumentation and explanation. The SWISH model demonstrates how scripts engineer productive learning by creating controlled "splits" that require students to interact intensively to reach shared understanding.

title: The need for considering multilevel analysis in CSCL research—An appeal for the use of more advanced statistical methods
authors: Ulrike Cress
summary_haiku: CSCL research involves hierarchically nested data—individuals within groups—yet standard statistical methods violate independence assumptions, causing alpha-error inflation. Multilevel modeling (MLM) addresses this by simultaneously analyzing individual and group levels, testing cross-level interactions between within-group predictors and between-group variables. However, MLM requires large sample sizes typically unavailable in CSCL studies, necessitating alternative approaches and careful reporting of intraclass correlations.

title: Appropriation of a shared workspace: Organizing principles and their application
authors: Maarten Overdijk & Wouter van Diggelen
summary_haiku: This case study examines how student groups appropriate a graphical shared workspace during computer-mediated argumentative discussion. Through micro-analysis of tool-mediated interactions, the researchers found that groups develop shared organizational principles through implicit negotiation of conventions. Four groups demonstrated distinct orientations—maintaining direct interaction, constructing personal reasoning, or submitting unrelated contributions—resulting in different principles for organizing contributions. The study reveals mutual shaping between students and tool, where early choices constrain later possibilities and strong graphical principles prove difficult to abandon.

title: Operationalizing macro-scripts in CSCL technological settings
authors: Pierre Tchounikine
summary_haiku: This article proposes SPAIRD, a conceptualization model for operationalizing CSCL macro-scripts—pedagogical activity structures that guide collaborative learning. The research identifies core design dimensions including script reification through technology, student presentation strategies, and uncertainties in script perception and enactment. SPAIRD disentangles structural models, implementation models, platform specifications, and student-oriented models while documenting design rationale. The analysis examines current technological approaches and advocates for flexible, model-based script engines supporting iterative design.

title: The effect of a script and a structured interface in grounding discussions
authors: Judith Schoonenboom
summary_haiku: This study examined how collaboration scripts and structured interfaces support grounding discussions among international students working remotely. Using a three-condition experiment (unscripted, script-only, script+interface), 42 students performed two grounding discussions structured into input, discussion, and consensus phases. Results showed scripts increased knowledge input quantity and discussion of differences, while structured interfaces further enhanced input length and adherence to prescribed activity sequences. However, no significant effects emerged for summary quality or learning outcomes.

title: Alternative goal structures for computer game-based learning
authors: Fengfeng Ke
summary_haiku: This field study examined how cooperative, competitive, and individualistic goal structures in classroom computer math games affect fifth-graders' math performance and attitudes. Using a pretest-posttest design with 160 students across four conditions, results showed all gaming groups outperformed controls on math tests, but cooperative goal structures proved most effective for promoting positive math attitudes. Socioeconomic status significantly moderated outcomes, with disadvantaged students benefiting most from cooperation.

title: A connective ethnography of peer knowledge sharing and diffusion in a tween virtual world
authors: Deborah A. Fields & Yasmin B. Kafai
summary_haiku: Researchers used connective ethnography to trace how tweens ages 9-12 learned and shared an insider gaming practice—teleporting—across an after-school club, classrooms, and the virtual world Whyville.net. Integrating video, field notes, logfiles, and interviews, they found that most participants traversed multiple physical and virtual spaces to learn this practice, employing observation, questioning, and peer coaching. Knowledge diffusion occurred through informal, unstructured interactions rather than explicit instruction, demonstrating how virtual spaces expand peer-to-peer learning opportunities beyond traditional classroom boundaries.

title: Affordances revisited: Articulating a Merleau-Pontian view
authors: Nina Bonderup Dohn
summary_haiku: This article develops a Merleau-Pontian account of affordances for CSCL, arguing that existing interpretations within the field contain unresolved ontological and epistemological tensions. The author proposes that affordances are dynamic, relational, and skill-relative properties existing independently of perception but relative to agents' body-schematic interaction potential. This framework shifts design and empirical research focus toward background structuring and learners' developing capabilities rather than mental models.

title: Time is precious: Variable- and event-centred approaches to process analysis in CSCL research
authors: Peter Reimann
summary_haiku: CSCL research often neglects temporal dimensions despite studying processes unfolding over weeks or months. Reimann argues that variable-centered variance theory inadequately captures long-term change, proposing event-centered analysis as a complementary approach. Event-based methods enable narrative explanation, accommodate multiple causality types, and facilitate integration of qualitative and quantitative analyses, offering CSCL researchers more appropriate tools for analyzing extended collaborative learning processes.

title: Earth science learning in SMALLab: A design experiment for mixed reality
authors: David Birchfield & Colleen Megowan-Romanowicz
summary_haiku: This design experiment examined how mixed-reality environments support collaborative earth science learning. Researchers implemented SMALLab, a semi-immersive platform enabling colocated students to interact face-to-face within computationally mediated spaces. A 3-day intervention with 72 high school students revealed significantly increased student-to-student exchanges compared to traditional instruction and notable achievement gains on concept assessments, suggesting mixed-reality technology's potential for enhancing K-12 collaborative learning when properly designed.

title: An ontology engineering approach to the realization of theory-driven group formation
authors: Seiji Isotani & Akiko Inaba & Mitsuru Ikeda & Riichiro Mizoguchi
summary_haiku: This research presents an ontology-based framework for theory-driven group formation in collaborative learning. Using ontological engineering, the authors formalize learning theory concepts to guide group composition, role assignment, and activity design. A proof-of-concept experiment with four instructors and twenty participants demonstrated that groups formed according to pedagogical theory specifications showed significantly better performance and more meaningful interactions than control groups, suggesting ontologies effectively operationalize learning theories for improved collaborative learning outcomes.

title: S-COL: A Copernican turn for the development of flexibly reusable collaboration scripts
authors: Christof Wecker & Karsten Stegmann & Florian Bernstein & Michael J. Huber & Georg Kalus & Ingo Kollar & Sabine Rathmayer & Frank Fischer
summary_haiku: S-COL is a browser-based tool enabling flexible reuse of collaboration scripts across diverse web-based learning platforms. Rather than embedding scripts within specific platforms, S-COL implements scripts in the browser and triggers them by recognizing functionally equivalent page types. An empirical study demonstrated that a collaboration script for online search implemented in S-COL effectively increased students' engagement in early-stage search activities, supporting the tool's feasibility for sustainable script development and reuse.

title: Using activity theory to understand intergenerational play: The case of Family Quest
authors: Sinem Siyahhan & Sasha A. Barab & Michael P. Downton
summary_haiku: # Summary This study examined intergenerational play between parents and children (ages 9-13) using Quest Atlantis, an educational 3D game, through activity theory analysis.
