Five-week observations of seven parent-child dyads revealed that successful collaborative gaming required shared intentions and expertise exchange. While outcomes varied across dyads, the research demonstrated that educational video games can facilitate meaningful family bonding and learning, particularly when designed to encourage parents and children to leverage complementary skills around personally relevant narratives.

title: The collaborative construction of chronotopes during computer-supported collaborative professional tasks
authors: Maria Beatrice Ligorio & Giuseppe Ritella
summary_haiku: # Summary This study analyzes how teachers collaboratively construct spatial and temporal frameworks during computer-supported professional planning using qualitative video analysis of six sessions. The researchers identified three distinct chronotopes—Adagio, Andante, and Allegretto—representing different interaction tempos shaped by tool features, activity complexity, and participant expertise. Results demonstrate that technology mediates collaboration by creating multiple overlapping spaces where different types of coordination emerge, revealing how space-time co-construction fundamentally influences group professional work.

title: Learning the physics of electricity: A qualitative analysis of collaborative processes involved in productive failure
authors: Suneeta A. Pathak & Beaumie Kim & Michael J. Jacobson & Baohui Zhang
summary_haiku: This qualitative study examines collaborative problem-solving dynamics in physics education using computer-supported learning. Two student dyads—one experiencing productive failure through initial low-structured activities followed by high-structured ones, and another receiving only high-structured activities—solved electricity problems using NetLogo models. Analysis of video, screen captures, and solutions revealed that initial struggle enabled deeper engagement with the model and reflective reasoning, while over-scripted activities hindered meaningful collaboration and conceptual understanding.

title: An information processing perspective on divergence and convergence in collaborative learning
authors: Robert L. Jorczak
summary_haiku: Jorczak proposes a Collaborative Information Processing (CIP) model explaining how peer discussion facilitates learning through information divergence and convergence. Using information processing theory, the model demonstrates that groups benefit from diverse member perspectives triggering conceptual conflict, followed by convergent processes achieving shared understanding. The CIP framework unifies cognitive and social interaction theories, predicting that heterogeneous groups and divergent information exchange enhance collaborative learning outcomes.

title: Comparing the effects of representational tools in collaborative and individual inquiry learning
authors: Bas Kolloffel & Tessa H. S. Eysink & Ton de Jong
summary_haiku: Collaborative learners significantly outperformed individual learners in combinatorics and probability inquiry learning, particularly on intuitive and situational knowledge. Using a pre-test/post-test design with 61 collaborative dyads and 95 individual students, three representational tool formats (conceptual, arithmetical, textual) were compared. Results showed collaboration's benefits persisted regardless of tool use, while individual learners benefited from externalization. Representational format did not directly enhance specific knowledge types as hypothesized, though approximately 50% adopted conceptual or textual tools versus only 20% using arithmetical formats.

title: Designing automated adaptive support to improve student helping behaviors in a peer tutoring activity
authors: Erin Walker & Nikol Rummel & Kenneth R. Koedinger
summary_haiku: Researchers used a four-phase iterative design process to develop adaptive support for peer tutoring in algebra. Through user needs analysis, system design, classroom experimentation, and qualitative case analysis, they found that adaptive assistance improved conceptual help quality and sentence classifier usage compared to fixed support, though learning gains were not significantly different. The study demonstrates how accountability-focused design principles can enhance collaborative help-giving behaviors.

title: CSCL for intellectually disabled pupils: Stimulating interaction by using a floor control mechanism
authors: Ulrike Cress & Katrin Wodzicki & Martina Bientzle & Andreas Lingnau
summary_haiku: This study examined whether floor control mechanisms—restricting simultaneous actions in collaborative learning environments—improve interaction quality for intellectually disabled pupils. Twenty pupils completed a furniture-sorting task in pairs using tablet PCs, comparing floor control versus unrestricted conditions. Results showed floor control reduced relocations, decreased coordinative communication, and increased content-related discussion, particularly when pupils disagreed or faced difficult symbols, while producing slightly higher-quality collaborative outcomes.

title: Agent-based dynamic support for learning from collaborative brainstorming in scientific inquiry
authors: Hao-Chuan Wang & Carolyn P. Rose & Chun-Yen Chang
summary_haiku: This study examines learning during collaborative brainstorming through two controlled experiments manipulating individual versus pair work and system support. Results reveal that while pair brainstorming produces process losses in idea generation, it enhances multi-perspective learning. The VIBRANT agent's automatic feedback improves connection-based learning. An enhanced version in study two shows promise for mitigating productivity losses associated with collaborative work.

title: Are two heads always better than one? Differential effects of collaboration on students’ computer-supported learning in mathematics
authors: Dejana Mullins & Nikol Rummel & Hans Spada
summary_haiku: Collaboration's effectiveness in mathematics learning depends on instructional material type. This experimental study compared individual versus collaborative learning with conceptual and procedural algebra instruction in a computer-supported environment. Results showed collaboration enhanced conceptual knowledge acquisition through mutual elaboration, but hindered procedural skill development due to task distribution and reduced practice opportunities.

title: Interfering and resolving: How tabletop interaction facilitates co-construction of argumentative knowledge
authors: Taciana Pontual Falcao & Sara Price
summary_haiku: Peer interference in shared tabletop interfaces can productively support argumentative knowledge co-construction during exploratory science learning. Analyzing 43 students aged 11-14 interacting with a tangible light-behavior simulation, researchers applied Weinberger and Fischer's consensus-building framework to interference episodes. Integration-oriented consensus building—where students reflected on and incorporated peers' contributions—consistently produced productive learning, while conflict-oriented approaches typically yielded counter-productive outcomes.

title: Guided reciprocal questioning to support children’s collaborative storytelling
authors: Giulia Gelmini-Hornsby & Shaaron Ainsworth
summary_haiku: Guided Reciprocal Peer Questioning (GRPQ) scripts significantly enhance children's collaborative storytelling through increased interactive discussion. Using a within-subjects design with 36 six-to-seven-year-olds creating stories with KidPad, the study found that question prompts promoted longer, more evaluatively rich, and more coherent stories. Benefits largely persisted after scaffold withdrawal, suggesting children internalized the questioning approach and can apply it independently.

title: The role of teacher assistance on the effects of a macro-script in collaborative writing tasks
authors: Javier Onrubia & Anna Engel
summary_haiku: This multiple-case study examines how teacher assistance patterns interact with macro-scripts to influence collaborative writing in university students. Analyzing two settings with different script types and teaching approaches, the study identifies distinct teacher assistance patterns and their relationships to group organization and knowledge construction phases. Results show that flexible, content-focused teacher guidance combined with open scripts promotes heterogeneous group strategies and advanced collaborative knowledge construction, while detailed scripts paired with organizational reminders produce homogeneous adherence but lower knowledge construction levels.

title: Connecting agents and artifacts in CSCL: Towards a rationale of mutual shaping
authors: Maarten Overdijk & Wouter van Diggelen & Paul A. Kirschner & Michael Baker
summary_haiku: This article examines how human agents and technical artifacts connect in computer-supported collaborative learning. Through theoretical review of affordance, structuration, and instrumental genesis frameworks, the authors argue that existing CSCL research emphasizing artifact-driven "shaping" of collaboration should shift toward "mutual shaping," where both learners and technologies reciprocally influence each other. Instrumental genesis emerges as the most viable theoretical approach for understanding this bidirectional relationship.

title: An instrumental perspective on CSCL systems
authors: Jacques Lonchamp
summary_haiku: Rabardel's instrumental genesis theory reveals that CSCL systems involve complex two-phase development: teachers customize artifacts during preparation, while learners and tutors collaboratively develop utilization schemes during use. The research distinguishes two system categories based on who drives instrumentalization—learner-instrumentalizable systems supporting emergent collaborative practices, and teacher-instrumentalizable systems enforcing predefined learning structures—each mediating different forms of knowledge construction through epistemic, pragmatic, interpersonal, and reflexive mediation.

title: Scripted collaborative learning with the cognitive tutor algebra
authors: Nikol Rummel & Dejana Mullins & Hans Spada
summary_haiku: Researchers extended the Cognitive Tutor Algebra system to support collaborative learning by implementing a jigsaw-based collaboration script with adaptive elements. In a classroom experiment comparing scripted collaboration, unscripted collaboration, and individual learning, process analyses revealed the script improved interaction quality and problem-solving during learning. However, quantitative between-condition comparisons showed no significant learning advantage for collaboration, though collaborative performance matched individual performance despite fewer practice problems, suggesting interaction compensated for reduced practice opportunities.

title: Learning physics through play in an augmented reality environment
authors: Noel Enyedy & Joshua A. Danish & Girlie Delacruz & Melissa Kumar
summary_haiku: # Summary This study demonstrates that first and second graders (n=43) can meaningfully learn Newtonian physics through augmented reality activities combining embodied play and progressive symbolization. Using pre-post assessments, students showed significant gains in understanding force, net force, friction, and two-dimensional motion. Two design principles guided the curriculum: participatory modeling leveraging socio-dramatic play to make intuitions visible, and progressive symbolization enabling students to invent and refine representational systems. Case studies illustrate how embodied prediction and collaborative symbol refinement supported conceptual integration, though challenges emerged when students relied exclusively on embodiment or formal reasoning.

title: Patterns of kindergarten children’s social interaction with peers in the computer area
authors: Eun Mee Lim
summary_haiku: This qualitative study examined kindergarten children's peer interactions in a classroom computer area through three-month observations and teacher interviews. The researcher identified six social interaction patterns: parallel play, verbal conflicts, sociable interactions, knowledge construction through positive processes, knowledge construction through negative processes, and non-verbal communication. Three patterns—positive processes, negative processes, and non-verbal communication—constituted "Cognitively Effective Social Interaction" leading to meaningful knowledge construction. Findings demonstrate computers support collaborative learning when integrated with classroom curriculum.

title: A model for flexibly editing CSCL scripts
authors: Pericles Sobreira & Pierre Tchounikine
summary_haiku: Researchers developed the T2 model, a table-tree representation system enabling teachers to flexibly edit CSCL scripts. Using intuitive table structures mapped to machine-readable trees, the approach prioritizes simplicity and adaptability over complex meta-models. Usability testing with five teachers confirmed the model's ease of use and demonstrated that teachers effectively leveraged representation flexibility to customize scripts according to their perspectives and contexts.

title: Facilitating learning in multidisciplinary groups with transactive CSCL scripts
authors: Omid Noroozi & Stephanie D. Teasley & Harm J. A. Biemans & Armin Weinberger & Martin Mulder
summary_haiku: # Summary This laboratory experiment with 120 university students examined how transactive memory and discussion scripts in computer-supported collaborative learning environments facilitate knowledge sharing in multidisciplinary groups. Students from different disciplinary backgrounds solved an authentic problem requiring complementary expertise. Results showed that each script individually improved transactive knowledge sharing, knowledge transfer, and solution quality, but combining both scripts produced negative interaction effects, likely due to over-scripting constraints within the 80-minute collaboration period.

title: Co-located single display collaborative learning for early childhood education
authors: Florencia Gomez & Miguel Nussbaum & Juan F. Weitz & Ximena Lopez & Javiera Mena & Alex Torres
summary_haiku: Small-group co-located single-display collaborative learning significantly improves oral language, logical-mathematical, and social skills in kindergarten children. Using a quasi-experimental design with 268 experimental and 172 control participants, researchers implemented computer-supported collaborative activities twice weekly for four months. Results showed the experimental group achieved substantially greater gains in logical-mathematical skills (21.78% vs. 6.09%) and social skills (10.09% vs. -8.19%), with teacher mediation proving essential for effective collaboration.

title: Advancing understanding using Nonaka’s model of knowledge creation and problem-based learning
authors: Meng Yew Tee & Shuh Shing Lee
summary_haiku: Integrating Nonaka's knowledge creation model with problem-based learning addresses Bereiter's critique that the model neglects understanding. This design-based research examined a 14-week course for in-service teachers developing technological pedagogical content knowledge. Findings demonstrate that combining socialization, externalization, combination, and internalization processes within problem-based learning phases cultivates advancing understanding of complex teaching-technology integration challenges.

title: The multi-layered nature of small-group learning: Productive interactions in object-oriented collaboration
authors: Crina Damsa
summary_haiku: # Summary This study examines productive interactions in small-group collaborative learning through a 20-week undergraduate research project. Using qualitative analysis and descriptive statistics, the researcher analyzed five student groups' interactions and emerging knowledge objects (research reports). Findings reveal that productive interactions manifest in two primary patterns: discourse-based interactions fostering shared understanding, and object-oriented interactions involving iterative co-construction. Groups demonstrating shared epistemic agency—deliberate, joint engagement with knowledge materialization—produced higher-quality knowledge objects, suggesting that productive collaboration integrates discursive interaction with tangible object development over time.

title: How to bring a technical artifact into use: A micro-developmental perspective
authors: Maarten Overdijk & Wouter van Diggelen & Jerry Andriessen & Paul A. Kirschner
summary_haiku: # Summary This micro-developmental case study examines how a student pair appropriated a digital shared workspace for project planning. Using qualitative analysis of classroom observations, interviews, and interaction protocols, the research reveals that artifact appropriation involves tension between existing classroom practices and new tool affordances. Resistance from the artifact—when it contradicted established planning conventions—triggered reflection and procedural adaptation, while absence of resistance enabled unreflective departures from regular practice. The findings demonstrate that technology use emerges through complex negotiations between learner intentions and designer intentions embedded in artifacts.

title: An examination of CSCL methodological practices and the influence of theoretical frameworks 2005–2009
authors: Heisawn Jeong & Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver & Yawen Yu
summary_haiku: This content analysis examined methodological practices in 400 empirical CSCL studies published 2005–2009 across seven leading journals. Researchers coded studies across research designs, settings, data sources, and analysis methods, then examined relationships with theoretical frameworks. Findings revealed descriptive designs dominated (54%), classroom settings predominated (74%), and quantitative analysis was most common (86%), though qualitative and mixed methods were frequent. Cluster analysis identified four distinctive method-theory combinations, demonstrating that theoretical frameworks significantly influenced methodological choices across all dimensions.

title: Different leaders: Emergent organizational and intellectual leadership in children’s collaborative learning groups
authors: Emma M. Mercier & Steven E. Higgins & Laura da Costa
summary_haiku: This study examines emergent leadership in children's collaborative learning groups through two investigations. Using a coding scheme adapted from prior research, the authors analyzed 32 students in Study One and 96 students in Study Two, identifying leadership moves as either intellectual (idea development, topic control) or organizational (turn management, planning). Results reveal leadership is distributed among group members, with approximately half of groups showing distinct intellectual and organizational leaders held by different students. Leadership patterns vary significantly across content areas and task types, suggesting leadership is context-dependent rather than stable.

title: An integrated way of using a tangible user interface in a classroom
authors: Jessica Dehler-Zufferey & Giulia Ortoleva & Pierre Dillenbourg
summary_haiku: Researchers designed a classroom activity using TapaCarp, a tangible user interface, to teach carpenter apprentices spatial skills while bridging school and workplace learning. The mixed-methods study with 40 apprentices across three classes showed high usability and strong engagement, with improved artifact quality from day one to day two. However, standardized tests revealed no significant learning gains compared to controls, though plausible objects proved more effective than non-plausible ones for complex tasks.

title: Collaborative group engagement in a computer-supported inquiry learning environment
authors: Suparna Sinha & Toni Kempler Rogat & Karlyn R. Adams-Wiggins & Cindy E. Hmelo-Silver
summary_haiku: This study develops an observational protocol to measure collaborative group engagement in computer-supported inquiry learning as multifaceted—encompassing behavioral, social, cognitive, and conceptual-to-consequential dimensions. Using qualitative analysis of ten middle school groups solving an ecosystem problem, researchers found that behavioral and social engagement differentiated low-quality groups, while cognitive and conceptual-to-consequential engagement characterized high-quality engagement. Results demonstrate these engagement facets are highly interrelated and mutually influential, with implications for designing technologies that scaffold deeper learning in collaborative environments.

title: Teacher support in computer-supported lab work: bridging the gap between lab experiments and students’ conceptual understanding
authors: Anniken Furberg
summary_haiku: This intervention study examined teacher support in computer-supported collaborative lab work, analyzing 122 student help requests during a genetics experiment. Findings reveal that 45.1% of requests concerned conceptual issues and 28.7% addressed procedural challenges. Detailed interaction analyses show students struggled linking lab procedures to underlying scientific principles, requiring substantial teacher support through elicitation, explanation, and conceptual guidance to bridge this gap.

title: The symmetry of partner modelling
authors: Pierre Dillenbourg & Mirweis Sangin & Nicolas Nova
summary_haiku: This study examines whether collaborative partners' mutual modeling accuracy—their ability to understand each other's knowledge, intentions, and emotions—depends on individual cognitive skills or interaction quality. Analyzing five experiments across different collaborative tasks, the researchers found that partners' modeling accuracy was significantly correlated in four studies, suggesting interaction quality matters more than individual abilities. However, correlations remained moderate, indicating both factors contribute to mutual understanding in collaborative learning.

title: You like it, you learn it: affectivity and learning in competitive social role play gaming
authors: Cyril Brom & Michaela Slussareff & Tereza Selmbacherova
summary_haiku: This study examined whether positive affect mediates learning gains in game-based education using a between-subjects design with 325 high school and college students. Participants learned about EU policy through a debate-based method delivered via computer game, non-computer game, or traditional workshop. Both game conditions induced higher positive affect and flow, and participants learned more with games. Positive affect—but not flow—mediated the relationship between instructional medium and learning outcomes, suggesting that affective engagement is crucial for game-based learning effectiveness.

title: Contribution to a theory of CSCL scripts: taking into account the appropriation of scripts by learners
authors: Pierre Tchounikine
summary_haiku: Tchounikine argues that understanding CSCL script enactment requires examining learner appropriation—how learners perceive, understand, and make scripts their own—rather than assuming direct script implementation. Through theoretical analysis, he demonstrates that appropriation involves complex cognitive processes influenced by technology use, institutional contexts, and domain-specific factors. The paper proposes that appropriation and implementation are intertwined processes requiring holistic analysis, extending the Script Theory of Guidance framework.

title: Appropriation from a script theory of guidance perspective: a response to Pierre Tchounikine
authors: Karsten Stegmann & Ingo Kollar & Armin Weinberger & Frank Fischer
summary_haiku: This response clarifies how Script Theory of Guidance (SToG) addresses learner appropriation of collaboration scripts. The authors argue SToG inherently concerns appropriation through three mechanisms: learners' goals influence internal script configuration, perceived situational characteristics shape script interpretation, and appropriation involves perception, interpretation, and implementation steps. They propose that internalization follows successful appropriation, and acknowledge that institutional and domain-specific factors merit stronger theoretical integration within SToG's framework.

title: What happens when you push the button? Analyzing the functional dynamics of concept development in computer supported science inquiry
authors: Hans Christian Arnseth & Ingeborg Krange
summary_haiku: This study examines how high school students develop scientific concepts through computer-supported collaborative inquiry into energy transformation. Using video ethnography, researchers analyzed students' interactions with material and digital tools while learning to explain how a heat pump works. Results demonstrate that students progressively developed sophisticated use of science concepts as explanatory tools through a functional system comprising teacher guidance, material artifacts, and digital models. Teacher practices—including eliciting understanding, providing strategic hints, and modeling coherent concept use—were crucial for supporting students' conceptual development across multiple representations.

title: DCLM framework: understanding collaboration in open-ended tabletop learning environments
authors: Matthew Berland & Leilah Lyons & Mike Tissenbaum
summary_haiku: This paper introduces the Divergent Collaborative Learning Mechanisms (DCLM) framework for analyzing collaboration in open-ended tabletop learning environments where participants pursue divergent goals. Extending the existing Collaborative Learning Mechanisms framework, DCLM adds six mechanisms including boundary spanning actions and perception, goal adaptation, and modeling. Analysis of the Oztoc museum exhibit demonstrates that participants with non-aligned goals can productively collaborate, providing insights unavailable in shared-goal activities.

title: Adaptable scripting to foster regulation processes and skills in
authors: Ingo Kollar & Karsten Stegmann & Xinghua Wang
summary_haiku: This study examined how adaptable collaboration scripts—which allow learners to modify script components based on self-perceived needs—affect regulation processes and skill acquisition in computer-supported collaborative learning. Using a three-phase experimental design with 87 university students, results showed adaptable scripts significantly increased metacognitive reflection and monitoring activities compared to fixed scripts, and substantially improved learners' self-regulation skills in subsequent unscripted tasks. Mediation analyses revealed reflection processes during scripted collaboration explained the positive effects on later regulation skill transfer.

title: Facilitating socio-cognitive and socio-emotional monitoring in collaborative learning with a regulation macro script – an exploratory study
authors: Jaana Isohatala & Sanna Jarvela & Piia Naykki & Johanna Poysa-Tarhonen & Paivi Hakkinen
summary_haiku: This exploratory study examined how a regulation macro script supports socio-cognitive and socio-emotional monitoring in collaborative learning among teacher education students. Using video analysis of 20 group sessions, researchers found that groups engaged more actively with orientation phases than intermediate or reflection phases. Active script discussions stimulated significantly more socio-emotional support provision than less active discussions. Importantly, socio-emotional support initiated during scripted phases transferred to subsequent unscripted task work, suggesting scripts can facilitate sustained collaborative regulation.

title: Investigating the effects of peer to peer prompts on collaborative argumentation, consensus and perceived efficacy in collaborative learning
authors: Owen M. Harney & Michael J. Hogan & Sarah Quinn
summary_haiku: Peer-driven prompts in computer-supported collaborative learning using Interactive Management significantly enhanced student outcomes compared to facilitator-driven prompts. With 101 undergraduate students across eight groups, peer-driven conditions produced higher perceived consensus, perceived efficacy, team orientation, and more sophisticated argumentation patterns, while reducing discomfort in group learning. Results demonstrate that structured peer prompting, supported through facilitator modeling and gradual responsibility transfer, effectively supports collaborative learning and critical thinking development.

title: I think you just got mixed up: confident peer tutors hedge to support partners’ face needs
authors: Justine Cassell & Amy Ogan & Michael Madaio
summary_haiku: Peer tutors with lower social closeness to tutees provide more positive feedback and use indirect language when delivering instructions and comprehension-monitoring, but only when they possess high tutoring self-efficacy. Conversely, tutees benefit from hedged instructions and comprehension-monitoring specifically in low-rapport dyads, suggesting that interpersonal closeness reduces the need for indirectness while self-efficacy enables strategic face-threat mitigation.

title: Visions of CSCL: eight provocations for the future of the field
authors: Alyssa Friend Wise & Baruch B. Schwarz
summary_haiku: CSCL faces critical identity and relevance questions through eight provocations: the field needs unified conceptual frameworks for diverse tools, should prioritize learner agency over scripting, rigorously define collaboration and community, address methodological divides, pursue computational approaches, prioritize learning analytics and adaptive support, expand to social media and large-scale environments, and reconsider its commitment to educational change through research-practice partnerships.

title: Using technological functions on a multi-touch table and their affordances to counteract biases and foster collaborative problem solving
authors: Inga M. Bause & Irina R. Brich & Ann-Katrin Wesslein & Friedrich W. Hesse
summary_haiku: Multi-touch table support functions with affordances for moving, structuring, and merging information significantly enhanced collaborative problem-solving in hidden-profile tasks. University student triads using the collaboration support kit showed greater discussion intensity, more balanced information exchange, stronger mutual understanding indicators, and five times higher correct decision rates compared to standard conditions, demonstrating that intuitive technological affordances can overcome biases from prior preferences.

title: One framework to rule them all? Carrying forward the conversation started by Wise and Schwarz
authors: Nikol Rummel
summary_haiku: Rather than seeking one unified CSCL framework top-down, this article proposes using a 12-dimension taxonomy of support characteristics as a foundation for collaborative empirical research. Through experimental studies varying dimensions like timing and foundation of instruction, the author demonstrates how systematic investigation across taxonomy dimensions can generate evidence-based design principles for computer-supported collaborative learning environments.

title: From Cognitive Load Theory to Collaborative Cognitive Load Theory
authors: Paul A. Kirschner & John Sweller & Femke Kirschner & Jimmy Zambrano R
summary_haiku: Cognitive load theory, traditionally focused on individual learning, is extended to collaborative learning by incorporating the concept of collective working memory and transactive activities. The authors argue that collaboration reduces cognitive load when tasks exceed individual working memory capacity, but transactive costs of communication and coordination can negate benefits. Design principles for effective collaborative learning must consider task complexity, team composition, prior experience, and domain expertise.

title: Learning through collaborative design of location-based games
authors: Jo Dugstad Wake & Frode Guribye & Barbara Wasson
summary_haiku: Students collaboratively designed location-based games to learn history using the SILO authoring tool. Through design-based research and video analysis, the study found that students engaged creatively with historical materials while making design decisions about game difficulty, narrative structure, and location placement. Students explicitly considered peer players' experiences, demonstrating accountability and responsibility in their design process.

title: The opportunities of networks of research-practice partnerships and why CSCL should not give up on large-scale educational change
authors: Ornit Sagy & Yael Kali & Yotam Hod
summary_haiku: This article argues that CSCL should pursue large-scale educational change through networks of design-centric research-practice partnerships (DC-RPPs). The authors counter arguments that the field has abandoned this goal by demonstrating how collaborative networks integrating researchers, practitioners, and policymakers can generate scalable, sustainable innovations. They illustrate this approach through Taking Citizen Science to School, a five-year Israeli research center connecting citizen science with classroom learning.

title: Instrumental genesis in the design studio
authors: Lucila Carvalho & Roberto Martinez-Maldonado & Peter Goodyear
summary_haiku: Instrumental Genesis theory explains how artifacts and their uses co-evolve within specific environments. This study applies IG to the neglected "upstream" phase of CSCL design, examining how educational designers use design studio artifacts to create collaborative learning tasks. Through two empirical studies involving design teams using the CoCoDes tool and design patterns, the researchers traced how artifacts move downstream to learners and how designer practices move upstream to inform tool improvements, demonstrating CSCL design as a distributed, dynamic system of instrument-mediated activity.

title: Conceptualizing the designs of authentic
authors: Yotam Hod & Ornit Sagy
summary_haiku: This study synthesizes 25 years of CSCL research using constant-comparative analysis to clarify authentic learning design. The authors identify three cultures—current, authentic, and intended—operating in authentic learning environments and distinguish between simulation approaches (classroom-based enculturation) and hybrid approaches (direct practitioner interaction). A coding scheme analyzing participants, settings, time, computer support, and collaboration reveals that timeframe most clearly differentiates approaches, offering CSCL designers a refined conceptual framework and visualization tool for understanding authentic learning environment variations.

title: Learners’ agency and CSCL technologies: towards an emancipatory perspective
authors: future of CSCL
summary_haiku: This conceptual article argues that CSCL should adopt an emancipatory perspective prioritizing learners' agency over technology-imposed constraints. Tchounikine proposes that learners should be empowered to select, adapt, and interoperate software applications while receiving informed feedback. The analysis identifies key challenges: enabling technology choice, supporting customization, and providing transparent information—requiring fundamental reconceptualization of CSCL technologies as services rather than fixed applications.

title: It is not either or: An initial investigation into combining collaborative and individual learning using an ITS
authors: Nikol Rummel & Vincent Aleven & Jennifer K. Olsen
summary_haiku: This study compared combined collaborative-individual learning to either approach alone using an intelligent tutoring system for fractions with 382 elementary students. Results showed the combined condition produced higher learning gains than individual or collaborative-only conditions, particularly for fourth graders. Process data revealed combined-condition students made fewer errors and requested fewer hints, while reporting greater situational interest in the activity.

title: Good for learning, bad for motivation? A meta-analysis on the effects of computer-supported collaboration scripts
authors: Anika Radkowitsch & Freydis Vogel & Frank Fischer
summary_haiku: This meta-analysis of 53 studies examined computer-supported collaboration scripts' effects on learner outcomes. Results showed scripts produced non-significant positive effects on motivation, small positive effects on domain learning, and medium positive effects on collaboration skills. Contrary to widespread criticism, scripts did not undermine motivation. However, combining multiple collaborative activity prompts generally reduced effectiveness compared to single-activity scripts, suggesting simpler designs may be more beneficial for learning.

title: Learning in embodied activity framework: a sociocultural framework for embodied cognition
authors: Joshua A. Danish & Noel Enyedy & Asmalina Saleh & Megan Humburg
summary_haiku: This paper proposes the Learning in Embodied Activity Framework (LEAF), which synthesizes individual and sociocultural theories to explain how bodies support collaborative learning. Using Cultural Historical Activity Theory, the authors analyze data from the Science through Technology Enhanced Play project, where first and second-grade students used mixed-reality simulations to learn about particle behavior and states of matter. LEAF extends embodied cognition research by explicitly examining how individual and collective embodied actions, mediated by tools, rules, community, and division of labor, jointly shape learning in collaborative contexts.

title: Does collaborative learning design align with enactment? An innovative method of evaluating the alignment in the CSCL context
authors: Lanqin Zheng & Panpan Cui
summary_haiku: This study proposes design-centered research (DCR), a novel quantitative methodology for evaluating alignment between collaborative learning designs and their actual enactment. Using three indicators—activated knowledge range, knowledge-building degree, and interactive approach—plus interaction path graphs, researchers analyzed 40 groups across two iterations. Results show significant alignment improvements in round two after design optimization, with corresponding gains in group performance, demonstrating that data-driven design refinement enhances collaborative learning effectiveness.

title: Regulating self-organized collaborative learning: the importance of homogeneous problem perception, immediacy and intensity of strategy use
authors: Martin Greisel & Markus Dresel & Ingo Kollar & Nadine Melzner
summary_haiku: Self-organized study groups achieve greater satisfaction when members develop shared problem perceptions, apply strategies that directly address identified problems, and use regulation strategies frequently. This longitudinal study of 122 university students across 52 groups examined how problem perception homogeneity, strategy immediacy, and strategy intensity predict satisfaction with collaborative learning experiences during exam preparation, confirming all three hypotheses through hierarchical linear modeling.

title: Bringing maker practices to school: tracing discursive and materially mediated aspects of student teams’ collaborative making processes
authors: Pirita Seitamaa-Hakkarainen & Kai Hakkarainen & Sini Riikonen
summary_haiku: This study examined how seventh-grade student teams engaged in collaborative making projects using digital and traditional fabrication technologies. Researchers developed the Making-Process-Rug video analysis method to trace social-discursive and materially mediated aspects of five teams' co-invention processes. Four successful teams demonstrated iterative cycles integrating model making with focused discussion, while the unsuccessful team lacked substantive prototyping. Shared epistemic objects and well-organized collaboration processes proved essential for successful co-invention.

title: A review of the International Handbook of
authors: Jeremy Roschelle
summary_haiku: This review examines the International Handbook of Computer-Supported Collaborative Learning 2020, analyzing its contributions to the thirty-year-old CSCL field. Using Kuhn's paradigm shift framework, the author identifies the handbook as both a consensus document summarizing established theories, designs, and methods, and a source of productive disequilibria—unresolved tensions in diversity/equity, scalability, learning analytics integration, and methodological coherence—that present opportunities for transformative scholarship and paradigm shifts.

title: Adaptable scaffolding of mathematical argumentation skills: The role of self‑regulation when scaffolded with CSCL scripts and heuristic worked examples
authors: Freydis Vogel & Ingo Kollar & Frank Fischer & Kristina Reiss & Stefan Ufer
summary_haiku: Two experiments examined adaptable versus non-adaptable scaffolding for mathematical argumentation skills in collaborative learning. University students (N=167) learned with either adaptable or fixed CSCL scripts and heuristic worked examples. Results showed maximal scaffolding supported domain-specific skills, while adaptable scaffolds benefited students with higher self-regulation abilities. Self-regulation skills proved crucial for effectively utilizing adaptable scaffolding, particularly for socio-discursive argumentation development.

title: ‘Supporting socially shared regulation during collaborative task‑oriented reading’
authors: Jolique Kielstra & Inge Molenaar & Roel van Steensel & Ludo Verhoeven
summary_haiku: A collaboration script designed to support socially shared regulation during task-oriented reading facilitated mainly low-level metacognitive discussions among 44 prevocational students working in groups. While the script elicited metacognitive regulation through role-based information distribution, deep-level co-construction remained rare. However, students individually improved their ability to recognize high-level task characteristics and reflect on appropriate reading strategies post-intervention.

title: Supporting children’s place-based observations and explanations using collaboration scripts while learning-on- the-move outdoors
authors: Heather Toomey Zimmerman & Susan M. Land
summary_haiku: This design-based research study examined how collaboration scripts embedded in a mobile augmented reality app supported children's learning during outdoor activities. Across two iterations with 87 youth participants, researchers found significant gains in tree life cycle knowledge for both groups. Iteration B, which included additional scripts for socially-shared regulation of learning, showed improved collaborative sense-making where children better coordinated observational evidence with explanations, though knowledge gains were comparable between iterations.

title: Fostering regulation of learning processes among programming students using computational scaffolding
authors: Leonardo Silva & Antonio Mendes & Anabela Gomes & Gabriel Fortes
summary_haiku: # Summary This randomized controlled trial evaluated RESPE, a computer-supported collaborative learning platform embedding computational scaffolding for self-regulation and socially shared regulation of learning in introductory programming. With 71 students across three conditions (self-regulation support only, combined self and social regulation support, and control), results showed regulatory support significantly improved course grades. Notably, only students receiving social regulation support achieved superior collaborative activity performance, confirming the importance of social-cognitive perspectives in learning regulation.

title: Identifying collaborative problem‑solver profiles based on collaborative processing time, actions and skills on a computer‑based task
authors: Yue Ma & Huilin Zhang & Li Ni & Da Zhou
summary_haiku: This study employed latent profile analysis on PISA 2015 data from 1,677 Chinese students to identify four distinct collaborative problem-solver profiles based on time-on-task, actions-on-task, and three CPS skills: Disengaged, Struggling, Adaptive, and Excellent. Results revealed that gender, socioeconomic status, and attitudes toward collaboration significantly predicted profile membership, while achievement motivation did not. Profile membership correlated with CPS performance differences.

title: Can CPS better prepare 8th graders for problem‑solving in electromagnetism and bridging the gap between high‑ and low‑achievers than IPS?
authors: Jiun-Wei Guo & Hsiao-Ching She & Meng-Jun Chen & Pei-Yi Tsai
summary_haiku: This study compared collaborative problem-solving (CPS) and individual problem-solving (IPS) approaches in an online electromagnetism unit with 109 eighth graders. Using simulation-based instruction across five classes, researchers found CPS significantly enhanced problem-solving performance compared to IPS, while both equally improved conceptual understanding. Critically, CPS more effectively boosted low-achievers' performance and narrowed achievement gaps, as low-achievers received greater peer support during collaboration.

title: Learning within fiber‑crafted algorithms: Posthumanist perspectives for capturing human‑material collaboration
authors: Anna Keune
summary_haiku: This study employs posthumanist analysis to examine how middle school students and fiber craft materials collaboratively produce algorithms during weaving and fabric manipulation activities. Using video data, the researcher identifies how youth-material intra-actions create computational performances through repeated, patterned movements. Findings reveal that both humans and materials actively contribute to algorithmic production, with variations in these patterns enabling algorithmic expansion over time. The study proposes human-material collaboration as a productive analytical unit for understanding computational learning in CSCL contexts.

title: Collaborative Problem‑Solving in Knowledge‑Rich Domains: A Multi‑Study Structural Equation Model
authors: Laura Brandl & Matthias Stadler & Constanze Richters & Anika Radkowitsch & Martin R. Fischer & Ralf Schmidmaier & Frank Fischer
summary_haiku: This study tested the Collaborative Diagnostic Reasoning (CDR) model using structural equation modeling across three medical education studies (N=504). Analyzing simulation-based diagnostic tasks, researchers found that content and collaboration knowledge influenced collaborative diagnostic activities (evidence elicitation and sharing), which subsequently affected diagnostic accuracy, justification, and efficiency. Notably, collaboration knowledge emerged as more critical than social skills, and diagnostic activities independently predicted outcomes beyond individual characteristics, highlighting the multidimensional nature of collaborative problem-solving in knowledge-rich domains.

title: Knowledge creation through maker practices and the role of teacher and peer support in collaborative invention projects
authors: Sini Davies & Pirita Seitamaa-Hakkarainen & Kai Hakkarainen
summary_haiku: Student teams engaged in open-ended collaborative invention projects applied maker practices—design, computer engineering, product design, and science—in iterative, nonlinear processes. Video analysis of three seventh-grade teams revealed that embodied practices like sketching and material experimentation were essential for advancing shared epistemic objects. Teacher scaffolding and peer tutoring effectively supported knowledge creation, though excessive direction could oversimplify designs and reduce engagement.

title: Comparing the effectiveness of CSCL scripts for shared task perceptions in socially shared regulation of collaborative learning
authors: Mariel Miller & Allyson F. Hadwin
summary_haiku: High-support group planning scripts significantly improved undergraduate students' accuracy of shared task perceptions and transactive planning discussions compared to low-support scripts, though individual-level support showed no detectable effect. However, enhanced task perceptions did not translate to improved group performance, suggesting groups may struggle to implement shared understanding during task execution.

title: Comparing the effects of a collaboration script and collaborative reflection on promoting knowledge about good collaboration and effective interaction
authors: Sebastian Strauss & Isis Tunnigkeit & Julia Eberle & Arlind Avdullahu & Nikol Rummel
doi: Comparing the effects of a collaboration script and collaborative reflection on promoting knowledge about good collaboration and effective interaction
summary_haiku: This experimental study compared external collaboration scripts and reflection scaffolds for fostering collaboration skills in 150 university students working in groups. Using multilevel modeling, researchers found that learners receiving collaborative reflection gained significantly more knowledge about effective collaboration than those using scripts or no support. However, neither intervention improved subsequent interaction quality. Results suggest reflection-based approaches may offer autonomy-supportive alternatives to directive scripting for knowledge acquisition.

title: Correction: Collaborative Problem‑Solving in Knowledge‑Rich Domains: A Multi‑Study Structural Equation Model
authors: Laura Brandl & Matthias Stadler & Constanze Richters & Anika Radkowitsch & Martin R. Fischer & Ralf Schmidmaier & Frank Fischer
summary_haiku: This is a correction notice for a structural equation modeling study examining collaborative problem-solving in knowledge-rich domains. The original article contained a sign error in Table 5, where most coefficients were incorrectly prefixed with negative signs. The corrected version has been published online.

title: Correction to: Many are the ways to learn: Identifying multi‑modal behavioral profiles of collaborative learning in constructivist activities
authors: Jauwairia Nasir & Aditi Kothiyal & Barbara Bruno & Pierre Dillenbourg
summary_haiku: This correction document addresses formatting and citation errors in the original 2021 article examining multi-modal behavioral profiles in collaborative constructivist learning. The researchers identified and corrected a missing colon in the title and multiple misattributed or incorrectly formatted citations throughout the paper, ensuring accurate reference to their prior work on collaborative learning analytics.

title: Measuring the quality of collaborative group engagement: Development and validation of the QCGE self‑assessment scale (QCGE‑SAS)
authors: Loris T. Jeitziner & Lisa Paneth & Oliver Rack & Susanne Bleisch & Carmen Zahn
summary_haiku: This study developed and validated the QCGE-SAS, a 13-item self-assessment scale measuring quality of collaborative group engagement across four dimensions: behavioral, social, cognitive, and conceptual-to-consequential engagement. Using confirmatory factor analysis with 246 higher education students, the scale demonstrated good model fit and construct validity through correlations with related measures. Three subscales showed acceptable reliability; however, the social engagement subscale exhibited suboptimal internal consistency, warranting future refinement.

title: Activity‑based collaborative virtual reality: Conceptualising immersive virtual reality for collaborative learning
authors: Lucas Paulsen & Jacob Davidsen
summary_haiku: Paulsen and Davidsen propose Activity-Based Collaborative Virtual Reality (ABC-VR), a conceptual framework grounded in activity theory for designing and researching collaborative learning in immersive 360-degree video environments. Unlike existing individual-focused concepts, ABC-VR emphasizes social knowledge construction through analyzing recorded real-world activities at multiple levels—examining what actions occur, how they're performed, and why. The framework positions learners collaboratively engaging with situated practices from educational, social, and work contexts.
